This Company has been formed to purchase the Mining and Muting Rights over certain districts in the State of Pahang, on the eastern side of the Malay Peninsula; to develop and work such poitiou or portions of the property as may he found desirable; and further, to sell or lease portions of the property to cothpanles or individuals. . . . .

The concession extends over an area estimated at about 2,000 square miles, and contains numerous and most extensive lodes of Tin, Copper, Silver-Lead, and, it Is believed, of Silver and Gold, as also a vast tract of 'very rich Agricultural Land, well adapted for growing Tapioca, Coffee, and other Tropical Products, and in parts densely wooded with the best descrip- tions of Forest Timber, available for mining and building pur- poses, and an unlimited extent lof jungle affording valuable At present it is proposed to confine the Company's opera- tions almost exclusively to working the tin lodes and the stream tin which is found .in tise valleys and fiat lands. For the former purpose a battery of 10 stamps, with a water-wheel andappliances for dressing the ore, has already been ordered In EarglaroVand Is now hi course of shipment; so that immediate retunts may be expected. Considerable and regular Consign- ments.of tin, raised and smelted on this concession by the present proprietors, have been sold in the Singapore market for the past two years, so that the Company will take over as a going concern a business which is already in profitable work- ing, and whit* is employing upwards of 300 labourer at the Mines of Kuatte, of whose trained Pavia, Use Cimpany

GOD BLESS OUR GIRLS. (Tune—" God save the Queen.")' God bless our English girls, Let them be pure as pearls. God bless our girls. May they acknowledge Thee, And learn that great Decree, "None other gods but Me." God bless our girls. Let them be in Thy sight, "Corner stones polished". bright, -- Spotless and white. Virtuous women too; Modest and good and true, . Loving kind acts to do. God bless our girls.

Kindness upon each tongue, To every girl belong This law and song. May they prove "friends indeed,* Reaching their hands to feed When there is want and need., God bless our girls. In "strength and honour" drest, Thy Spirit for its guest In each warm breast. Daughters of England's brave, Let not one prove a slave To fashion's restless wave. God bless our girls.

And on each fair young face, Oh! do Thou plainly trace Thy love and grace. Help them to imitate Her who now rules in state— Woman, both good and great. God bless our Queen! Him who lived "here below," , Pattern for high and low, May they all know. And, when Thy voice shall call, May Queen and subjects all Eder the Festal Hall. "God bless us all!"
—Newcastle Chronicle.

I 'Domestic life has no finer picture ot confiding love than that the husband wearing a smoking-jacketiof his wife's making and trying to make believe that it fits

bins divinely. Science is trying to find out how quick a man can wink. The instantaneous photographer should try to catch the eye of a Connecticut deacon in front of a temperance soda fountain. A gentleman who claims to know, and who, by the way, is a scholar and a Christian, says the only differ- ence between Kansas and Paradise is that Kansas ea receiving much the heavier immigration and has the best roads. Just think of it! Cider, doughnuts. rambo Apples, euchre or seven-up, and a rip-roaring fire, and sitting alongside your best bright-eyed girl! The good old winter nights are comine, boys, when a slice of below zero is worth a cycle of July.--.4merica4 Paper. A Dakota paper thug stabs its hated rival: "A man living about twelve miles from here died from poisoning en Monday afternoon. It seems he ate a lunch that had been wrapped up in a copy of our loathed and disgusting contemporary, and it killed him. Others should take warning." A Hum TRTRITTIL—A Texas gentleman travelling in a Pullman palace car in Pennsylvania happened to r;say that he was from the Lone Star State. "Do you live in the western portion of the state?" asked a man opposite. "I do." "In Tom Green county?" "That's my county." "Live near Carson?" That's my town." "Perhaps you.know my brother. William Henry Jones ?" "Know him? Gimme your hand, stranger. I helped hang William Henry the night before I left. He was a horse thief, but a good one." Hein LIFT IN DAKOTA.—AMOTIZ the presents received by the young people were the following :—FrOm groom to bride. one bull pup, one yeller dog, pair of water spaniels, and a pure meerchaum pipe with tobacco. From bride to groom, one good shotgun, one bowie-knife, rifle, and three dogs. From parents of bridegroom, one fiddle, one banjo, spotted pup, and six pounds of tobacco. From the Shotgun Club, of which the young couple were members, one English mastiff, and a pair of silver-mounted pistols. It is seldom that a young couple start out in life so well equipped for perfect happiness, and Jock and Jule have the best wishes of this office.— Dakota ,Sunfirnmer. "NOT A PALACR, ntrr se Istsr."—ln Sir John Chardin's account of his travels in Persia in the seventeenth century will be found a quaintkatory about the curious mistake made by a dervish or monk. When this monk reached the town ot Balkh he went into the king's palace, thinking that it was an inn. After a time he entered a gallery, and spreading out his carpet, laid him-I self down to sleep. The guards soon7found out this strange guest, and asked him what business he had in that place, to which the monk replied that he was in an inn, and had taken up his lodging there for the night. Of course the guards got very angry, anertold him he was in the king's palace. At this moment the king came into the gillery and heard the talk. Though he was amused at the mistake, he inquired of the dervish how he came to make it. "Sir." answered the monk, "who lodged in this palace when it was first built?" Said the king. "My ancestors."" And who last lived here ?" The king replied, "My father." "And who lodges here now Why. Ido myself," was the royal reply. "And who will occupy it after you ?" "The young prince, my son," said the king. "Ali, sir," rejoined the dervish, "a house which changes its inhabitants so often, and has such an endless succession of guests, is not a palace, but an inn."—Little Folks 31aciazzne. SIR HENRI' LAWRIGNCE AT LUCICNOW.—When the pre- parations for a poasible mutiny began at Lucknow Sir Henry Lawrence cleared away many of the small houses near the Residency, but leaving some of them standing so as to build walls from one to the other, thus making a rampart or wall all round the Residency. Inside this enclosure be conveyed a large number of cannon. ' powder, and quantities of food, and all the English women and children were put in there for safety. It WILA not till the end of June that the first real struggle took place. Hearing that a large rebel army was ap- proaching the city, Sir Henry Lawrence determined to go out and meet them. On June 30th, therefore, he marched out of the Residency with all the men he could spare from the work of building the walls—about seven hundred in all, including some hundreds of faithful natives—and met the enemy near the village of Chinhut. The rebels mustered about six thousand, and on seeing them the natives on the English side began to run away. The English soldiers, as usual, fought with the greatest bravery, but unfortunately they were worn out with bard work, and could not beat back the thousands of rebels, who rushed forward like a torrent. They fell back in retreat; this soon became a rout, and those who were not shot or cut down got back to the Residency as best they could. The enemy rapidly followed, and on the night of June 30th the siege of the Residency, which was to last many months, commenced. A sad calamity now fell upon the little party of English men and women who were preparing to defend themselves against a merciless foe. During the night a shell burst into Sir H Lawrence's bedroom, and inflicted wounds from which -that brave and good man died, after lingering till the morning of July 4th, amid the constant thud of cannon- balls against the walls of the building, and the ceaseless rattle of guns night and day.—Prom " Littie Folks" Magarine for December. Brostases WlFE.—Wherever the English language is -spoken, there we find Bunyan's immortal story of the Pilgrim and his Progress. Troubled souls and trustful souls have found their own experience mirrored there. It has given us descriptive phrases which can never perish. We need not go out of our way for words while Vanity Fair and the Slough of Despond, Doubting Castle. and the Herb Heart's-Ease are ready-made for us. If the roofs of British homes could be raised for us on any Bunday afternoon, how many"of the aged and the suffer- ing should We find listening to the strangely melodious description of the Land of Beulah, how many brave boys pondering over the dread battle with Apollvon, how many little maidens gazing on the charms of the House 'Beautiful? Does it never occur to us that the wonder- ful allegory would scarcely have been written but for the unselfish life and holy influence of the poor working woman who married Bunyan in the days when he was, not the unexampled sinner which the unsparing words of his earnest repentance might lead some to imagine, but what was perhaps almost less likely to change into the Christian saint and devoted preacher— to wit, a roystering and careless youth, knowing no pleasures but those of skittles and quoits and beer? Did it seem as if it could possibly signify to the whole Christian world, whether the penniless wife of that humble Bedfordshire villager was a sincere, godly woman, intent on keeping her little household in ways Of purity and piety. or a mere good-humoured slattern, who, if her husband brought her home a fair share of his wage, would be quite content to humour his "little ways" and indulge his "harmless pleasures?" Nobody could have been astonished more than poor Mrs. Bunyan herself, could she have foreseen the final result of the innocent wiles which she exerted to keep John interested in the Bible, or the "Plain Man's Pathway to Heaven," while the shouts of his playfellows on the village green penetrated to their little kitchen, which we may be sure was neat, and clean, and cosy, for all its bareness. Probably, if she could have known that John was a genius, she would have been frightened to marry him, and still more frightened to attempt to influence or con- trol him. But God showed her all that it was necessary for her to know—that it was her plain duty to try to get her husband to do what she felt was pleasing in God's sight; and she found strength to do this. She laid her hand on the rudder of the Ship of life, keeping it in its course, and the winds of God came down and filled its sails, and bore it triumphantly where she did not dream. —The Qvirer for December. . WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. There were present the Mayor (Alderman T. H. Sutton). Alder- men Crosfield. Chandley, Holmes, Burgess, Webster; Councillors J. Pierpoint, Platt, Wright, Tinsley, Heaton, Blackhurst, Jolley, Greening, Percival, Barker, Dixon, F. A. Roberts, Hutchinson, Fleming, Belton, J. Shaw-Green, Ashton, H. Roberts, Grin- all ; Messrs. W. IL Brook (town y ' clerk). J. L. hit- tle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treas- urer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), and J. Pater- son (gas manager). TUB LATH CAPTAIN REYNOLDS. Before the business proper of the Council was pro- ceeded with, the MAYOR referred to the unfortunate death of the late Capt. Reynolds, who, he said, although not at the time of his death a member of the Council, once represented one of the wards in the borough. fig, was sure that they would all join with him in the follow- ing resolution, which he proposed :—" That this Council receives with deep regret the announcement of the death of Sylvanus Reynolds, Esq., „formerly a member of this Council, and desires to express its sincere sympathy and condolence with Mrs i Reynolds and her family an.,their sad bereavement." Alderman Butiogss seconded the resolution, which was carried.

WATCH COYMITTHE. This committee reported that at their Meeting Alder- man Harrisort was appointed deputy-chpirman of the committee foi the ensuing 'year, and Camel Hors Fran- comb and Tolley the Visiting Committee of the Bridewell. It was resolved that the bye-laws as amended by the Secretary of State be approved and submitted to the Council for adoption. The MAYOR proposed, and Councillor PlArr second,d, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BOLTON asked when the Council were going to finish passing bye-laws? They seemed to have 700 or 800, and a person had remarked to him that if they were all painted on a board it would require one a hundred yards long. Were they the same bye-laws that had been passed two years ago? The TOWN CLERK said that the bye-laws did not ex- actly comply with the form sent down by the. Secretary of State two years ago, and they:had been before the Home Office of and on ever since. There had been no fresh bye-laws passed during the last two yeas. The minutes were then adopted,

_ FINANCE COMMITTEE. The committee have appointed Alderman Holmes chairman, and Councillor Greening deputy-chairman, and a resolution was adopted requesting Councillor Brown to audit the collector's accounts.' On the motion of Alderman llotims, seconded by Councillor GREENING, the minutes of the committee were adopted. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee, Councillor Platt was ' appointed chairman, and Councillor Greening deputy- chairman. It was resolved that the following members of the committee be appointed the Lighting Sub-Corn- mittee—Councilloni Greening (convener), Platt, H. Roberts, Dixon, and Wright; that the following members be appointed a Visiting Committee to visit the sites of proposed buildings or alterations to buildings when re- quired—Councillors Platt, Greening, Wright, Marsh, and H. Roberts ;'and that the sum of £l2 lOs be paid to Mr. John Hughes for a strip of land at the corner of Thelwall and ICnutsford-roads. The following report of the Light- ing Sub-Committee was read:—" After visiting, the Sub- Committee recommended the following alterations to be made to old Umps, and new ones fixed as follows, viz.— Orford-lane: New pillar lamp on south side opposite road leading to Barracks; new Pillar lamp opposite Orford- avenue; remove pillar 'lamp opposite Conies Corner: alter position of lamp between Battersby-lane and new lamp proposed to be fixed opposite road leading to Barracks. Green's-court, Fennel-street: One bracket lamp." The minutes were approved on the motion of Council- lor PLATT, seconded by Councillor WRIGHT. THE LONGFORD DEPOT.—A LIVELY SCENE. It was reported that at a meeting of the Sanitary Com- mittee Alderman Burgess was appointed chairman and the Mayor the deputy-chairman, and Copncillori Dakin (convener), Francomb, and Wright wet% appointed a sub-committee to superintend the horses, vans, stables, and provender, and all matters pertaining therto, and to report to the committee. It was resolved that the. chairman, deputy-chairman, and Councillors Fmncomb and Taylor be appointed a sub-committee to visit the infectious diseases hospital; that the chairman, deputy chairman, and Councillors Greening-and Roberts be ap- I pointed a sub-comnittee to visit the Longford and. inter- cepting depots, and a minute stated that the committee met on land behind Messrs. Roberts, Dale, arid Co.'s works in Wharf .street, which the Paving and Sewerage Committee proposed to purchase, and afterwards dis- cussed the matter with the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee, and agreed to recommend the General purposes Committee to buy the land. Alderman BURGESS moved, and Councillor CRGSFIELD seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the commit- tee. Councillor BARKER asked how it was that the informa- tion previously requested by him was not given to the Council at the last meeting in November. He had a mo- tion on the paper for information with respect to Long- ford and the intercepting depots; the information was promised for the first meeting in November, and nothing had been heard of it since. Councillor PERCIVAL asked if any one could visit the depots without a written order, or upon what conditions they could do so. Councillor BOLTON said that he also should like an answer to Councillor Barker's question. The members of the Council, he thought, were entitled to more con- eideration from the Sanitary Committee than they got. A member of the Council had published a letter in the newspapers, saying that the scheme was a valuable one, and that great profits were made at the Longford depot. He contended that they should be put in the same posit- tion as the member to whom he had alluded, and as the Sanitary Committee_ There was no doubt that the rate- payers of the borough and certain members of the Coun- cil were dissatisfied with the manner in which things concerning Longford depot were brought under the notice of the Council. He proposed that certain sums entered for wages at Longford on the minutes be not paid until a satisfactory answer was received. The in- formation had been promised, but they had not received it, and had been treated with contempt. It was not even explained why the information was not furnished, and he thought that such treatment was neither gentle- manly nor fair. The members of the committee should be open and above-board, and let them have the infor- mation without any trouble. Mr. J. Snsw-Girsini asked for information with regard to the purchase of land in Wharf-street; nothing was said as to what it was intended it should be used for? , Councillor ROBERTS asked how it was that Coun- cillor Barker was not in his place at the meeting to ask the questionof which he had given notice. Councillor BARKER said that he was not required to be in his p ace; it was not a question but a motion, granted by the Council and promised by the committee. Councillor BURGESS; Certainly not: I said I had noth- ing to do with it. I did not consent. Councillor BARKER reiterated that Alderman Burgess did consent. Alderman BURGERS I said I offered no objection. Councillor Pnarr considered that before the matter was discussed further they ought to have an explanation from the Chairman of the Committee. He (Mr. Platt) asked Alderman Piclmiere at the meeting m question whether it would.not be advisable that the Committee should give information in the form of a report to be circulated to every member of the Council, and he understood that the suggestion was agreed to. He be- lieved that Alderman Burgess was present, and the then Mayor said he had no doubt the , suggestion would be agreed to. It had not been complied with, however, although it was information to which they were fully entitled. It was no use the members saying the Long- ford scheme was going on in a first-class manner if they gave no facts to go upon. Councillor BARKER said there seemed to be an opinion amongst some people that he was asking for this infor- mation out of animosity to the Committee, and Alder- man %mows interjected the remark that it was so. PAYING AND SBWBRAGII COMMITTHB. This Committee recommended that Alderman Davies be appointed chairman, and Councillor Wright, deputy chairman for the ensuing year. The minutes also stated that a letter had been received from Messrs. Bartlett and Atkinson, offering to sell five acres of land at Wharf Meadow at one penny and one-eighth of a penny per yard, capitalised at 20 years' purchase, subject to a con- tract. It was recommended that this offer be accepted. It was resolved that permission be given to the Man- chester Ship Canal Company to construct a crossing over Wash-lane for the purpose of their works, subject to a contract to be prepared by the Town Clerk. Councillor WRIGHT moved the adoption of the minutes. Referring to the land it was proposed to purchase at Wharf Meadow, he said that the capitalised price would be £2,268 to buy it out and out. He mentioned that the land could be used among other purposes as a stone yard. Councilor DIXON seconded the adoption of the min- utes. After some disci4ssion, in the course of which most of the speakers expressed approval of the proposed pur- chase, the minutes were adopted.

Councillor BOLTON seconded this motion, whick, after some discussion, was unanimously agreed to. CITTBSTIONEI. The following notice of question had been given by Councillor Dixon, and was down on the agenda papers, viz. :—To the Town Clerk of Warrington. Sir,—At the next meeting. of the Town Council I propose to ask the Mayor permission to visit the works at Longford, and take with me a gentleman, who is engineer to a large chemical works, and from there to go and inspect the sulphate of ammonia plant at the gasworks; also to ask the chairman of the Gas Committee the per centage of sulphur there is in the oxide of iron taken from the puri- fier, and the weight made per year. Councillor Dixon having formally put the question, The MAYOR, in reply, said that as the Council gave frAlderman Burgess the privilege of allowing any one to inspect the Longford works, he did not see that he could interfere. The only proper course was to give notice of a motion to rescind the resolution in question. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Holmes was understood to say that the Gas Committee did not feel disposed to give permission to the engineer in question to inspect the plant at the gas- works. The meeting than ended.

_ The minutes of the Museum, Library, and Arts Com- mittee contained as follows :—That the following gentle- men be aprinted the officers for the ensuing year: Pre- sident, William Beamont, Esq ; vice-president, Mr. Alderman Webster. That the sub-committee appointed to report on the Was from the Friary, Messrs. Owen and Worsley, recommend that a sufficient portion of the tiles to represent the design of the pavement be framed and hung on the wall of the antiquities room; that specimens of each kind be exhibited in the cases; and that the remainder not required for the Museumbe given to the vicar and wardens of Holy Trinity, on condition that they lay them down in a suitable place in Trinity Church. RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. 4 , MI GRONFAYMER S SWOARD. Thad swoard hung up theer wur mi grondad's— His name's long bin deawn Deoth's book,— Un his hand used thad blade when th' frog-eyters wor scattered bi th' owd "Iron Duke." , When t' French swarmed up, army bi army, Un fun th' English plenty to do, Id wur then as mi gronfayther gript id, Till Peace coom wi:grim Wattero. Ay! It's ftasht eawt i' Wellington's battles. Wlaeer th' British wur second to noan, For mi grondad worn d one o' or milk-sops, Bud a Harrud lad, stubborn to t' booan. Wi thad pluck as is t' prop ov owd England, . He win; prtawd o' hur nights to defend ; Bud, tho' ruff as a lion ut feightin, He wur gentle un kind as a friend. When aw wur a lad, aw oft wondered Why War, un id horrors should be; Un aw've shivered ut th' tales as he toad me— We WM' mates, mi owd grondad un me! Un aw'Te thowt sin, as kings, wither splendour • Un pride, cud this lesson be towt. As kindness cuts deeper than bullets, Un goodwill costs nobody nowt. Hey, mony a time we've set campin, Un aw'ie axed him to tell me o'er t' swoard, Then he's oeawr d still awhile, thowtful, smookin, When mi tawk's touched some quiverin chord In his heart, un he's towd me, while teardrops , Hung big in his eeu, he,aw his mates Wur cut deawn just like cattle i' th' slaughter, • Un he'd tell me booath t' places un dates. Ther's a dingo in id edge; aw remember A tale as he towd me o'er thad. They wur feightin like mad neon t" Mounseers,” Un his regiment dropt in for't bad. Deed un weawnded wur foin bi dozens, Bud they budged fro' ther greawnd nod an inch. For he sod as a gradely trained sowjer, l' danger, wur near known to flinch. Un theer, they gave volley for volley, • Un med th' French battalions reel. Then up dashed a lot o' French hossmen, Un they MOE em wi bullet un steel. Mi gronfayther slipt, o ut sudden, As a Frenchmon coom gallopin deawn, Bud mi granfayther's mate picked his swoard up, Un met th' blade as wur flasht wi a freawn. Thad wur th' last deed e'er done bi thad Frenchmon, For a shell scattered rider un hoes, Un th' hero as stopt him wur butchered— Heaw mi gronfayther grieved o'er his loss 1 He sobbed as he towd me heaw noble His mate wor, wi eon red un dim, Un aw raylee believe as th' owd fella Kept th' swoard, just i' memory ov him. Mi gronfayther never wur weawnded, Un his pension he drew mony a year; They'd sum thowt in his days for owd sowjers, No Governments skinny un near. • But at last Captain Deoth co'd o'er th' muster, Un mi owd grondad went at his co; Th' owd chap's laid i' Harrud's quate churchyard, Thads his swoard in id scabbard on t' WO. CHAPTtR XHI. , , TliE FUNERAL. The preliminary inquiry by the inagi3ti ates at Tavistock was over.

"The prisoner," so the next nitmber of the ravistock Gazette concluded its report of the proceedings, "who preserved throughout an n nmoved dem eanour, reserved his defence. and was committed for trial at the next Exeter assizes." Martin was allowed a few minutes' interview' With his sister. " Harrison thinks I ant guilty, I: pla vaife of it," he said, and for the.firSt time since Ins arrest, Anne thought he looked a little discouraged: "Never mind him,", Anne 'tried to, say. bravely. "We shall get the cleverest barrister on the circuit to defend you, and then we shall; hear what he says by-and-by." I don't think .we could do better than have Grimsby, the one who defended Me before; he is a rising man, they say." Then Martin smiled rather bitterly. "But I doubt if he'll get me off suite so easily this time.;, my character is all against me now, you see." . Anne returned alone to Row-tor Farm. Last time that terrible last time of which Martin sometimes spoke—he was with her, and she had devoted herself to the work of trying to cheer and console him, trying to keep up Ins courage to bear the accusation of a crime of which he was guilt.' less in intention, though be felt himself to be guilty of it in act •Etit .tioNf‘ he was far away, a close prisoner ,in the ,gaol at. Exeter, where she could see him only occasionally or a brief visit of one
quarter (if an hour. . ' , She sdlid to herself, as she went back to her de- solate home, "Now 1 have just one thing to live for, and that is to find out the man lyho murdered
Susan. I was the cause, the innocent cause, of all Martin has suffered these lmt two years; it was ih defending me he accidentally killed Dick Lawson • now please God, I will be the one to set

him free." Sonietimes, in looking back upon certain epochs oi our lives, we wonder how we could have borne such repeated and crushing blows without dying under theni. Hut human nature has &wonderful power of enduring pain. It is afterwards that we realise what we have stiffered, and sometimes the calmest and bravest bear the reminder of that suffering in the form of scarred flesh and shattered nerves fer the rest et their lives. - Ir 6". The day following Susan was buried. All the village seemed to follow her funeral, and St. Stephen's churchyard was crowded with people.. Many of them ' were surprised, and almost scan- dalised, by Anne's being present. "One would have thought," they said afterwards, "that sh& would have been 'ashamed to chew her face-with her sister murdered, and her brother took up for it." The.old traditional instinct which is typified by the. "Tower of Siloam," made the villagers feel that . oae upon whom such strange and terrible woes had ' fallen must be accursed of God. Anne had forced herself to write a note to Captain Stambridge telling him of the arrangements for the funeral, and asking him to be present. He did not reply tq her letter, but he joined the dark proces- sion as j eatered the churchyard, and stood near the grave;- with his face hidden in his hand- kerchief, while the serice we! being read. ' After it was over Anne lingered a tnthtif Jid looked in his direction. Her heart had softened towards him, her former easpieions seemed to her like a delirious fancy;" the longed to exchange a few words with the man who had loved Susan--for surely he would have some kindly feelings, some little sympathy for his betrothed's sister But Stambridge carefully avoided looking at her, and Anne turned away, keenly realising that she was shunned because she was Martin's sister. The crowd parted—almost shrank—away from her as she walked down the churchyard alone in her supreme desolation, yet, with firm step, ...and bead held erect. Stronger than grief was her desire to show an unmoved front to the world—to hold up her heal proudly—knowing that whatever cruel blows had fallen upon Martin and herself they had no cause for shame. It bad been a mild, even bright afternoon, the sun Alining with the veiled lustre of December. But as the day declined, threatening clouds gathered round the horizon, and the wind blew chill, when In the early grey twilight Anne was being driven home by Richards after the funeral. She had closed her eyes • she was growing stupitied by all that she tad gone throcifei during the last few days, when she was aroused by the trap coming , to a sudden standstill about half a mile from Row. tor Farm. She saw standing in the road , beside her, a care-worn middle-aged woman, dressed in rusty black. It was the widowed mother, of the dead Dick Lawson. " Miss Derrick,* began the woman, with a timid, hesitating air, "I've made bold to stop aud speak to you. I hope you won't think me intruding upon you, particular just now, but I want to know if there's any little thing as I can do for you. I heard as how your Eliza was took quite bad with the fright and all, and wasn't fit for her work; and I thought, perhaps as how you'd let me lend a hand lit the dairy, or with the poultry, or I'd scrub the floors and dean up for you Satur. day—there isn't anything as I wouldn't be pleased to do for you Miss Derrick, if so be you'll let me do it as a friend. I've never liked to stop and speak to you before. I know the sight of me can't be a very cheering one to you; but now you're in such trouble I plucked up courage to come and meet you on your way home to-day." Anne felt as if she were choking. "How kind you are—how kind you are—" was all she could say. "I'm that sorry for you Miss Derrick, and for your poor brother too; and new the ice is broke, as one may say--1 want to 'tell you, I've been as sorry as sorry can ' be; for you both all these two years, butt I've never liked to say a word to Mr. Derrick. I know he can't abide the sight of me, and 'taint nateral that he should. But I've knowed all the time," and Mrs. Lawson, having got over her first shyness, beeaine quite impassioned in her earnestness, "I've knowed all the time that he was fretting his heart out about my poor lad. And what did he do, only last Thursday night as ever was—as Richards here can tell you—but make me a present of the beautifullest oow as ever you see! I knowed it was him, though I daresay he thought I shouldn't. He's as kind a man RS ever lived; and don't you be downhearted now, Miss Derxick'; he'll come out of this fresh trouble as white as snow." It was too much—when Anne was feeling that thd whole world was against Martin—to hear these words from the mother whom he had bereaved of her son, and she burst into a storm of tears. "Come and see me whenever you can," she said, preeently,clasping Mrs. Lawson's band with both her own. "The very sight of you will comfort me more than anything else." The next market day Anne sent her butter, eggs, and poultry to Tavistock by Mrs. Richards. She could not -bring herself just yet to face the people who flocked to the little town on Fridays. Every- body was talking of the murder at Row-tor Farm, and the arrest of Martin Derrick. "He has been in trouble before, I understand," some one would remark. "Yes," the reply would be, "and got off by the skin of his teeth, as one may say. But he won't be let off so easily the second time; no, no, the jury will do their duty lIQW they see the sort of man he is." "Hanging's too good for him," another would say. "His own sister, and such a fine young woman as he was too, to be murdered in cold blood like that I They say Captain Stambridge that was just going to marry her will never hold up his head again." The murder, if unexplained, would have spread fear ana trembling throughout many a lonely hotne- stead on the moors; but it was a relief to everybody to know that no mysterious enemy, no ferocious convict, escaped from Dartmoor prison, no ,blood- thirsty tramp was lurking round their barns and hay-ncks. The crime was capable of an easy—and considering all that had „"one before—a very natural explanation. It was a family affair of the Derricks, and nobody else had any cause for alarm. (To be continued.)

div.head: DEATH OF LORD LYONS.
div.p: DEATH OF LORD LYONS.

_ Lyons died at half-past eight on Monday morn- ing. He had been lying seriously ill at Norfolk House, St. James's, the town residence of the Duke of Norfolk, since Tuesday last. His lordship passed away quietly. , The Duke of Norfolk and other members of the deceased's family were present, including Lady Mary Howard, Lady Philippa Howard, and Lady Margaret Howard.. Mr. Sheffield,. his r private secretary, was also pre- sent, together with Dr. Stewart, who had been in attendance at Norfolk House during his lordship's ill- ness. Intelligence of the death was telegraphed to the Queen and the Prince of Wales. Many persons who had intended calling to enquire after his lordship refrained Din doing Ito on seeing the blinds drawn. The Right Hon. Richard Bickerton Pemeli Lyons 4 G.C.8., G.C.M.G., Only surviving son of the first Lyons (who commanded the, British fleet in the Black Sea in 1855-6), was born at Lymington, April 26th, 1817, and succeeded to his father's title November 23rd, 1858. Having been educated at Wineliecfer and Christ Church, Oxford, he was. appointed unpaid .Attaché at Athens in 1839, and paid Attache in 1844, at Dre-;den in 1852;iat Florence (residing at Rome) in 1853. Secretary of tea- tion there (residing at Rome) in 1856, and Envoy to Tuscany in 1858. He was accredited as Envoy Extra- ordinary to the United States in December, 1858. re- turned to England on account of ill-health in February. 1865; was appointed Ambassador at Constantinople ITI August, 1865. and was transferred to Paris in Ju1y,1867. That post he has held uninterruptedly till the present time. He was made a K.C.B. in 1860,a G.C.B. in 1882; was sworn of the Privy Council, March 9th, 1865; and made an honorary D.C.L. at Oxford. June 21st, 1865. In November, 1881, he was created Viscount Lyons, of Christ Church, in the county of Southampton.

div.head: WYCJIFFE CHOIR CONCERT.
div.p: WYCJIFFE CHOIR CONCERT.

The members of Wycliffe (Warrington) Church choir, assisted by the Tonic Sol-fa Association and an orchestra, gave a concert on Tuesday evening, before a large audience, in Wycliffe Hall. The pro- gramme. consisted of miscellaneous vocal and in- strumental MuSic, andlhe sacred cantata by Alfred R. Gaul, The Holy City." The solo vocal- ists were Mrs.. R. H. Pearson, Miss Monks, Mr. Harold Lee, and Mr. W. H. Wallington, Mrs. Lane, who was to have taken part in the concert, being pre- vented by indisposition from being present. Mr. R. H. Pearson ably fulfilled the responsible duties ef conduc- tor, and in additiou should be credited for his valuable services in trairibag the orchestra. Mr. John Roberts wasi leader• of pie. band, Miss Toft harpist, Mr. Z. Armitage choirMaiterond Mr. J.W. Caldwellaccorrepanist. Each of the solo vocalists contributed songs in the first and miscellaneous portion of the programme, and won the plaudits of the audience. Mrs Pearsen sang " Gou- nod's serenade" with taste and expression, and was skilfully supported by Mr.' Pearson in the delightful obli- gato, on the due interpretation of which so much of the success'of this pleasing morcian depends. ' Mr. W. H. Wallington gave, a vigorous and jaunty rendering of "The pirate, -" and Was lotialy applauded, and Mr. Harold .Lee sang " and amy fathers' with feeling and some- thing of pathos, besides an additional song mtlieabsence of Mrs Lane, Miss Monks, in "Ora pro nobis " was lieard to advantage, and for an effective interpretation of this' somewhat difficult song received loud applause. I A Ballata for three violins and piano, by Papini, plaged by Messrs. Pearson, Roberts, Atkin, and Caldwell served to give agreeable variety to this part of the entertainment. Of the two orchestral items in the first part of the pro- L gramme, the first, a gavotte, was undoubtedly the best, and here as to the band generally we must at once say that, taking into account ,its purely amateur charatter, its performances were fairly satisfactory, and evidenced painstaking training during the short time the cantata had been in rehearsal. There was a noticeable weakness in the wood wind especially; and in the difficult keys ih Which some of the numbers are pitched the ensemble. was not always perfectly in tune as to the violins. A good beginning was made in the instrumental introduc- tion to the cantata, and what in Wagnerian phrase- ology may be called " The Holy City motif," occuring several times in the course of the work. was heard to advantage and agreeably impressed On the memory.. Several unaceompamed pieces of vodal har- mony stood'out in bold relief and gave nice 'light and shade in gradations of tone volume. Notably may be mentioned the quartette "No parting yonder," the subsequent chorus "None wanting yonder," and the Chorus " The fining pot is for silver." The absence of Mrs Lane, as previously explained, necessitattd the omission of an air for the principle soprano and trio. The quartette `: List ! the cherubic host," was, however' saved, thanks to the efforts of the Misses Roberts, and , proved a very interesting item. Miss Monks and Mrs Pearson were both somewhat handicapped by an un- steady accompaniment in the respective solos "Eye hath not seen" and " Then shall the King say," but espite this fact each sang with fervour and an intelligent regard for the sentiment expressed in the words. It was a little un- fortunate that the music falling to the lot of Mr. Harold Lee was somewhat beyond the range of his voice; which is distinctly baritone in character and pitch. Never- theless, he made the most that was possible under the circumstances of "My soul is athirst for God," and other items. Mr. W. H. Wallington sang the solos scored for the bass voice, but scarcely did himself justice by reason of too marked a stdlldity in style and enuncia- tion. The air" I saw also the Lord" was his nearest approach to an ideal rendering. A' meed of praise is due to Miss Toft for her musicianly performance of an effec- ive harp accompaniment in this number, and in the instrumental intermezzo "Adoration." The choruses were highly satisfactory as a whole. - "Great and marvellous are Thy works' is almost Handelian in its breadth and massiveness, and was a marked success in performance.

PARIS, SATIIRDAY.—M. Grevy has left the FAysee, aad has taken up his residence at his house in the Avenuede Jena.

VERSAILLES, SATURDAY NIOUT.—M. Sadi-CATIIO/, mein- ber of the Chamber of Deputies for the Cate d'Or and Minister of Financein the late Cabinet of M. de Trek- cinet, was to-day elected President o'f the `French Iteputtic'by an immense majority. This event, which up tothis morning was entirely unexpected, wasbrought sbottt by the withdrawal from the contest of M. Jules 'Ferry and of M. fie Freycinet, who retired after the an- nouncement of-the results of the first ballot in order to allow of the Whole Republican strength being concen- trated on one .candidate. The following is the result 'officially anno'cnced by M. Le Royer to 'the 'Congrein (amtiber of voters 833). M. Sadi Carnot 616 General Saussier M. Jules Ferry M. de Freycinet General Appert. M. Flog uet 'M. Felix Pyat Twenty blank voting papers were put in. The procla- mation of the result of the election was hailed with prolonged cheering by the members of Congress and 'reiterated shouts of " Vive In Republique. '—M. ILe Rover then said: "M. Sadi Carnet having obtained the suffrage;' I proclaim him President Of the 'Republic." 'llere there was a fresh outburst of cheering, especially from the Left and Centre. M. 'Le Royer afterwsMe declared the session of the National Assembly te'be closed, and the Assembly rose at B 47. PARTS, 81/NDAY.—M. Sadi-Carnot took up'his residence at thd Elysee this afternoon, and one of the first to wait upon him was M. Grevy. Sclbsequently he received several politicians. In conversation with 'these, per- sonages M. Sadi-Carnot expressedihis intention te ask the Chamber, as soon as the new Cabinet was formed, to vote provisional instalments of the 'Budget, and then to close the session on the 15th,hurt., • owinE ,to the •proxi- mity of the senatorial elections. 'This •evening the Ministers went to the ElysO e to Vice 'their resignation In the hands of the new chief isf the State, who, how- ever; requested them to remain in Office 'temporarily in order to carry on the business of the country.. 'The newspapers, almost without .exception. give a. very favourable welcome to the new 'President, and 'con- gratulate the country on the peaceful issue of 'the contest. The patriotic condrict of 'MM. 'Ferry and Dd'Freycinet in retiring rather than snlit the'Repdhlican vote is warmly praised by marry of 'the papers, and the 'unity of feeling and action displayed by 'the different. Republican groups at the critical inoment'is regarddd as a happy augury for the future of the Republic.

div.head: RECORD BEATER.
div.p: THE RECORD BEATER.

Though the history of cycling in England extends only as far ihack as 1870, the , strides which fbia sport has made are really phenomenal. tweedy years ago the man who dared to suggest, that the day would•beine when* gide: pi4ler voald. cover 29Z miles in 4 hours would have been laughed at. Bat for all tbat, such a performance :has been ac- •camplished. The sportef wheel-racing may be recognised AS one ;of firmly eetablished institutions of this country. Every Saturday during the spring, summer, and .autumn eyrie aces take place all over the country., and attract the greatest attention from all lovers of good aped. Most prominent amongst the many famous bicvcaetweing-nien is Richard Howell, of Leicester, the champion of the world. When intssing through this city the other day, we took.advantage of the occasion to call opn the 'chain- pion who was then actively engaged intraining for one of races. . Howell, who is a splendidly-made fellow, of ' betireeh, twenty-five and thirty years ,ef age, stiiading six feet highi in his stockings, and weighing, intraitiing, thirteen • stone, looked the picture of health, ambreadily responded to our suggestion as to a few minutes' tillk en some of his greatest achievements. Replying to a query as to 'whew he first began riding, lllowell said— " In the year 1879. It was not, however, till 1881 that fiat brought my name into prominence before the , 'sporting public. A the Whiteuntidetweeting, .1881, at the Belgrave Grounds; Leicester, I men the one-mile Lchampionship of the world, 'beating ;all the best men of the day, including Jack Keen .and Fre() eooper, the two Old champions. From that time my.aaner, with the ex- ception of two or three months in 1883, when I was a ' bit off colour,' has beensnoof unbroken successes. I have stood 'right here during the bicycling season, 'ready to race any man in the world who fancied he -could beat me. I should like to say that all through I, have ridden a 59 inch Badge' bieyele,aand would not change toy mount underany consideration." ; "Have you raced in the tnited State& " • " Yes, I crossed the pond in 1884,. and 1885. It the; great Springfield tournament in IP,M Fwon seven out of 'eight races there." "What do you reckon your best performances ?" "Well this year I .4!fid IL full mile on the track at Coventry, the home of the cycle 'manufacture, in 2 minutes, 35 seconds. I -was hampered bv my pace- makers, and good judges think with everithingin my ,favour I could. do 2-30 for the dietaries, :a• time which I 'myself think I could get pretty•dlose to." What is your system of training'?" •:" Well, I reckon I know howto •take eon of myself, • and how to ;id fit. I don't believe :in the old-fashioned ideas of strict diet and heave gruelling-work. I eat plain, good food, and plenty at it,: and drink port wine and sound beer in moderation. In themorning I take a -litiViiiik-WfMne breakfast, and thea,mfter that meal, if lam heavy, ride eight or nine Miles on the track here, in thick flannels: • After dinner I do 11013a41 more slogging 'work and maybe a watic inthesevening,.aad early to bed. When lam about right in weight I content myself with short, sharp bursts as hard as ever lean go, on the track, and when I can ,cover 440 yards in 30 seeonds with a fly- ing start I reckon to be moving -as well as I want to. But there is one secret—at lave., no secret—but idea of mine the practice of whichl have found invaluable. If I feel' dull and out of sorts, heavy. or depressed. 111 have done too much .work, or my NOM= is out of order— if, in short, I don't feel quite actund; I take some medicine the same as I have used lance I was queer in 883. , I .have always found this sot me up:and put me to rights again, and it is a remedy which 1 I:believe in and tell all my friends about." " Well, and what it It?" " It is called Warner's Safe Cure, and it is safe, to cure every time: In the winter-time especially, when you can easily understand I am not so careful•of ray health as in the spring, summer, and autumn, I 'have found it in- Valuable. All I want, to beat the fastest bicyclist in the world, is plenty of practice, an occasional dose of the medicine, and my favourite raathine."—Cycling News, Oct. Ist.

The Catholic Primate ef Ireland, 'Dr. Mc.Gettigan, died at 12 30 p.m. on Saturday. The -Mast Rev. Daniel ' Mc.Gettigan, Archbishon of Armagh, and" Primate of all Ireland. was consecrated coadjater 'for Raphoe in 1856; succeeded to the bishopric in 1861; and was translated to Armagh on March 11th, 1870. At Newmarket Fergus, on Saturday., before Messrs. Eaton and Seagram*, five nien mooted 'ltichard Allen, Michael Barry, William Alien. IVSYliaari 'Jones, and John -Beechmor were sentenced te one morrth's Imprisonment, under the Orimes Act, for ottendings suppressed meet- ing of the National benzin,. at Newirinetket on November 'l3th. -The meeting of the ?Arbil a Oorportion, fixed to. be held on Monday, was adjourned, on the motion of Mr. Sexton, seconded by Ahlerman Magee, 'to mark the sym- pathy of the municipal body with the leirdMayor on his • Imprisonment. An adjourned meeting will be held on Saturday, when a resolution will be proposed to the toffeet that the freedom of the city ,he conferred on the 'Lord Mayor. On Monday, three children of MarthatOasey were left alone in his house, at Tertrugh, near Swatragh. co. Lon- 'donderry, and they went into a fihed, where some flax waastored, for hand-scutching purposes, and lighted a fire. The flax caught the denies, andthese set fire to the children's clothes. Twe of them, aged six and seven years, were burnt to death, and the third.was seriously -injured. A violent storm from the north-west, accompanied by •thunder, lightning, and heavy hail showers. swept over •thediStrict of West Cork, on Monday night, working considerable havoc amongst property. In Skibbereen, .on" Tuesday morning, the streets were -strewn with tiles, broken chimney pots, and refuse, and several windows have been bielren by hail. A number, of mac- kerel fishing boats put to sea from the Castle Towns- •end Bay. and had to run for shelter before the storm. A National League demonstration was -held. on Sunday at 'Watergrasshill, and was addressed by Messrs. Lane, MP., and °glen, M.P. Mr. Gilhoolv. M.T„ against whom warrants have been kowed, attended mass at ,and addressed a large gathering of people 'before they started for Watergrasshitl, when the de- monstration proper took place. It lea carious fact that •while -Mr. Gilhooly was in the church he was in the im- mediate -vicinity of two policemen: who evidently were 'unaware who their neighbour was.

'The prison efficiaa ai:Tullamere returned O'Brien his greatcoat on Friday. Since the mew suit of Clothes was smuggled into him Mr. O'Brien has been !Wing continually, night and day, in those garments, so fla not to give the warders a second opportunity of removing his clothes when he was asleep. On Friday, the •Govemor of the gaol (Captain Featherstonhaugt), in the presence of Dr. Morehead, one of the visiting justices, gave Mr:O'Brien an undertaking that his clothes wouldmat be taken from him again so long as he wasin the infirmary. The Freeman's Journal says: "A rumour is current that warrants have been issued for several members of Parliament and other gentlemen prominently connected with the recent movements, to the number rot 40. Mr. Balfour has tried the plan of sapping the Nfrticrud organisation. His failure has been con- spicuous; and now, in Mr. Harrington's arrest, which is reportedlo be only the first. of a long series, he hopes apparently to effect, by a vigorous attack and the-ex- treme deve;opment cif Cis policy. what he has failed to accomplish by the slower method." - -

LOW HARTECOTOg Ar RAWTENSTALL..—The Marquis of Hartington addressed a meeting of his constituents at Rawterstall on Saturday afternoon. Before referring to• what be described as the "everlasting question of Ire.: land," ba offered a few remarks upon the eourse which he had thought it his duty to pursue during the last two years. At the election in 1885 a, definite programme was put before the electors. On that programme in the main the Liberal party were agreed, and he submitted that the proper 'course to have taken was to have ,dealt with the chief items thereof, instead of dividing the party and, indefinitely postponing the realisation of the hopp;anoz, wishes that .bad been expressed concerning various mea- sures. Discussing some of the difficulties which he die., cerns in the Rome Rule polieyj Lord Hartington sub- mitted that it was perfectly preposterous to assume that the people of Great Britain would allow Irish repre— sentatives to interfere in their local affairs when English members were debarred from 'any voice in the local af- fairstf the sister country. As to the Crimes Act, he consitlered that the condition 9tlreland consequent upon the action and influencerdf the National League justified it. ir.,When order had ' beenrre-established the whole, Unionist party, he believed, would gladly co-operate in extending a great measure.of nelf-goveriment to Ireland; afid so sosn as the Liberal party ifelt it to he their duty to co-operate with the Unionists in thel'ext.ension of local liberty, local self-government, and load freedom in Ire- land, they would no longer find in them opponents but their closest ant warmest friends. These indicatians encourage the hope that we are Willy on the eve of better times." AWFUL TRAOI37Yr IN LONDON. A murder and suicide of the most shocking and revolting char- acter were perpetrated in the neighbourhood of Cam- berwell New Road, London, on Satueday morning. It appears that at about half-pest ten cries of "Help." were heard, and smoke was seen issuing from the ground floor windows of No. 118, Thomas-street, by ocune paesers- by. Information WAS at once given to the polioe. In a very short time Police-constable Arthur !Catalan, 198 1., arrived on the scene, and on forcing an entrance die- ecvered that the house was full of smoke. The fire was at once extinguished, and on the constable making his way into the premises, he found a child named Way flore, aged four years, lying on the floor of the kitchen in a pool of blood, with its throat cut by some share instrument ; in another portion of the house WGLS a woman, the mother of the child—Marie Bore, 35 years of age—in the same condition. On the arrival of Dr. Arnot be pronounced both to be dead. From evidence which teas been obtained by the police, it appears that the mother, through some cause at present unknown, murdered her child, then set fire to the house, and after- wards out her own throat. Considerable excitement was caused in the neighbourhood by this shocking deed; but from inquiries it appears that no one knew the woman's name, she, witii her two e.hildren, the mur- dered one, aged four, and another, aged about two years, being the only innwites of the house. The woman hid been deserted by her paramour, and was known to be addicted to drink.

14:xPOLTTION. OF A JEALOUS MURDERER. -- MOM SE Payne. 38 years of age, and a labourer, was executed at Warwick Prison, on Tuesday morning, for the mur- der of his sister-in-law, Charlotte Taylor, at Coventry. in August last. Payne and his wife had charge of ma office at Coventry, and the deceased, for whom he had eNhi- bited great fondness, resided with them. , Becoming jealous of the attentions of a "Salvation Army" mem- ber. named Leonard Day, Payne had from time to time used threats towards the couple, And on the morning of the crime seized the woman from behind, while she was engaged cleaning the officn, and cut her throat, nearly severing the head from the body. The culprit, since his condemnation, had manifested the greatest penitence, and repeatedly declared himself ready to die. Ffe was daily seen hy the gaol chaplain (the Rev. G. Sumner), and fre- <vent ly hy the Rev. J. Gibson, Congregational minister. Hit was hn Monday afternoon visited by lds wife and mother, and the parting was an affecting one. He re- tired to rest on Monday about nine p.m., slept fairly well, and rose shortly after six a.m. on Tuesday. Havirg -partnken of n tight breakfast, the chaplain-and the Rev. Mr: Gibson went to his cell soon after seven o'clock, and remained with him in prayer some time, the culprit en- gaging-earnestly in devotion. He submitted quietly to the pittioning, and walked firmly and Unsupported to the scaffold, cordially shook hand; with the executioner, cad said he lipped "to meet hini in heaven." On Use 'Scaffold, he repeated several times "Receive my soul, my I.ord !" "God bless my wife;" "Save her soul ; " "God help me!" Berry gave a drop of seven feet, and death was instantaneous. The culprit had throughout admitted the justice of his sentence, but left behind no confession. Field reporter. witnessed the execution.

RIINCORN..—These tAarns met en Saturday on the ground of the former, at Rushohne. The Runcorn men were minus nine of their usual team, , the absentees being Speakman, Cawley, H. Hughes, W. 'Hughes, W. Broady, W. Faulkner, Wainwright, Wright, and Lewis, six of whom were assisting their county against Durham at Birkenhead. Only two thirties were indulged in. The visitors won the tossaand the Ran- gers started the ball, and for a considerable length of time Taylor and Sabin made strenuous efforts to get away, but the tackling of Davies, Woods, and W. Riley was too good for the home forwards. Half-time was called with the score :—Runcorn one goal, Rangers nil. The Rangers towards the close played anything but the game, continally lying on the ball is the scrimmage whenever they bad a chance. The score at the close was one goal and one minor each. The visitors played a plucky game all through, and deserve every credit. Teams :—Runcorn: J. Brazendale, back; T. H. Davies, T. Woods, and W. A. Riley, three-quarter backs ' • H. Andrews and G. Whitby,half-backs : I. Clarke.' J. Gat- ley, J. Barns, P. Riley, F. Hancock, Cox, lianipson, J. Bowyer, and A. Raffe, forwards. Rangers A. Dickson, back; Radcliffe. Sabin, and A. Hainnett, three-quarter backs; W. Perlane arid Taylor, half-backs; Herbert Hasleham, Harry Haslehain, Mee, Jones, H. Hamnett, J. Parlane, Barrow, Haaron, and Frost, forwards. WIDNYIS v. Weesersi.—Played at Widnes, on Satur- day, before a huge assemblage of spectators, the home team winning easily by two tries and six. minors to nil. Smith kicked off, and by smart play, in which Morris, Plumpton, and Smith were prominent, Widnes added two touchdowns, on both oecaione having hard fines or tries. Then Tassel' secured the ball at the centre, ran smartly, and.passed to Plumpten, he to Hardman, and that player to Sampson, who crowned this bite really splondid play by grounding the ball over the opponents' goal. Farrell failed to add the major points. Half-time was called before anything else was scored. Shortly after the resumption of play, Parkinson dribbled over Werneth line, and fell on the ball, but lost possession, and a touchdown was added. Long kicking by Morris compelled the visitors to save; and Hardman's smart following up did ditto. Plumpton now ran splendidly in the home quarter, and, though surrounded by his oppo- nents, passed nicely to Smith. who ran in and gained the second try. Morris was entrusted with the place-kick, but could not effect an improvement. The game closed soon after, as above stated. Teams: Widnes-.-S. Bing- ham, baek • Plurapton, Parkinson, and Morris, three- quarter betas ; Farrell and Wilkinson, half backs; Smith (captain), Kiddie, Hardman, Sampson, Gandy, Barber, \Woods, J. Bingham, .and Pennington, forwards. Umpire, Mr. A. Hatton. Werneth—R. Brown, back; S. Shirt, J. Simpson, aad J. Wyatt, three-quarter backs; Rayne and J: Buckley, half backs ; -F.-Fitton,. A._Wood, J. Wood, Shortrielge, Hankinson, Kent,. Crabtree, White- head. and R. Wyatt, forwards. Referee, Mr. Vickers, of :Salford. ." WARRIMOTOW "A" Taira V. ARDWICK (IST).--7Plaved at Ardwick on Saturday, in beautiful weather. the Warrington team were placed at a disadvantage owing to Hackett'm knee (which he had injured a few weeks ago) again giving way prior to the commencement of the game. and also to the uneven state of the ground. They, however, found a substitute for Hackett in Lalley (of St. Paul's), who happened to be on the field. Ardwick won the toes, and, two 35 minutes being the, time agreed upon to 'play, the visiting captain kicked off at 3-20, the ball going,into touch. The Warrington forwards broke away, atei,Warburton getting hold put in a good run, being brought down by Heade. Whittle next passed to Antrobus, who threw to Appleton, this player being pushed into touch near the line by Hall after a splendid run. Ardwick relieved the pressure by touching down. Brindiey dropped out, Appleton returning to centre: The home forwards carried a scrimmage ; then the War- rington forwards broke away, and Whittle kicked across to Warburton who put hi a strong run, being brought down by Rearie In the home 25. Brindlev transferred play to centre, tut the visitor,' again dribbled to the line, Jones and Molyneaux being conspicuous. The Ardwick forwards next got the ball away, and dribbled nearly the length of the fold. A try appeared inevitable, but Webster overran the ball, and Antrobus rushing up averted further dearer. The Warrington forwards re- lieved hi grand style. Moores passed to Heade, who was collared by Warburton. Antrobus now passed to Evans, who kicked to Hall, the latter player being allowed a free kick for offside tackling, but Jolley returneil with in- terest, Jones and Thornley taking play to the line. Good passing between Whittle, Evans, and Appleton took place, the latter player again being pushed into touch' near the line. Moores put in an opportune kick to the quarter jiag ; then Antrobus passed to Evans, who had his kick charged down, but Warburton secured and Made a dashing run, being brought down by Hall. From a pass by Antrobus, Evans kicked to Appleton, who made a smart run and to Randles, Brindley collaring him before he coldugssetdoff. From a line-out in the Ard- wick quarters Antrobm got possession and passed to Evans, who ran in between the posts, Warburton's kick at goal striking the upright. Brindley kicked off, the ball going into touch. From a scrimmage the ball became loose and 'Whittle kicked to Cheetham, who put in a long drop kick, to which Jolley replied with a gigan- tic punt, Adamson preventing any return. The Ardwick forwards now made another dangerous rush, but Jolley saved well by kicking into touch in the Warrington 2. The Warrington men worked the hall into Ardwick ter- ritory, where Jones picked up from a dribble and al- , most got over, being brought down by Hall near the ' line; half time being called with the score—Warrington 1 try and 1 minor to Ardwick nothing. On change of cads Cheetham restarted for the home team, Evans mak- inga good return. The Warrington forwards dribbled to the home full-back, who got the ball away nicely and kicked to Jolley, this player making a good return into touch. Whittle now passed to Evans and he to Apple- ton, who kicked to Hall, the last-named player return- ing into touch. From the line out the Ardwick forwards broke away, Jolley saving. From a scrimmage near the Warrington smarterflag, Morris got away almost un- noticed and was making "tracks" for the Warrington line, but Jolley brought him down beautifully. Ardwick now preased the visitors, who had to relieve their lines by touching down. Jolley dropped out, but the kick was charged by Parker. Warrington were placed on the defensive for some time, wadi the forwards,headedbv Eyes Adamson and Donohue, took play to neutral ground. Some Adamson, passing between Morns, Dawson, and heetham was witnessed, but Warburton's tackling was too good for them to get far. 'whittle next passed , wide to Appleton, but he was to well watched by Heade to get away. Play now settled in the Ardwick 25, a dead ball accruing to Warrington. Nothing of note occurred from now to the call of time, the final score bck ing—Warrington, 1 try and 2 minors; Ardwick, 1 minor' point. Teams :—Warrington: Full back, Jolley; three- quarter hacks, Appleton, Evans, and Warburton; half barks, Whittle (captain), and Antrobus; forwards, Siolyneaux, Eyes, Adamson, Thothley, Jones, Donohue, Lalley, Bate, and Bandies. Ardwick: Full back, Hall; three-quarter backs, Reade, Dawson, and Cheetham ; half backs, Morris and Moores: forwards, Webster, Buckley, Wood, Brindley, Burgess, Barba., Henderson, Parker, and Ward. WARRINGTON v. NENDAL HORNETS,

The above teams met in splendib weather on the Wil- derspool ground, Warrington, on Saturday, before a fair attendance of spectators. Both teams failed to put their full strength in the field, Warrington suffering most in this respect by the absence of Massey (who, by the_wayjs_progres..sing very favourably), Rigby' and the brothers Turner ; whilst Armstrong-and Pisher were

away from the Kendal ranks. The fine open game and the splendid passing which the visitors are accustomed to display caused much specnlation to be rife as to the result of the match, and it was a matter of regret that both teams were wt.itkened by the absence of the players mentioned above. .

Soon after the selected time the Kendal men kicked off, Barnes making a neat return to centre. The first scrimmage was formed at that place, and from it War- ren Passed to Barnes, who ran and passed to Jolley, that player making tracks fot the visitors' lines; but his career was stopped by laines at the quarter flag. A bad pass:by Barnes tto Daniels spoiled a certain eliancl of scoring, and the visitors relieved to half-way. The War- riegtonians again forced the game on the visitors' lines; but Battersby got the ball away by a timely kick to neid- field. Berry tried hard to get away; but found niore than a match in Warren, and the honer team pressed the Hornets back again. From a line out the leather was rushed over, only a minor accruing. The drop put brought little relief, for the Warrington men again forced the game on the Hornets' lines; but the home team were placed at a serious disadvantage through Warren having to retire hurt, Davies going half-hick. The lat- ter got in a pass to his captain this player kicking over the lino, and Alien sawed in the sick of time. Bcru: re- started, and exchange kicking by Nevins and Battersby ended in the latter putting in a neat pass to Walker, who transferred hick to Nevins, the latter being awar- ded a free kick for off-side tackling. This availed his side little, for the Kendal men invaded the Warrington territory, but Warren, who had returned to his place, got away from a pack, and relieved his • side gallantly. Walker ohortly after made his mark in a favourable position, but nothing came of it, for Jolley negatived by a brilliant run gong touch to half-way flag. A good kick by Barnes again threatened danger, and a miss by pme of the Kendal Hornets' backs let in the home team, and the hill was taken over, Speakman grounding. On appeal this was disallowed, though its legitimacy was freely commented On. The ball was brought back to the twenty-five flag, , and from some loose play Berry got away, and made a splendid run to the Warrington line, Nevins stopping him. Ashton relieved his side by a short run and kick to centre, and half time was called with the score—War- rington two minors to Kendal Hornets nil. So far the game had been all in faro* of the Warringtonians, and it was thought that at least they would make a draw or come out of the fray successful. Isherwood recom- menced hostilities, and for a tsime the Warringtonians held the upper hand. Passing by the Hornets' backs was now indulged in, and the home goal was threatened, but the home forwards, headed by Ashton and Little- wood, took play to half way. Exchange kicking by Barnes and Crass settled play in the Kendal ground, but Walker put in a useful kick to Nevins, the latter failing to get the leather away. Speakman got in a neat run to midfield, and E. Dillon seconded his efforts by a smart dribble to the north countrymen's lines. A sharp pass by Speakman to Barnes gave the latter a chance, but he kicked over the line, Allen going in touch in goal with the oval. Isherwood almost got over soon after the drop out, but Cross relieved. Povey now looked like scoring, and took the leather again over the line, and the visitors were forced to act on the defensive. Walker dropped. out, and the visitors now played up with renewed vigour, invading the Warrington quar- ters. Davies, however, took play back to midfield, and from some loose play which followed Retry got away„ and passing to Walker, that player transferred to Baines, the latter after a strong run getting in under the post. Cross kicked& neat goal. The game was re- started from mid-field, and considering the above re- verse, the home team played with great confidence, and more than held their own, strenuous efforts being made by Barnes, Ashton, and Speakman to equalize. The superior tactics of the Kendal men again forced the War- ringtonians to act on the defensive, and a passing move- ment by the visitors' backs againended in Barnesgetting over, Cross agaid doing the ne•dfnl. It only wanted a few minutes new from the MU of time, and both teams strove hard to obtain another point, but all in vain, and after seventy minutes hard and pleasant play the result read as follows :—Kendal Hornets, 2 goals ;Warrington, 4 minors.

. During the latter portion of the game the home team had to play fourteen men, owing to the retireme.nt of Daniels, who had stained serious injury. The score certainly does notindicate the nature of the game, for the Warringtonians had equally as much of the play as their opponents. On behalf of Warrington Nevins did not play so well as we have seen him. Of the three- quftrters Barnes wa.s decidedly the best, and at half back Speakman played t sterling game. Warren, having been hurt during the first portzon of the game, failed to , show during the remainder his old fire and dash. In the forward ranks Harry Ashton was by far the best on the field, his play surpassing any of this season's efforts. He was ably assisted by Davies and E. Dillon. On the Ken- dal side Baines, Cross, Franklyn, and Wilson were the best of a splendid team. The following were the teams Warrington—Full back, W. Nevins; three-quarter backs' J. Jolley, T. Barnes "(captain). and W. Daniels; halfbacks, J. E. Warren and W. Speakman forwards, 11. Ashton. W. PoVey, R. Littlevrood, W. Dillon, Davies, E. Dillon, W. Haves T: Craghan, and Isherwood. CALTFORNLA. AND FEMALE EMIGRA- TION. On Wednesday evening, at a meeting of the Pen- keth Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society, held in the Wesleyan Day School, an interesting lecture on "California" was delivered by Mrs. M. E.Parker, in whose emigration scheme much interest has bean excited since her return from California in August last. There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. Robert Garnet, J.P., who, in intro- ducing Mrs. Parker to the meeting, said that she was a lady who, by her philanthropic character, had endeared herself to a large circle of friends and acquaintances, not only in this country, and not bounded by this country. Mrs. Parker had travelled in many countries besides our own, and they had assembled to listen to what he had no doubt would be a very interesting subject, dealt with in a very interesting and entertaining way. (Applause,)-- Mrs. Panav,a, who remarked that she hoped that when shelital finished her lecture those present would agree with her that California was the paradise of the world, then spoke of hei"sthird visit to America as a temper- ance delegate. Passing lightly over the ocean voyage, she touched upon the visit to New York, Boston, and Chicago, and proceeding, described in vivid language the scenery,climate, and natural advantages of California. California in itself, she said, would produce more food to nourish, and more fruit to gladden, the heart of man, than many countries of mighty millions of acres. The state of California Was indeed the poor man's paradise, with its boundless resources. The rapid growth of pro- duce and fruits was most wonderful, game and fowl there were in abundance, while the rivers swarmed with fish. Her intention was to show what kind of a field for emigration California was, both for men and woman, and as a means to that end she gave a list of wages paid to the artizan class, 'which ranged from El a day to Bs. a day, and of the wages paid to women for household work, ranging from LSO or £4O a year to £3O or £7O, or there- abouts. In England female employment could scarcely be obtained, but in California there were thousands of bright, happy homes there sensible, educated women would be warmly welcomed, and treated with considera- tion and respect, if they would lay aside false feeling of gentility and go as real helps" to the wives and mothers there, who were obliged to do their own , work, or resort to the help of Chinamen. She had trav- elled thousands of miles in California, and found the same want everywhere. Wealth abounded, and if our British women were sensible enough to take the woit of the household, they would soon earn competencies for themselves under pleasant surroundings. She pointed to California as the golden way to happy independence both for men and women. They could not realise how warmly the domesticated women of this country would be welcomed, there, but they must look upon nothing they had to do as being too menial. People who ob- jected to housework as being menial were not required there. Surely it was worth while to leave a scanty pit- tance, with little chance of an independence, for such a home, surrounded by everything that could make life en- klyable. In conclusion, she mentioned that she had or- ganised committees to receive women that she might send out, but all whom she sent must be total abstainers and have a capacity for housework. School teachers need not go to that country, for there education was provided absolutely free by the Government. —A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Parker, on the pro- position of' Mr. James Watson, seconded by Mr. 11. Hobson.

It is not known whether he will go to the south of France or to Egypt. He will remain abroad until the reassem- bling of Parliament in February, and perhaps until a later period. THE LIBERAL UNIONISTS.—A Liberal Unionist Confer- ence was held in Westminster Town Hall on Thursday afternoon, Lord Hartington presiding. Resolutions in favour of the maintenance of legislative union, and ex- pressing confidence in Lord Hartington as the leader of the party were adopted. In the evening a ban- quet in connection with the conference was held in St. Stephen's Hall, Westinin.ster, Lord Harting,ton`again pre- siding. Vide ",WESTERN MAIL," CARDIFF, Saturday, dd. t 5, 1551.
MISS E..IIELEUISH, of 7, Clive-road, Canton, Cardiff, was sufferiug from a moat bevere form of

llness. She had the advantage of the very be,t, skill and care, but all appeared vain; and she was at last recommended to go to the Glamorgan and Monmouth Infirmary. Here she was treated for several weeks for Bright's disease. Milk diet, vapour baths, and other prescriptions had no effect. On the

contrary, she became much worse, and her body commenced to swell. At last, in March, she underwent an operation, and some 16 or 18 quads of water were removed. from her side and legs. She continued to get worse, and in Mai was discharged as incurable. Her journey to her home (then at Kings- brompton. near Silverton, in Somersetshire) was performed with the greatest difficulty and suffering, and occupied several days. Though a cure had been pronounced hopeless, her lather nsisted on further professional advice, and again instru- ments were applied, with the frightful result of withdraw- ing 20 quarte tit water from her /Leh week. Again the medi- cal men pronounced the case hopeless, and finally they re- linquished attendance on that ground. The unfortunate victim was now in despair. Her sufferings wefe indescrib- able, and there was no prospect except that at sink- ing through slow torture into an early grave. At this time she became acquainted with the details
of an extraordinary cure (the well-known cam!.
of William Grayson) by Hop Bitters, and bhe resolved to try them. Medical men sanctioned the experiment, but warned'
her that it could only be a useless expense. HuVf ?WEN', Mires
Melhuish persisted, and in June she begun to take the Bitters.
Her condition changed almost immediately.
The waer
diminished. to the surprise ot the doctor, who had triemburel
her at intervals, and who declared that the change was nothw
ing short of miraculous. The improvement continued ; she gained appetite, and slept well. Fer months previout* she
had been unable to retail food, or to enjoy continuou3 rest. Within two months the water was practically checked. She

continued to use the Hop Bitters, finding that they strengthned her. M addition to relieving the disease, and within three months of he.; commencing to take them she was able to walk in the fields without help. This astonishing cure of one
of the most awful diseases that affect humanity bas made the

deepest impression on both professional and lay inhabitants or the district. Miss Melhuish, the fortunate subject of what she regards as almost a miracle, is now able to walk her seven or eight miles with ease. With a proper sense of grateful ap- preciation of the remedy, and with a laudable desire to beip other sufferers by the diffusion of the precious information, she announces that her greatest happiness will be to show her

fellow creatures who may be soffering the tortures of thin hideous disease how they may rind relief. She will gladly give all information in her Power to anyone who writes to her,. We have recorded her address above.

6' 3, Carter's-yard,
Salthouse-lane, Hull,
March 14.

"Dear Predr—You will be surprised at receiving a letter from the, but, thank God, I am pleased to say am getting better every day. I shall be so glad to breathe the fresh air again. It has seemed a dreadfa long time to be in bed. You know I was taken to the hospital last April to be treated for Bright's Disease of the kidneys. Well, on July 31 they tapped me, and took away 304 ounoea of water. The same thing was done again on September 18, and 408 ounces of water obtained. On Oct. 9 I Was discharged from the bob- pital as inourable. In January this year (the 20th) was again tapped at home, and 360 ounces of water taken away. The St. Bartholomew's Hospital in Lando* refused me admission as a hopeless case, and the St. Bartholomew's Hospital, Chatham, also refused me, as being the worst case they had seen for 'years, and two local doctors gave me up as hopeless. When I came from the hospital it took three to pot me to bed. My clothes had to be cut off. I was an . object of misery and despair. After the. hospitals had refused me, and doctors given Inc up, my wife persuaded me to try HOP BITTERS, and from the commencement have improved daily. I have only taken them seven weeks, and can now get downstairs and walk about without even a stick. With the aid of a few more bottles of the Bitters shall be well again. The water has left my body and legs. The only trace left is in my feet. It Is a wonderful medicine. I wish I had tried it sooner, as I have nearly ruined myself and family with doctors' bills and other expenses. I might, • have been well long ago. At the hospital I had no appetite whatever, but since using the Bitters eat everything with a relish. The only difficulty is the expense, but mast not mind that so long as Tam getting well. Am cheerful now that recovery is near, for every one had given me up as a bad job.—With best wishes
.. Your affectionate brother,
