div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 10, lip 7.

Tim z French Republic has, in a most peculiar crisis, stood the great strain of a change of Presi- dent much better than was anticipated. It is 01)- 1th:4113-not only that Republicanism holds the field, but that Republicans aie prepared to make sacri- fices to maintain the Republic. When it became evident that public feeling could only be allayed by the resignation of M. GREVY, it was also appa- rent that the selection might plunge the ,nation into a still greater crisis There were those who foresaw the possibility of the ruin of the Republic as an outcome of the struggle of rival claimants, for it must not be forgotten that there are con- spirators in France ever ready to seize an oppor- tunity of overturning the existing , order of things. Happily, the election of President has come and gone, and the Republic is all the stronger for the ordeal from the fact that its strength is proVed. It seems somewhat strange to those who have been keeping an eye on the more prominent can- didates for the Presidency to find that the choice of the Congress has fallen, upon one who was looked upon as an outsider. But it has happened before in history that, when the supporters of two strong candidates found that they stood in each others way, they have stepped aside and agreed to concentrate their votes on a third candidate. It was in this way, if we mistake not, that Presi- dent LINCOLN' and President GARFIELD SRC* cessively came to he the final choice' of the Electoral Congress; and it may, it

is to be hoped, be taken as happy augury for France that both of these Presidents of the Great American Republic proved to be ex- ceptionally well qualified for the high office which they were thus called upon to, hold. M. SADI CAB,' liar, the new President of the French Republic, is not looked upon as a brilliant man; but he has that which is better than nwre brilliance—he has
I

a high character for integrity, and for disinteres- ted devotedness to the cause of the Republic. He has not sought the office; the office has rather Bought him, and this, after all, is the highest form of appointment. He has not been amongst those who have intrigued to effect the downfall of M. GREVE and it is therefore the less likely that he _
will himself be intrigued against. He declined,

When asked to allowbimseli to be nominated, to t canvass for votes, and yet, as the result thows, he has by far received the largest numberlof votes, shtaihing 616 supporters, in the finarballot,, against 18S for General SausstEs., who still stood in the running against him. The fact that the various sections of Republicans have been able to unite in

LORD Cnoss.—Speaking on Wednesday night at a meeting of Liberal Unionists at Chippenham, Lord Cross remarked that if it were thought for the ad- vantage of the country that Lord Ilartington should be Prime Minister, with a cabinet of Liberal Union- ists, the Conservatives would readily make way for him.

his favour is some sort of guarantee for the sta- bility of his position, though, having "tasted blood" by removing one President, there is reason to fear that the populace will be stimulated to repeat the operation. We cannot but think that M. GREVY has been badly treated in being compelled to re- sign because of the sins of his son-in-law. By all means let M. WiLsoN be punished when it has been proved that hehas dishonoured. France; but to turn, meantime, against M. GREVY and make him a scape-goat is, to say the least, ungrateful. ' The hopeful features about an otherwise bad piece of business are that the French have shown them- selves "jealous in honour," if "sudden and quick in quarrel;' and that they are practically unani-s mous in electing. a President with a character above suspicion. ,

TIE Liberals of Warrington were favoured in having the Marquis of RIPON to address them at the demonstration which was held' in the Public Hall on Monday night; and it is obvious from the crowded character of the attendince; and from the enthusiasm which was manifested that they knew how to .appreciate the favour. It is undoubtedly true that, in the main, the classes are against the masses on the question of Hoine Rule—just as they have, in the first instance, been opposed to every other great reform. The dukes and lords, "and other tremendous personages "—to quote Lord DERBY'S famous phrase—have deserted Mr. GLADSTONE (Lord DERBY amongst the rest), but it is to the iredit of their order that such dis- tinguished statesmen as Lord RIPON and Lord GRANVILLE still stand by the cause of the people. A little leaven leaventh the whole lump, and it may yet happen that Lord. RIPON Will have the satisfaction, all opposition being overcome, of piloting a Home Rule 811 through the House of Lords just as he piloted the Ballot Bill through that stiff-necked assembly. His lordship directed his attention to replying to the speech which the Marquis of HA.nrixorox delivered before his con- stituents, at Rawtenstall, on Saturday evening. It was a speech which called for a reply,for it bristled with objections to Home Rule; and it gratify- ing to know that it 4ras effectually answered by Lord RIPON. There was grain as well as chaff in the good-natured reference which his lordship made to the recent meetings at Dublin, which were not proclaimed, and were not attended by the Government reporter. It pointed to the fact that in Ireland, as the law is at present administered, there is free speech for the Tories and Liberal • Unionists, and a brutal gag for the Home' Rulers., Lord *row did well to describe as monstrous the action of the Government in prosecuting news- agents for selling papers which contained, reports of meetings that had been proclaimed. Such petty tyranny would be incredible if history did not re- veal that it is the special priyilege of the Tory Party to assail the title to a free use of tongue and pen. As the stupid party, it has always been easier for them to gag an opponent than to answer him. Lord HABTINGTON, of course, holds his chin too high in the air to notice these things; but Lord RIPON is not so unbending, and he is moreover fresh from a humanising experience of government in India. He saw how the poor in our great Dependency suffer through being denied rights and privileges which are common in this country; and it is to his everlasting honour that he did not hesitate to cross swords with the classes in order that he might stand by and be of benefit to the masses. He is the same Lord RIPON at home as abroad; he believes Irishmen suffer from the misgovern- ment of a dominant race; and he would give them self-government in order that they may have a fair chance of becoming prosperous and .con- tented.

Lord Hs.inNnToN has had a good deal to say about the strength of the minority in Ireland but, as Lord RIPON put it, nobody disputes the fact that there is a minority in Ireland opposed to Home Rule. There needs no ghost to come from the grave, or anyone to go to Dublin, to tell us that. The main consideration is—are we to have regard to the minority or to the majority ? Absolute unanimity is impossible, and we should have thought Lord HARTINGTON had too much good sense left to give any sort of countenance to such a doctrine. Absolute unanimity was not attained by the apostles, and it is certainly not likely to be reached by 'either politicians or, peoples. The member for Rossendale always was a bit Whiggish, and now that he is mixing so much with the dry bones of politics, it would seem that he is ossifying into Toryism. It is not forgotten by those who have watched his career, that when the agitation for the extension of the county franchise com- menced, he expressed his doubts as to the wisdom of making the basis of the franchise as wide in Ireland as in England. He gave way on the point when he found himself in a minority. He did not then claim that nothing should be done till the minority could be won over, although we do not , doubt that he could have shown that a large num- ber of the "tremendous personages" who are now opposed to Home Rule were at that time opposed to any extension of the franchise either in Ireland or in England. But he has now taken his stand as champion of the propertied classes, and it seems to be a matter of Course with him to object to sqh an elementary proposition as that involved in the phrase one man one iote," thus showing how Gos- chenised—how much of a Tory he has already became. But, assuming that the commercial and industrial classes are to be taken into account, is Lord HANTINGTON quite sure that he is rendering them real help by opposing Home Rule? What of the statement quoted by Lord RIPON that even the trading community are coming to the conclu- sion that there is no chance in Ireland of a satis- factory state of things until Home Rule is granted? What hope has he of the future of Ire- land under the ever-and-ever Coercion Act? There is not a grain of comfort in his speech for the class in Ireland for whom he professes to be most anxious. There was a time, and that not long since, when Lord HARTINGTON looked to an extended system of local self-government as a remedy for Irish discontent. Now he dreads that; he fears that to increase the authority of the people of Ireland will be to put a weapon in their hands to be used in the struggle for home Rule. Local self-government is to be granted to Eng- land; but it is to be denied to Ireland until the Irish declare that they are comfortable under a policy of Coercion! Was there ever such madness with so little method in it? And what a c9ntrast to the views and declarations of Lord RzPorr! Lord HARTINGTON is plunging, hopelessly plung- ing, in an endless bog; while Lord RIPON goes steadily forward on firm ground in the' full assur- ance that Home Rule will, ere long, be rc;ached as an end achieved, and that it will be a blessing to Ireland; and to the rest of the United Kingdom.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATITRDAY, DECEMBER 10, 1887
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATITRDAY, DECEMBER 10, 1887
"TOUCH AND GO."
It is just as we expected—the Fair Traders are being told to sit still, or they will upset the Unionist boat. Lord Hartington will have hone of it, and he is " boss " of the craft.

The way in which Alderman Burgess tackled the "terriers," at the Warrington Town Council, on Tuesday, was enough to curl their hair; but they were even with him in the end, for, as they say in the vernacular, he had his own hair "combed and Platted."

--- There is another case of smallpox at Sankey Bridges. The Rural Sanitary Authority ought:to bestir themselves, and make arrangements for con- veying the sufferers to the Warrington Hospital. They are, to be sure, making inquiry, but when a house is on fire people as a rule do something more than. make inquiry.

That the Lord Mayor of Dublin should be treated as a first-class prisoner seems to have been gall and wormwood to Mr. Balfour, who has had Mr. Sullivan removed to Tullamore gaol. Here he was placed, on arrival, in an ordinary cell like the meanest criminal. The Irish Secretary is like this Irish cell—anything but first-class.

As soon as •Parliament meets, Mr. W. H. Smith will put a scheme forward for further changes in the rules of procedure. There will be nothing else done, of course. The Tories are like the workman who spends all his time in preparing his tools. Byron says—" good workmen never quar- rel with their tools ;" but the Tories are not good workmen.

It is usually a pleasant time "when the cows come home ; " but it was the reverse of pleasant for Mrs. Barr, of Newton, to see a cow enter her kitchen on Monday, and proceed to demolish the whole of the furniture. It was as bad as the pro- verbial bull in a china shop. But that cow will not trouble the peace of a household any more; it received an effectual remonstrance—in the slaugh- ter-house.

Elizabeth Tither,of St. Helens, has won fame as one who has been convicted no less than 120 times. Brought before the magistrates, on Mon- day, for being drunk and disorderly, she said— " Give me three months this time, please." She evidently likes the inside better than the outside of a gaol, and was quite disappointed when they gave her fourteen days only. We want another Moore to write another "Paradise and the Peri;" but what a Paradise, and what Peril

The Viaduct Institute, Earlestoivn' continues to make good progress. At the annual soiree and distribution of prizes, on Friday evening, it was re- ported'that the increase in the' number of passes, in science subjects, was no less than thirty per cent, in three years. Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., and other speakers referred to the industrial progress which was being made in other countries, and urged the students to prepare themselves for the face that was before them.

It is a pity Mr. Vaughan could not see his way to granting a summons against Mr. Bradlaugh for perjury alleged to have been committed in the 'statements he made as to Lord Salisbury's connection with certain Trafalgar-square meet- ings. The member for Northampton knows what he is about in matters of this kind, and it would have been ,sport for the gods if be could have got Lord Salisbury under cross-exami- nation. Think of Lord Salisbury being shocked at a statement possibly inaccurate ? Why "a Salisbury "--;-what :a a Salisbury."

Mr. Gladstone has addressed an important letter of thanks to Lord Edmund Fitzmaurice. He thinks the speech his lordship made was " pre- cisely and pre-eminently the speech that was wanted." The leader of the Liberal party pro- ceeds to show that the Whigs are breaking with their best traditions in turning aside on the Home Rule question. "It has been a Liberal, not a Tory, aristocracy which has supplied the country with the necessary guidance." Exactly; we want all the help that they can give, but if the Whigs will go wrong, we dare say the Liberals will find their way without them. .

Mr. John Crosfield had a word or two to the point, on Monday night, as to the Fair Trade meeting recently held in Warfington. Mr. John White was he said, the agent of big landlords ; big landlords would get bigger rents if they could put a tax on corn, and Mr. John White would got a bigger screw. 'This was a forcible way of driving the argument home, and it was much enjoyed by the audience. It is a fair illustration of the un- fairness of Fair Trade. Let the case be examined whenever and wherever it is put • it will generally be found that there is a John White somewhere looking out for a bigger screw.

The question of all Owing beer with the Christ - mail dinner at the Workhouse was under discussion at Warrington, on Wednesday, and it was even- tually decided,-by a majority of one, that the in- mates who wished it should have beer. The issue is not a great one, but it involves a question of principle, and, seeing that drink has brought so many of the inmates to the workhouse, it Is -cer- tainly in the right direction to put the evil thing away from them. ,But the majority of the Guar- dians have a different opinion; their idea is that certain paupers will be all the better for a hair of the dog that bit them.

The tide must be out at Fleetwood, for a con- temporary states that the Conservative Club there is "in low water." Joseph Park, who occupies the club premises, has been summoned for non-pay- ment of improvement rates amounting to i 2 13s. 70: This is rather hard, seeing that there is no sign of improvement in the condition of the Fleetwood Conservative Club. Indeed, it was stated, at the Police Court, that the term for which the officers were elected had expired, and, as the club is in the throes of dissolution, it is scarcely kind to say anything about either an improvement rate, or a rate of improvement. •

Lord Hartington objects to Home Rule being brought to the front, seeing that it was not, in 1885, a plank in the Liberal platform. Speaking at •Iliwtenstall, on Saturday, he said :--" I am not going to say anything now about such questions as disostablishment, free education, or a host of other questions upon which we were all so com- pletely united." It would be interesting to know when Mr. Gladstone committed himself to Free Education as a part of the Liberal programme? It was only the other day that Lord Randolph Churchill reproached him for overlooking it. How- ever, it is something to know that" Randy " and " Harty " are two of a party in favour of Free Education.

A LOCAL LAW SlllT.—Crookes ,v. Crookes.--A jury was empanelled at Sheffield on the 2nd initant, be- fore the Under-Sheriff of the County (Mr. E. Gray), at the Law Society's Rooms, to inquire, under a writ of degit, what property George Crookes was possessed of, and to assess the annual value of the same, that it might be delivered to Mrs. Mary Hayden Crookes. of Penketh, the successful plain- tiff in an action against George Crookes.—The Under - Sheriff stated that the plaintiff rel- covered judgment against the defendant for the sum of £127 19s 6d, and it was said the de- fendant had no goods and chattels. But he was in- formed the defendant had certain real estate in Sheffield, and evidence of that would be given, and also of its annual value.—Mrs Crookes, examined by Mr B. Burdekin, junior, solicitor (who appeared on her behalf, and as the agent for Messrs W. D. Jeans and Co., of Warrington, her solicitors), said she now resided at Penketh, near Warrington, and was the wife of George Crookes, who, she believed, lived at Murcia, Spain. He purchased the house No. 20, Nether Green-road. and she considered it was still his property.—Mr John Lister, the tenant of the house, proved that he paid the rent, £l6 a year, to George Crookes, and Mr Francis Dickenson, builder, , stated that he sold the property ti Mr Crookes.— The jury then agreed that the house belonged to George Crookes, and that it was worth .£l6 a year, and the Uunder-Sheriff made an order that the rent be paid to Mrs Crookes until the amount of her judgment Was paid off.

Mataxae.—Along with our not paper, there will be pre.ented to each Of our readers a large sheet Almanac: printed in two colours, and containing a large amount of local and general informatien. It will be adorned with a beautiful view olLathom House in the olden time. Pre- sented NExt Wicax: Order early of newsagents. Examiner- and Almanac—price one penny. The large sale-of the paper 'on Almanac Day affords a special opportunity to advertisera.
MELANC4OLY SUDDEN DEATH AT DITTON.—Mr. Lee, an elderly woman, who resided in Bull-lane, Ditton, died very suddenly shout half-past six on Friday morning. She expired in her daughter's arms.

GAun TRESPASS AT Witiwick. —At. the Warring- ton Occaoional Court-house, on Monday, William Mains, of Eariestown, was charged under a warrant with trespassing in search of game on land at Win-' wick in the occupation of the Iter.Cinonllopwood; oO the 13th February, last. Ile was fined 20s and ,costs, or,..in default, 14 day's imprisonment._

, THE WAEILINGT6N INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPI- TAL.—We learn that the above hospital is not so full as was reported at the meeting of the Sanitary Authority, held at the Workhouse last week. The tents, further, are not full, and the authorities are quite prepared to grapple with any outbreak that may occur in the town. A number of typhus cases have been admitted from Newton.
THE TALK OF THE Towzi.—Howell's Golden Herb Pllls. Advt.

ELEcTioN OF MRILSICY COMMISBTONERS. The following gentlenfen have been elected members ou the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission for the ensuing year :—Mr. William Hayes. merchant, of Runcorn ; Mr. John Simpson, merchant, of Run- corn ; ' and Mr. Thomas Roberts, manufacturing chemist, of Warrington. Mr. Henry Collier was the returning officer, and as the nominations were not in excess of the number of vacant seats, the above- and gentlemen were declared to be elected, the term of office commencing on the Ist of Janu- ary next. BURNING ACCIDENT AT WlDNES.—Martha Con- nellVvaged the, son of Patrick Connelly, S, Dock- street, Widnes, was playing with matches on Mon- day, when he set his shirt on tire, and before it could be extinguished he was burnt very severely on the chest, the right side of the face, and, the right arm. He is now in a critical condition. While asleep before the fire, on Wednesday night, Mr. John Donaldson, a foreman at 'Messrs. Muspratt's, had his clothes set on fire with a spark, and the inftam- triable material was not Bxtlnguished until Mr. Donaldson had sustained severe burns on the legs

REV. JOHN YONGH.—The numerous friends of the Rev. John Yonge, of Wycliffe Church, Warrington, will be glad to learn that, on Monday, he was duly elected as chairman of the Manchester Congrega- tional Board for 1888. This is a position of great honour and responsibility, for Mr. Yonge will not only be called upon to give an inaugural address, but he will have to preside at monthly meetings, gomposed of ministers, professors, and several of the ex-chairmen of the Congregational Union of Eng- land and Wales. We congratulate Mr. Yonge, and wish him health and strength to fill this important office. •

WIDNES FREE PUBLIC LIBUART.—The monthly meeting of the committee of this institution was held on Friday afternoon at the Town Hall. Mr H. Wade Deacon presided, and there were also present Dr O'Keeffe, Messrs J. Morrison, E. Carey, S. Sadler, W. Sadler, J. P. Allen (Local Board cleric), and Miss Proctor (librarian). The Librarian reported that the total number of books issued during the month was 3,487, an average daily issue of 211, and an increase of 151 over the number issued last month. The total attendance at the Library was 13,003, an aver- age daily attendance of 500. It was agreed that a number of old illustrated journals be given to the Infectious Diaeases Hospital. • CONCERT AT Ruscon:v.—On Tuesday evening the Mill-brow Military Band. gave their first popular concert of the season before a large and 'highly ap- preciative audience. The programme was a most attractive one, and was rendered by such popular artists as Miss Bonfilun. Mr. Coope, Mr. Harry Collins. the unique City Banjo Band, and the Mill- brow Band. A novel feature of the concert was the playing of the "City Banjo Band," every one of ' their pieces being well received. The Mill-brow Military Band opened the concert with• a splendid performance of Balfe's overture to the Bohemian Girl," and during the evening acquitted them- selves admirably. Mr. W. B. Kay and Mr. J. K. Cane shared the honors as accompanists. PILM are eured bY Howell's Golden Herb Pills. of 0.11 Medi- cine CON,CERT AT BITAToN'WOOD.—On Tuesday evening a miscellaneous concert was given in the school- room, Biatonwood;in connection with St. Michael's Church, and in aid.of the church funds. The Rev. H. Wilson presided, and there was a good audience. The programme, a well selected one, Was contribu- ted to by the Burtonwood String Band, under the conductorship of Mr. Massey, Mr. Baxter (Warring- ton), Mr, J. Mercer (Warrington), Misb Horton, Mr. Taylor (Warrington), Miss Talbot (Manchester), andl Mr. Greenhouse. The evening's entertainment was brought to a close by a comic sketch, entitled "Advertising for a servant," in which Mr. J. Mercer land Miss Talbot took part. Mr. G.Riley accompanied throughout. The concert was a great success, and Mr. Mercer, who organised the affair, is to be con- gratulated. INDIOES TIOICURED by one box of Howell'e Golden Herb 1 Pills.—Advt.

RITNCORN POLICE COORT.—On Thursday, before Major Hazlehurst, Mary Ann Walsh, a young woman, was charged under a vdrrant with having used violent and obscene language on the 14th April, and on the evidence of P.C. Kettle she was ordered to pay £l, or go to gaol for 14 days.—The same constable also proved a charge of begging against John Walsh who was sentenced to 14 days hard labour. SODDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—At five minutes to nine on Tuesday morning a young man named John Rigby, belonging to Bootle, and employed as an engine driver on the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway,went into one of the company's closets at the Widnes station. About twenty minutes afterwards a porter went into the same closet, and found the unfortunate young man on the floor in a fit. He was at once taken to a waiting- room, where he was attended by Dr. Saul, and subse- gd i ently removed to his lodgings n Witt-road, where he died at six o'clock in the evening. Deceased had been unwell for some time. ALLEGED POACHING AT BOLD.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, John Middlehurst, who is employed in St. Helens, was charge'd with having used a gun for the purpose of killing game.—Mr Swift, of St. Helens, appeared for the prosecution, and stated that on the night of the 28th November the defendant was the guest of Philip Locock, of Moathouse Farm, Bold, and he went out with a gun for the purpose, it was said, of shooting pigeons; but he was observed to shoot at a pheasant in , a preserve belonging to Mr Tipping, whose farm ad- joined Mr Locock's.—The defendant said he was shoot- ing at a rabbit, and had no intention of shootinga pheas- ant.—The case was dismissed, but the Bench pointed out that the Excise could prosecute him for carrying 44 gun without a license. SALE or Won't AT WIDNES.—In connection with Milton Congregational Church, a sale of work was opened in MalMs Temperance Hall, on Thursday afternoon. Al- though the weather was ef the most inclement, charac- ter, a good company assembled to witness Mrs. Brock, wife of Mr. John Brock, J.P., perform the opening cere- mony. After the usual devotional services, the Rev. R. G. Hughes, the pastor, explained that the object of the 'sale was to raise the slim of £5O, which amount was re- quired in a.ddition.4o what had been contributed in church, to meet the annual expenses, ministerial and otherwise, of the church.—Mrs. Brock then gracefully declared the bazaar open, and in doing so congratulated the ladies ivho had been working so busily for many months on the success, so far, of their labours. They must remember that old saying that a little help was worth a vast amount of pity. (Applause.)—Mr. Brock also addressed a few genial remarks to those present.— On the motion of the Rev. R. G. Hughes, seconded by , Mr. C. Whitfield, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Brock •, and on the motion of the Rev. D. Davies, seconded by the Rev. Hugh Owen, the services of those who had been engaged in managing the bazaar were heartily acknowledged:—The Rev. R. Burden and the Rev. E. Nall also took part in the proceedings.—Articles of the usual character were displayed for sale in the usual manner on three stalls, and there was besides a refreshment stall. During the evening a concert and other entertainments were given for the amusement of visitors.

TRANSFERS AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Major Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handley granted the transfers of. various licences. • THE 800 SCARE AT WIDNES.---At Widnes Petty Ses- sions on Thursday, the following persons were each fined 5s and costs for allowing their dogs to be at large : Esther Singleton, butcher, Victoria-road; Charles Clif- ton. greengrocer, Waterloo-road; Charles Evans, Bank-. street; and William Twist. , WRECX OF A FLAT OUTWARD 116IIND.—A flat named the Mary Jane, laden with coal, was being towed down the river from Widnes late on Timidity night, when the tow rope snapped, and the flat drifted away. A sudden squall coming on, she heeled over and sank in the Sloyne. The I crew managed to escape in a small boat. Ilzoom.—llefore Mr. T. Sutton Timmins and Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes Petty •Sessions, on Thursday' an old man named William Tone was charged with begging from house to house in Birchfield-road on the previous day.--He was sentenced to seven days' imprisonment. Wastots POINT WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—OR Tues- day the schoolroom adjoining the Wesloyau Chapel at Weston Point was crowded to ts utmost capacity, the .occasion being the inauguration of a band of hope in connection with the Sunday school. Mr. J. W. Wood- land, of Runcorn, occupied the chair. A collection was made at the olnse.

Tna Rounzur Imola A RUNCORN BOATMAN.—Thomas azden and William Dugniore Won charged, before Mr. W. H. Higgin,- Q.C., at the Salford Hundred essions, en Tuesday, with receiving a horse, halfer, and bridle, the • property of Thomas . Bellfield, boatman, of, Runcorn. After hearing Bellfield's evicienc4. the magistrates AC- quitted both prisoners. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—At Whines Petty. Sessions, on Thursday, John Tobin was charged with having, on the 23th November; committed a broach of the peace in Water-street. He was also charged with having, at one o'clock that (Thursday) morning, slept in the chemical works of Messrs. Hutchinson.—For the "sleeping out" the prisoner was seritenced to*7 days' hard labour, and on the other charge he was ordered to be bound over. WIDNES "GYMNASIUM Hannums.,-,-Saturday being a glo. rious day, the members of this club enjoyed an excellent spin across the country. Leaving the Milifield Inn at 345 p.m., the party started towards the Bongs, then on past the Horns to the Bold Arms, and then to Clock- face. From thence they proceeded to Marshall's Cross,. and then turned for home. A capital race ensued down Peelhouse-lane, Cowley leading most of the way, but he was eventually beaten by McMahon and Franklin, Roscoe, Lee, Brocklehurst, Kershaw, Brown, Jones, and Etheridge finishing in the order in which they are named. WIDNES CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.— I The members of the juvenile section of the Widnes branch I of the Church of England Temperance Society gave a concert in the National Schools, Waterloo-road, on Thurs- day evening. • There was a crowded audience, the Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar, presiding. The Chairman, in his opening remarks, alluded to the importance-of chil- dren being trained in principles of total abstinence: At the conclusion a vote of thanks was accorded Mr. and Mrs. Farratit for their tramming of the,. children. The . proceeds of the concert are to be devoted to the fund for the juveniles' annual Christmas treat._ • AtLEOED ASSAULT ON A BAILIFF AT 1/ ESTON. OR Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, William Didsbury, a young man, was charged with assaulting Joseph Foulkes. The complainant said he was a bailiff, and on Monday I afternoon, the 28th November, he went • to a house at Weston to distrain for rent.. Immediately he entered the defendant's wife struck him on the head with a poker, and said she would find a man that would put him out. I In about half an hour the defendannt Came. in, turned up his shirt sleeves, and said "Now, its your life or mine." He then -*seized hold of him (witness) by the neck and put hint out of the house.—Theslefenclant stated that when he got to the house the complainant was sat in a corner in a beastly state of drunkenness.— The complainant called a boy; who confirmed his evi- dence, and P.C. Breeze, who said he saw Foulkes about half-past five. Although he then smelled of intoxicating liquor, he was not drunk.—The Beneh dismissed the

MAD DOG AT RUNCORN.—ALARMING STATEMENT.—At Runcorn Petty sessions, on Monday, Superintendent Hollingsworth applied to the magistrates (Major Hazle- hurst and Mr. James Handley), for an order under the Dogs' Act, compelling the owners of dogs, to keep their animals in confinement or under proper control. He made this application, he said, in consequence of a dog that was destroyed in Runcorn on Friday last, and which a veterinary surgeon, who had made a post modem examination, certified was suffering from rabies. The dog, before it was destroyed, had either bitten or been in contact with 14 dogs to the knowledge of the police, and perhaps with many more. Under a section of the Infectious Diseases (Animals) Act, the owners of these dogs had been cautioned to keep them in confinement, and be (the Superintendent) pow asked that all dogs should be confined for a period of three months. The mad dog had also been in contact with throe children, but serious results were not anticipated. Themagistrates had power to direct that all dogs should be led when out. I—The Bench, after a brief consultation, granted the order.—Superintendent Hollingsworth said it had been I thought that if a dog had merely a strap over its mouth it was mpzzled, but the police would take prOceeding,s against any person who allowed his dog to be at large insecurely muzzled. A DISTURBER AT RUNCORN SMAIATIONARKY CITADEL.— At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Major Harlehurst and Mr. James Handley, Ralph Bate, a boat- man, was charged with having, on the 27th November, been guilty of riotous or indecent behaviour in the Salvation Army Citadel, and also with having assaulted Peter Jones.--.Yones stated that he was a labourer for Mr Ralph Bate, farmer, and was, a soldier in the Salvation Army. On the day in question he was appointed to keep order inthe Citadelduring, diyineservice. About half-past three the defendant entered, and sat down with his hat on and commenced to call out. Malcolm Jones asked him to behave himself, stroked his hair down, and took off his hat. Before Malcolm Jona had got half-a-dozen yards away the defendant said "Wait until the comes up again and I Will give him a smack in theteeth." The complainant then asked the defendant to be quiet, and he replied "Not for a-- like You." and gave complainant a violent blow on the face .—Malcolm Jones, a shipwright, gave corroborative evidence.—Mary. Gib- son, a domestic servant, also corroborated the com- plainant's evidence.—Mr. Knowles then addressed , the Pouch for the defence.—Charles Gatley, a labourer, who said he was not a friend of the defendant's, but had been in his company in an ale-house. and Geo. Pye, a labourer at the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company's Works, gave evidence bearing out Mr. Knowles' state- ment.—The Bench convicted the defendant on both charges, and ordered him to pay a total of £2 25., or go to gaol for .a month, ROBBERIES AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. if. Gaskell. junr., and Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes Police Court on Monday, two youths named James Dwyer, of 47, Sutton's-lane, and John Carroll, of Warrington, were chargedawith having stolen from the fiat "Toiler," two vials an one pair of boots the property of Walter Atherton, of 102, Terrace-road; Widnes. It was stated that the flat was secured in the Canal on the evening of the 16th ult., and next morning the cabin was found to have been broken. open and the articles named stolen.—On the 20th ult., the prisonors were arrested on suspicion of being the culprits, and Dwyer in answer to the charge said he and Carroll left Hutchinsons works where they were em- ployed during the night, and Carroll broke into the Cabin and took the coats and boots. Carroll also made a statement, laying the blam4 on Dwyer. A coat was afterwards recovered from a heap of slack coal at Mews. Hutchinson's works.—As both prisoners had been previously convicted they were committed to the quarter Sessions for trial—James McGrew, aged 10, ' of 32, Wellington-st.. was charged with having stolen two pigs feet, worth 7d., from the shop of John Collins, Waterloo-road. On Friday night, P.C. Evans saw the prisoner come from the shop with the feet in his hand. Immediately the boy saw the constable he threw the feet into OA street and ran away. Next day he was appre- hended, and in reply to the charge said "I was hungry." The prisoner's mother inferthed the magis- trates that the boy had no need to steal, and he was ordered to receive 6 strokes with the birch rod.—Daniel Clay, aged 10 years, of 38, Eleanor-st., pleaded guilty to having stolen from a stall in the market, six dolls value is. 6d. the property of James Watterson, of 8 Mersey- road. He was ordered to receive four strokes with the birch rod. RUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There were pre- 'sent Col. Ashton, (Chairman), Revs. J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron. Stockes, W. Whitlow, Campkin, Parr, I3randreth, Hadfield, Turner, I Hamilton, Wallington; W. H. Linaker, (assistant I clerk).—A Delayed Account: A letter was read from the Local Government Board in reply to a request for sanction to pay an account sent by Mr. Littler, of Fred- sham, for repairs, &c., to the Ship-st. sewer, Frodsham. They stated that as more than 12 months had elapsed since the date on which the account becime due the time had expired within which the Board could have issued an order to extend the time for the payment.— In answer to a question the Assistant Clerk said that the Authority had no power to pay the,account. The account had passed through the hands of Mr. Farring- ton, the inspector, but it had been delayed in some manner or other.—Mr. Farrington said he did not know how the delay had been caused. He always passed the accounts on. He would however see Mr. Littler in order to learn, if pOssible, what had been the cause of the delay.—lt wits decided that a copy of the letter from the Local Government Board, should be forwarded to Mr. Littler.—The Accomodation of Ship Canal Navvies: Mr. Farrington stated that it was intended to raise in the Authority's district a large quantity of huts, in connection with the Ship Canal. He wished to know whether these huts should be dealt with as dwelling- houses, and insist upon a supply of water being made to them. He mentioned that because in some former cases in which huts had been built for navvies, they afterwards were made into dwelling-houses, and it was possible that these huts might be dealt with in the same way.—lt was decided that the huts should be regarded as dwelling-houses, and that a copy of the Authority's regulations should be sent to the Ship, Canal Company, and also to Mr. Walker, the contractor for the canal. —This was all tue basineas of public interest.

, ACCIDENT AT Ittescoax.—On Monday morning a boy namedNewsome, who lives with his parents at 41, Shaw- street, was playing in the street when he slipped and • fell. Two of• his companions tumbles], upon him, and his leg becoming twisted beneath him, he suthined a • fracture of the thigh. Dr. MacLennan was called in. . and set the injured limb, and the boy is now progressing favourably. Ltenossa. OlciAnni r. Widnes : This match was played at Hough Green, on Saturday. Ogden and Hal- sail faced at three o'clock, and Kempsey getting the ball rushed to the Widnes goal and passed to Carter, who shot the first goal for the visitors. After some give-and- take play, Oldham increasedtheirscore tofivegoalsbefore half-time, Widnes being one. In the second half .Oldham had all the best of the play, and won by eleven goals to three. Wasrost WESLEYAN CHAPEL—In aid of the organ fund of this place of worship a service of song entitled" John Wesley was given by the choir on Monday. evening. Mr. T. Handley occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance. The narrative was read by the Rev. Geo. Wood, and the service was rendered additionally inter- esting by the singing of old Methodist tunes. Mr. Jas. Handley, J.P., and Mr. James Ball presided at the organ, and Master Handley, junr., of Garston, and Mr. J. Ford ably assisted with the violin and cornet respectively.. Mr. R. Norman gave an amusing and instructive account of early Methodism in the village. WOUNDED WITH A BREAKFAST CAN AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Police Court on Monday, Thomas Price, labourer, of Regent-st., Runcorn, was again brought up charged with having Ign the 26th uk., in Church-st., Widnes, unlawfully wounded a labourer named Michael Lever, also of 'Runcorn, by striking . him on the lrad with a breakfast can.—Dr..Nealan certified that' the in- jured man was unable to attend court, and the prisoner was remanded until Thursday. The as prisoner was again brmght up on Thursday, but the injured matt was still unable to appear, he was again remanded. He was liberated on bail. ' FIRE AT A RUNCORN PAWNBROKER'S SHOP. Shortly before twelve o'clock on Monday night, Mr. Weldon, the lessee of the Theatre Royal, informed a constable that the chimney of the pawnbroker's shop belonging to Mr. Arthur Davies was on fire: P.S. Woolley and P.C. Brew attempted to arouse the inmates, but being unable to do , so, the officers broke open the door and found that the pledge office was on fire.-- Steps were at once taken for ' extinguishing the flames; and after the arrival of the ' fire brigade the tire was put out in a few minutes. A large number of pledges were consumed and damaged, and part of the wood work of the room was destroyed. The damage amounts to about £lOO. Rut:coax BOOM OF Gusamsxs.—The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the workhouse, But- ton, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present., Col. Ashton, (chairman), Revs. J. Lockwood and J. W. N. Turner, Messrs. Mclntyre. Aaron, Stokes, W. Whitlow, . Campkin, Parr, Brandreth, Hadfield; Turner, Hamilton, Wallington. (Dice, Hewitt, Fisher, Lightburn, Jackson, and Forster; W. H. Linaker, (assistant clerk).— Weston. School • Committee : Mr. Aaron said that the Weston School Committee had lost four of its inembhll4, and the committee requested him to propose that the Rev. Mitchell Wood, the Rev. J: H. NVileockson. Mr. J. Roberts, and Mr. W. Armstrong, be addtxl, to the com- mittee.—Mr. Stokes seconded this proposal which was agreed to.— Appointment of Nurse: It was stated that ; there had been twenty-three applicants for the vacant post of wotkhouse nurse, and of these, four appeared before the Board by request, and ultimately Miss Elizabeth Harrison, of Manchester, was appointed.— Christmas Treat : A collection was made in the Board- , room in order to provide a treat for the workhouse ; children at Christmas, and it was stated that a. sum of between 20s. and 30s. had been realised.—The rest of the business was formal.

A VIOLENT WIDNES Woitsii.—At Widnes Police Conrt. on Monday, before Mr. H. Gaskell, junr., Bridget Bran- non, an elderly woman, of 4, Elizabeth-street, was brought up on remand charged with having, on the 26th ult., unlawfully wounded Mary Treacy, wife pf John Tracey, of Water-street. In the evening of the day named Mrs. Treacy went to the house of the prisoner for the purpose of collecting some .money the latter's' son owed her. The prisoner, after using some abusive ex- pression, threw a quantity of cold water upon Mrs. Treacy, who then left thehouse, followed by the prisoner. On the way down the street the prisoner pulled her clogg off her right foot, and running up to Mrs. Treacy struck her upon the forehead. In guarding herself from fur- ther blows Mrs. Treacy was also injured on the hand and elbow. She, however, succeeded in wresting the clog from her assailant, and subsequently handed the ugly weapon over to Sergeant Strickland, who arrested the , prisoner. In answer to the charge the prisoner then said • Maybe I did strike her with the clog. I had the clog In my hand. Some one took the clog from me'. I don't know who it was ."—Mary Tarpey, of 12, Elizabeth-street, proved the assault, and D. Hutchinson said Mrs. Treacy 'visited his surgery about eight o'clock on the night in question. She was suffering from a contused wound on the right side of the forehead, the wound penatrating to the bone and leaving quite bare a portion of the skull. He stitched the wound. There was at one time great danger of erysipelas setting in, and Mrs. Treaey was not yet out of danger.—The prisoner, who had now nothing .to say, was committed to Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. She was allowed out on bail in her husband's recognizances of £4O and two sureties of £2O each.

div.head: ItT.TNCOILN. SCHOOL BOA.R.D.
div.p: ItT.TNCOILN. SCHOOL BOA.R.D.
The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present Dr. McDougall, Messrs. liaison, Beckett, Lake, and Moss (clerk).
UNANIMITY WA4TED.

Upon the minutes of the ordinary and special Board meetings coming up for confirmation. Dr. McDougall pointed out that when the amendment that Miss Kennan ,be appointed mistress at Mill Brow School was put to the vote, as a substantive resolution, Mr. Beckett and Mr. Frith did not vote. Ile therefore contended that the resolution was carried unanimously.—Mr. liaison: It is carried unanimously. There is no contradiction.—Mr. Beckett: Bet you • cannot call it carried unani- mously.—Mr. Lake: Put it tienf. eon.—Dr. Mc- Dougall: Not having voted against it, they cer- tainly agreed with the resolution. Had Mr. Bec- kett and Mr. Frith wished to carry out their oppo- sition to the resolution, they would have voted against it.—lt having been entered upon the minutes that the gentlemen named did not vote they were passed as correct. THE LATE FATHER FENNELLY.

The Clerk said he had the sad duty to perform of reporting the death of the Rev. Fatl.er Fennelley. He had received a letter from the Rev. Felber Boa- win, of Ditton Hall, in which that gentleman said "Allow me to render you most heartfelt thanks for the very kind and charitable sympathy you have manifested for our common friend, the late Father Fennelley. I would beg you also to convey to the gentlemen of the Runcorn School Board the assur- ance of his sincerest gratefulness for their 'esteemed presence at the funeral of the deceased, and to ex- press to them how highly the Catholic community of St. Edward's appreciate the honour done their departed pastor by the attendance of his associateS of the School Board.'—The Chairman said he was sure that all the members of the Board regretted the removal of Father Fennelley from amongst them. He proposed that a letter of condolence be forwarded to the brother of the deceased and to the Catholic Bishop of Shrewsbury.—Dr. McDougall seconded the motion which was carried unarn- mously.—On the suggestion of Mr Beckett, a special meeting for the purpose of filling up the vacancy was fixed for Tuesday next. Mr. Beckett gave no- tice that he would then move a resolution.
BAITING MR. BECKETT: CONTRADICTORY STATEMENTS.

• Before the minutes of the committees were con- sidered, Dr McDougall moved the adjournment of the Board for the purpose of calling Mr Beckett's attention to a speech he made at the Board on the 12th November, and a statement he afterwards Published in one of the newspapers. In his speech, Mr Beckett said Mr Moulton, who was now head- master at the Board School, had been the means of gaining the excellent grant in connection with the Brunswick school. On the 26th ult. a letter was published from Mr Fitton, muter at that school.— Mr Beckett: I don't know why these personal matters should enter into thebusiness of the Board. —Dr McDougall said this was a matter of material importance, and he should proceed with what he had to say, and give Mr Beckett an opportunity of saying which was the correct statement. One statement said that Mr Moulson had been the means of earning the excellent grant at Brunswick school, and the other that he had been the means "to a certain extent."-Mr. Beckett contended that he used the expression to a cgrtain extent, but he exonerated the reporter from all blame, as it was almost im- possible for any reporter to take a correct account of his speech because of the continual interruptions of Dr. McDougall.—Dr. McDougall said he believed that Mr. Beckett might have one thing in his mind and say another.—Mr. Beckett replied that he had not intended to say anything further upon this question. It was perfectly wrong to raise such a point for the purpose of danpg- ing the character of anyone whatever.--2-Dr. McDougall said he should only be too pleased if IMr. Beckett could reconcile the two statements.— Mr. Beckett: Dr. McDougall wishes to put every- body else in order, but he won't remain in order himself. Mr. Beckett then maintained that he used the words "to a certain extent"• in connection with Mr. Moulton's work at Brunswick School.— After further discussion, the Chairman said if any statement by Mr. Beckett formed the opinions of the members of the Board,
and influenced the votes they gave, he thought it was highly to Mr. Beckett's credit. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—The subject then dropped.. TRH RE-AARANGEMENT OF THE STAFF. _

Dr. McDougall moved the -c-o-nfirmaii-o-n- of the minutes of a meeting of the Schoql Attendance Com- mittee, held on November 15th, which recorded the removal of Miss Simkin from the Mixed School to be assistant mistress in the girls' school, her salary to be increased from ZIO to £5O. Dr. McDougall pointed out that this change was recommended be- fore the appointment of the mistress to Mill Brow School took place, and that, therefore, the state- ment circulated that Miss Simkin was thrown out of employment was not a fact.—Mr. Lake seconded the motion, and the minutes were adopted.—lt was also resolied to have personal interviews with three of the applicants for the post of assistant master at Greenway-road School.
A CONTRACT.
The contract for the stationery of the Board was secured by the executors of Mr. Charles Ger- rard.
A REPLY TO MR. MIME.

Dr. McDougall moved the confirmation of the minutes of a committee held on November 15th, at which Miss Simkin was appointed assistant mis- tress at the girls' school, at a salary of £5O peryear, an increase of .£lO a year. The doctor pointed out that Miss Simkin was given this improved position before the appointmont of head mistress to Mill Brow School, and she still held the position. An impression had got abroad that Miss Simkin had been treated badly, and Mr. John Simpson had written a letter in which he drew a most heart- rending picture. They all knew how kind, how generous, Mr. Simpson was, and how a matter of this kind would touch his heart, He thought Mr. Simpson had been very much like the good Samaritan who went down to Jericho, and found himself amongst thieves. Mr. Simpson said that at a committee meeting four out of six members were in favour of Miss Simkin's appointment.—The Chairman said it had been decided that what was done was informal, and he thought it would not be discussed.—Dr. McDougall continued to say that the letter stated Miss Simkiu had lost the chance of another good situation, that she lived with a widowed mother, and was now thrown out of a situa- tion altogether. The fact was Miss Simkin was not out of employment, and would not be out of employment, and he hoped she would con- tinue in the situation which the Board considered most suitable for her.—Mr. Lake seconded the motion. With reference to Mr. Simpson's statement that four out of the six members at the informal meeting were in favour of the transfer of Miss Simkin to Mill Brow School, at that time he was a supporter of that course, and his reason for that was that he saw no other mode of retaining her services. But so far as four members agreeing to that, one of them said he did not think it was the best plan, and that it might be improved upon, therefore Mr. Simpson was quite wrong in saying that four out of the six members were in favour of that view. (Hear, hear.) As that scheme proved abortive altogether, they had a right to discuss the whole matter and take the course they had adopte4.—The Clerk said that, with the Board's permission, he wished to ex- plain that he certainly did not give Miss Simkin any promise that she would be appointed to Mill Brow School. All he did was to tell her, when she asked him, that the.members were favourably dis- posed towards her, and that probably she might ob- tain the appointment, but that, of course, he could not say what might happen, as nothing was settled. —Mr. Imison supported the passing of the minutes, and, however painful it might have been to the rival candidates to have so much prominence, he could not hold himself responsible for it—it was owing to the candidates' own friends. Mr. Simpson's letter, which had been so mercilessly dissected, was headed:—
Justice standeth afar off,

Equity cannot enter." He thought the most appropriate words would have been those of lagoin " Othello" "As I umfess, it is my nature's plague To spy into abuses ; and oft my jealousy Shapes faults that are not." (Laughter.) Mr.. Imison proceeded to contest the statements of Mr. Simpson as to Miss Simkin's qualifications being equal to Mi.ss Ken- nan's, and as to the respective attendances at Widnes and Runcorn Board Schools. The Chairman said he was glad to hear the re- marks made about its being painful to the rival candidates to discuss their qualifications or dis- qualifications in a public manner in that way. It had been a thing that he himself had always avoided. (Hear, hear.) He considered it was un- just to the candidates to dismiss the merits and de- merits of the rival candidates in the manner the Board had done. With regard to Miss Simkin, the Board thought they were doing justice to her ser- vices and her merits by promoting her as first assis- tant teacher in the senior girls' school—(hear, hear) at a salary of £5O per annum. So that they would see that she gained by position and by stipend in that promotion. For himself he failed to see why she or her friends, by service or by merits could claim that she should be appointed head-mistress of the Mill Brow Schools. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were passed and the meeting con- cluded.

div.head: ALLEGED PERJURY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ALLEGED PERJURY AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday. before Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Police Court, George Rigby, gamekeeper to Sir Rd. Brooke, Bart., was charged with having on the 17th Oct, at Runcorn. falsely and maliciously committed corrupt perjuryits a witness in an action against Jno. Shelton and Philip Handley for poaching.—Mr. J. W. Knowles, of Widnes, appeared for the prosecu- tors, and ,Mr. Cartwright, of Liverpool, appeared for Rigby.—Mr. Knowles stated that Shelton was a brickmaher, and lived in Bold-street. and Handley was a labourer, and lived in Heath-road. On Mon- day the 17th October they were charged in that court with having on the sth October entered upon certain land in the occupation of John Ackerley at , Halton, for the purpose of taking game. They were each fined 40s and costs, or, in, default a mqnth's hard labour. Shelton paid the fine, but Handley went to prison in default of payment. The perjury alleged was that Rigby swore in that court that he was going along .Astmoor-lane at a few minutes to nine on the evening of Wednesday, the sth October, and watched four men, amongst whom were Handley and Sheltor, leap over a fence and walk to the end of Haddock's Wood. He fetched the assistance of a man named Fitton, and they went tower the men. Three made their es- cape along the wood side, but he captured a man named Lydiate, who was afterwards fined 40s and costs. On the spot were found several coats, nets and pegs, and a quantity of stones. Rigby, before the magistrates, stated that he saw Handley and Shelton at the wood. With regard to Handley it would be proved that at the time in question he was drinking in the Moulders' Arms, Heath-road, and was there until closing time. Five witnesses would prove that statement. As to Shelton he was drinking in the Barley Mow Hotel, Church-4reet, until about eight o'clock, when he left. He ar- rived home at half-past eight, having spoken to several persons on the way. and went to bed at about nine o'clock. Lydiate who had been convic- ted of poaching that evening, would swear that neither Handley nor Shelton were of the com- pany, which was composed of himself, Joseph Rowlands, Thomas Astbury, and John Rowlands.— The solicitor's statement was supported by about fourteen witnesses, who were cross-examined by Mr. Cartwright to show that their ei idence as to the data and time was not to be relied upon.—Mr. Cart- wright, in addressing his worship for the defence, pointed out that a great portion of the evidence brought forward that day was heard by the magis- trates who convicted the men, and that conviction was recorded and in reality a bar to this action. They had brought forward the universal poachers' I defence of an alibi, and Mr. Cartwright having for- cibly dissected the evidence, contended that it was la case of manufactured evidence, and that there was nettling to show that wilful and corrupt perjury had been committed. —Without a moment's hesita- tion. his worship dismissed the case.—The summons against Fitton was then withdrawn by Mr. Knowles
