div.head: T,HE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMIIER 10. 1887
div.p: T,HE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMIIER 10. 1887
GREAT LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT
WARRINGTON.

SPEECHES BY THE MARQUIS OF RIPON. MR. JOHN CROSFIELD, AND OTHERS. A Liberal demonstration was on Monday evening held in the Public Hall, Warrington, at which the principal speaker was the Most Hon. the Marquis of Ripon. The demonstration was in every respect a great success, the attendance being in excess of the accommodation afforded by the hall, while those who did obtain admittance were unanimous and enthusiastic in their endorsement of the Liberal sentiments of the speakers. The doors of the hall were thrown open a littie before seven o'clock, and although the chair was not to be taken till a quar- ter to,eight, there was at once a great influx.of peo- ple, and the sitting • space in the gallery was very quickly filled. The interior of the hall had been very prettily and appropriately embellished by Mr. John Danbobbin. Around the front of the gallery were the mottoes, in conspicuous letters, "A hearty welcome to the Marquis of Ripon," "Free Trade," and Home Rule." High up on the end of the hall. opposite the platform, were the now famous words. "Remember Mitchelstown." and on the sides of the hall the. mottoes "Long live our President" and 'Crosfield for ever." A. novel feature of the deco- rations were the words "God bless our Grand Old Man," hanging, as it were, in mid air, over the head of the chairman. A number of beautiful plants were ranged along the front of the platform, and, altogether, the decorations were such as to do credit to their designer. During the long period of wait- ing several tunes were finely rendered on the organ by Mr. Thomas Mather. Mr. E. Wright also contri- buted to the harmony by the singing of "The Pilot of the State," the 'audience joining in the chorus. The only disappointment of the evening was caused by the announcement that Mr. McMinnies and Mr. Brunner, M.P., were unable to attend, the former through illness, and the latter by an accident to his wife. In the absence of Mr. McMinnies the chair was taken by Mr. P. A. Roberts. There was a very large platform of gentlemen, amongst whom were The Most Hon. the Marquis of Ripon, K.G. ; Alder- men John Crosfield, Holmes, Burgess; Councillors Greening, J. S. Green, G. Blackhurst, J. Barker, F. Dixon, J. H. Fleming, H. Roberts; Miss Crosfield, Miss J. Crosfield, Miss Dickson, the Misses Crosfield Mr. A. H. Crosfield, Mr. J. J. Crosfield; the Revs. J. Yonge, W. R. Parry, W. Brookes, J. W. Varley, E. Jackson, W. Graham; Fathers Thompson, Fianna- gen, Brown; Drs. Smith, Gornall, Fox; and Messrs. D. Garnett, A. G. Symonds (National Reform Union) J. Winser, Thomas Hall, jun.. C. S Burgess, R. Dut- ton (Lymm), A. Browne, Thomas Morrie, P. Cald- well, T. Grime. D. Dutton, E. Plinston, Wm. H. Bay- ley, Wm. Roberts, F. Loughlin (president of local branch of National League), Whitehead (secretary of local branch of National League), W. Mallard, Connor, James Mason, George Evans, To3arolt Salt, Samuel Jones, William Furness, C. Furness, M. Lyons, James Winstanley, C. Simpaon, J Mullins, Joseph Allainson. J. H. Norbary, William Walker, Jabez Plinston, Charles Plinston, William Gleave, W. Y. Lawton, John Gandy, George Weaver, T. Barber, H. H. Dutton, H. E. Roscoller, Thomas Birchall, John Williams, James Bowcocic, John Evans, George Beard, Hayward, John Sutton, C. Jackson ,Holmes, James Strange, A. G. Webster, P. T. Winskill, John Bonnell, George Holford, T. B. Carter, Richard Roberts, S. Kenyon. George Plump- ton, Job Swalee, John Podmore, W. C. Baines, T. Dinwiddie, William Taylor, R. G. Henshall, J. Laverock, 'F. Jenkins, John Ogden, R. Dowd, J. Summersgill, W. A. Bowden, E. Wallington, M. Chambers, George Parr, Jos. Mounfield, J. W. Hall, Henry Thornton. Charles. Twiss, E. Ford, Edward Plinston, N. Legge, A. H. Rathbone, David Rankin. A. F. Dixon, J. S. Garland, Samuel Down, William MAC, silCnek, f. J, sATldtrson, C. Sudlow, tte. The Cteintitile called upon Mr. Henry Ro'serts, the secretary, to read some letters of apology. Mr. ROMARTS said he was very sorry to have to apolo- gise lathe first instance for the absence of their presi- dent, Mr. McMinniell, who wrote as follows :—" I regret exceedingly that tile kate of my health will not permit me to be present at your meetini, on the sth. I sheuld have been glad to join with you in ebtidemning the Irish policy of the present Government, so disgraceful to Eng- land and so injurious to Ireldnd. I hope you will have a successful meeting, and add one more powerful protest against the wretched and worn-out policy which is doing so much to prevent the real union of the two eountries." Mr. Brunner, M.P., who should have been there that night, was prevented from being present owing to an accident to his wife, and wrote as follows from Rome "It is with the deepest regret I find myself unable to be present at your meeting on the sth December. We cannot reach home before the evening of the 10th. It would have given me ""J.Wure to do honour to Lord Ripon, for he is thoroughly in earnest; he never strikes below the belt, like so many of Mr. Chamberlain's gen- tlemanly friends. (Laughter.) I sincerely trust that Warrington will take the first opportunity that offers itself to get rid of its member. Your motto should be 'Down with Kieg Grog and up with Home Rule.'" (Laughter and loud cheers.) —Mr. William Crosfield wrote as follows: "I have to be in London on Monday. else I should have been present at your meeting to add my support to your demand for a change in the conduct of the present ad- minstration with regard to Ireland. While the recog- nised leaders of their people are being pounced upon and imprisottd with a vindictiveness which savours of personal spite, it behoves us all, whilst freedom is left to us to speak out for the cause of right and liberty. (Cheers). I should have wished under other circum- stances to have been with you to honour your noble visitor, and thank him for the brave service which his lordship is rendering to the oppressed." (Cheers)-140- ters of apology for non-attendance Incl also been re- ceived from-31r. Zito Armitage, Mr. C. M. Percy, Wigan; Councillor John Brown, Mr. F. W. Monks, Mr. 4.1_4. Reynolds, Mr. J. A. Swanwiek, Lymm ; Rev. G. E. Young, Mr. John Platt, and Mr. Robert Garnett., The CH lIRSIAN, who was received with applause, said they had heard—and he knew with a considerable amount of regret—of the absence of Mr. McMinnies and of the cause of that absence. (Hear, hear.) He ought to have been in that chair, and they in Warrington knew what an excellent chairman he made. (Cheers.) They in Warrington had watched the career of the Marquis of Ripon in India, and they welcomed the happy changes he had been the means of effecting in that country. (Applause,) It was only knowing the welcome they would give to the Marquis of Ripon that evening, and the.usual atten- tive behaviour of a Warrington audience, that had in- duced him to occupy the position of chairman. They had been unfortunate, for beyond the absence of their chairman they had to deplore the absence of one of their principal speakers, Mr. Brunner. (Cheers) They wished to see Mr. Brunner amongst them, and to congratulate him in per- son for the gallant and victorious fight he had conduc- ted in the Northwich Division. (Cheers.) rortunately however, he had been able that day to secure a speaker in the person of Mr. Symonds of Manchester. who would address them on the Irish question. He (Mr. Roberts) believed that that would be the first occasion the Secretary of the National Reform Association had addressed a Warrington audience. He presumed that the great question in all their minds, and which would be particularly touched upon that evening was the great and all-important Irish question—(cheers)—and he did hope that Warrington would bestir itself and act upon the advice which he was certain they would receive from the speakers who would address them in doing their best to reverse what they believed to be a cruel and coercive law which had been imposed on the Sister Isle. (Loud cheers.) Alderman John CROSTIELD was received with long. continued cheering. He said the resolution which he had the pleasure to move that night read as follows :—" The. Liberals of Warrington desire to offer to the Most Honourable the Marquis of Ripon, their sincere and hearty welcome, and while recognising with pride, the great development of the principles of equality and justice in the Indian Empire, with which the name of the Marquis is so honourably associated, would at the same time take this opportunity of recording their strongest condemnation of the unnecessary and cruel coercive policy of the present Government; and in ex- pressing their unabated confidence in the great Liberal leader—William Ewart Gladstone (loud cheers.) They would also pledge themselves to assist him by every pos- sible means in his noble efforts to restore the freedom of our Irish fellow-subjects, by bestowing upon them a wise and just measure of Home Rule." (Cheers.) He was sureit did not need a word from him to recommend that resolution to them. They were all of them deeply indebted to the Marquis of Ripon for taking the trouble to come all the way down from London to speak to them that night. They knew that he (Mr. Crosfield) was, not in the habit of speaking in very high terms of the House of Lords (Loud laughter and cheers.) There were some members in that House who, in his humble opinion, would be a good deal better out of it. (Laughter and cheers.)—and as a principle he did not approve of what was called hereditary legislation. (Cheers.) He did not believe that it was right that a youth, because he ' was the son of his father, should sit in the House of Lords to veto measures that were pissed by the repre- sentatives of the people. (Cheers). But, in the House of Lords there were men whom he called nature's noble- men, and the Marquis of Ripon was one of them. (Cheers.) lie did honour to his class, and he elevated himself in the opinion of his countrymen. Why? Be- cause he showed sympathy with the people. (Loud ' cheers.) As they were driving there that night the Mar- quis had told him what he did not know before, which was that the Marquis had charge of the Ballot Bill, ancl carried it through the House of Lords. (Cheers.) There was no measure, he believed, in his lifetime that had

done more for freedom and liberty, and especially of the Liberal party in this country than the ballot. (Hear, hear.) He was telling the noble Marquis, as they were coming down that evening, that he could remember the time when in Cheshire the poor farmers were driven to the poll like sheep, and when they could not call their souls their own, and when it was as helpless and hope- less to get a Liberal member in for the county as it would beeo set off from the earth to the moon. (Laugh- ter and hear, hear.) But how was it now? What hap- pened the other day, when his friend, Mr. Brunner, re- earned by over 1,000 ? .(Loed cheers.) He changed a majority of 800 against him into a majority of 1,000 for himself. (Cheers.) Did that indicate any feeling amongst the people on the Irish queetien ? (Hear, hear, and cheers.) Lord Hartington spoke of an overwhelm- ing majority, but it seemed to him that the overwhelm- ing majority was the other way. What about Bridgeton, in Glasgow, and what about the last half -a-dozen elections that had taken place? (Hear' hear.) In everyone of these elections the Liberal party, when they had nob won, had reduced the majority of the Tories. (Cheers.) He wanted to say a word to them about fair trade. (Hear, hear.) There was a meeting held ir Warrington the other night, and Mr. John White was in the chair. Well, Mr. John White was a very proper person to be in the chair. (Laughter.) He did not think they could have found a more suitable gentleman in Warrington. Mr. John White was the agent of big landowners in this part of the country, and he had no doubt whatever that Mr. John White spoke sincerely when he said he would like to see a &ss duty on corn. (A Voice: 10s.) They all knew that in Warrington they had had some little experience in political fights, and they were up to one or two of the dodges of the Tory part—(hear, hear, and laughter)—and this fair trade dodge was just a red herring which they were drawing across the path to di- vert their minds from Ireland, because tho Tories knew perfectly well they could never succeed, but they were in hopes that they might catch a few misguided voted in Warrington by supporting fair trade. (Hear hear.) He dare say they were fond of Mr. John White, ieut he did not think they were fond enough to support a duty on corn, which would raise the price of a 41b. loaf by, per- haps, 2d. The object of that fair trade cry was to raise the rents of farms, to put money into the landowners' pockets, and to raise the screw of the agent. (Loud laughter and cheers.) He dare say most of them in that hall had read a letter from Mr. John Bright on that sub- ject. (Hiesee.) Let thorn not hiss ; it was one of Mr. Bright's sledge-hammer letters, and very characteristic of the old man. Mr. Bright said, "if these fair traders in their silly and childish dreams, propose again to raisethe price of food by partial exclusion of foreign corn, how do they propose to protect the crowds of men and women working in the cotton and woollen trades of Lancashireand Yorkshire? You have observed what the Conservatives have been saying at Oxford. They returned—shall I say? —like the dog to his vomit. They Yeryslowly accept new teaching and new opinions, and the old delusions still attach to them, but they are all in confusion, and know not what they ask." (Laughter and cheers.) Just • word to them about Ireland. There was no man who in the last 50 years had said more powerful or eloquent words than John Bright. (Hear, hear.)He said some years ago,when speaking about the Irish question, that "force is no remedy"—(hear, hear—and it was perfectly incomprehensible to hint (Mr. Crosfield) that a man hold- ing opinions like those which he knew Mr. Bright held could go into the lobby of the House of Commons with the Tories and in support of a measure, the cruellest, the most wicked, and the most unwarrantable that had been passed in this century. (Cheers.) The Tories said they must all support law and order. Well, but he should like to know who had supported law and order in this country? If it had not been for the Liberal party and for the measures passed by the Liberal party there would have been civil war in England long ago, and if tho Tories had any gratitude in them, which they had not, they would go down on their knees three times a day and thank God for what the Liberals had done for them. (Loud laughter and cheers.) They spoke about main. taming law and order, but there was something that was grander and loftier than law, and that was justice. (Loud cheers.) John Bright once said these beautiful words "I plead for just law justly administered." (Cheers.) He (Mr. Crosfield) asked them if there wa4 just law justly administered at Mitchelstown. (' cNo.") Was it a just law that aanfe. Ec-poledr.fin with their batons to break the heads of the people assembled to discuss a political question? Was it just law that en- abled the policeman to hide themselves in their barracks smash the windows with their rifles, and then deliber- atelp kill three men fifty yards away ? (Cries of "No " and" Shame.") He said it was murder, and he said Mr. Balfour was guilty of that murder. (Cheers.) He was thankful that his 'friend Mr. Brunner was there, for he knew then that they should at all events hear the truth from him. (Hear, hear.) And Mr_ Brunner had given a detailed account of all that went oci at MitchOlfi- town, and it showed that thill slatelfient made by` Mr. Balfour in the House of Commons, and which he said was the official statement, was a tissue of falseheads from beginning to end. (Hear, hear,) And they had even gone so far as to clap a patriot a noble-minded patriot, like Mr. O'Brien in prison, put him on a plank bed, and gave him bread and water. And what was it for ? Simply because he dared to open his mouth and speak for the people. (Hear, hear.) Why, there would have been juat al much right when Cobden and Bright were speaking in 1840 to 1846 for a posse of policemen to break into one of their meetings and smash the people's heads. (Hear, hear.) What would John Bright have said then ? He thought John Bright would then have said, "Let's have justice beforo law." (Cheers.) And so if they wanted peace in Irelind it was no use humbugging about the thing at all, for there was only one man that could settle it. (Loud cheers.) He would spread peace, contentment, and prosperity. (Cheers.) Ho was the man who would put down the National League, because the National League would not need to exist. The Anti-corn Law League ceased to exist afterthey did away with thecorrilawe, because after it got what it wanted it naturally died out. So it would be with the National party in Ireland. When they had got what they wanted and what they had a right to have they would cease to exist. (Hear, hear.) There were 35,000 soldiers in Ireland to-day, costing, he supposed, £2,000,000, but if they had 350,000 soldiers they could not put down the National L'ave, ;Loncl cheers.) If he Uyed in Ireland did they not think he would be a frienaher of the National party? (Laughter and cheers.) , Yes, and he would be more than that, for he would boy- cot those fellows as hard as ever he could. (Laughter.) He mentioned the other 'day that ha remembered well enough when in Warrington the Tories boycotted every shopkeeper that dare vote for the Liberals. (Hear, hear.) They did so; they boycotted without any hesitation, but then as he had often told them the Tory party considered, they had a perfect right to boycot. (Laughter.) They were the gentlemen and had a perfect right to do it, but it was different when it came to the poor Irishman whose life was dependent upon the land, whose wife and children were perhaps starving, and who was rack-rented. to such an extent that he could not pay his rent, and had 'death staring him in the face. Would they not bos-cot under Ouch circumstanctes ? (Cheers.) His sympathy was entirely with the tenants; they were the people to be felt for. (Hear, hear.) He was delighted to see tlpt the other day the Duke of Devonshire had the good se&e and common feeling to send word to his tenants that he would take 30 per cent, off their rents. (Cheers.) That was the kind of spirit they wagted exhibited. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Crosfield) was delighted to meet them there that night. They were On the highroad to tectory; the tide was flowing fast. He was sorry for those miser- able Tories—(laughter and cheers)—and as for the Unionists, well, he thoutht they were wrecked high and dry. (Laughter.) Whatever was to become of them he did not know—they would vanish, he supposed. (Laugh- ter.) Let them :go on in the path of progress and of jus- tice. never turning back. Do noble deeds, not dream them all day long. And so make life, death, and the vast for ever, s One grand sweet song." (Continued cheering.) Alderman John BURGESS said that it afforded him very sincere pleasure to be privileged to second the reso- lution that had been so ably proposed to them by Mr. Crosfield. It afforded him great pleasure and great satisfaction inasmuch as he had not been unmindful during a somewhat long political period, of the fact that it was no new thing for a member of the Ripon family to be to the fore doing great work on behalf of the people of this country. And while his family had been to the fore for so long a period, the noble Marquis during the whole of his life had been giving the best time he had at his disposal to the well-being of his fellow-men in this kingdom of ours. (Cheers.) That was not all, for Lord Ripon had rendered eminent service in India that would never be forgotten. (Cheers.) But if the Marquis had been what he had been in India, and what he and his progenitors had been in this country, he (Alderman Burgess) did not think there was ever a period in the history of this country when the Ripon family had the opportunity of doing what the Martinis of Ripon and his coadjutors were at the present time doing on behalf of down-trodden Ireland. (Cheers.) They all of them knew and felt that Ireland had been oppressed at the instance of England time out of mind. For, himself he was weary of that thing; be wanted his own country free from the stain and stigma that at- tached to it, inasmuch as because they were strong and the others were weak, they were oppressors and the others oppressed. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they were not far from the time when that state of things would be bronght to an end. (Cheers.) That led him to the last matter mentioned in the. vote proposed by Mr. Crosfield, and that was that, they expressed their una- bated thanks to Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues for what they were doing on behalf of Ireland—(loud cheers)—and he hoped and trusted sincerely that the life of that great man might be spared to see the con- summation of his great wish, and that his life might be crowned by seeing Ireland made, through his great in- strumentality, free as a people, and free as a nation. (Loud cheers.) He licked them to give the most hearty and cordial welcome they could to the Marquis of Ripon who was rendering sucligreat services to Mr. Gladstone in that glorious cause. (Cheers.) Let him not think that in Warrington he was not appreciated, but let him see that when an advocate of freedom stood before ' them they were prepared to appreciate his efforts to the utmost degree. (Loud cheers.) The resolution was then carried unanimously amidst loud cheering.

The Marquis of RIPON, on rising, was received with much cheering, the audience rising and waving hats and handerchiefs. He thanked theixi flroin the bott4nl of his heart for the very kind and cordial reception they had been good enough to give him, and ho could assure them that he was very grateful to them for their kindness on that occasion. He thanked them heartily for that por- tion of the resolution which related to his administration of Indian affairs. It was not upon that topic that he was present to address thorn that night, or he could have , spoken at no small length upon the many intonate of that great country. Her would only say that while he had the great honour to fill the place of Viceroy of India it was his earnest endeavour at all events to do his duty: and he ventured to believe that he did some little, at all events, to bind together the vast populations of India in closer union to the Crown and people of this country, (Cheers.) He must also express the great gratification with which he had observed how heartily they had re- ceived the last sentence of that resolution, in Which they -expressed their undiminished confidence in his right hon. friend and leader, Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) He had at heart with eminent singleness of purpose the interests!' of the great body of the people of them kingdoms, and it had been all throughout his life, and it would be, he ventured to say, to his dying day, his earnest desire to labour continually for their benefit. (Cheers.) It was especially gratifying to him that night to see gathered in that great hall such a large number of per- sons who still appeared to be enthusiastically devoted to the interests of the Liberal party and to the policy of that arty with regard to Ireland, because they had been mformed during the last few days, in varying tones and different phrases, by the Tory papers throughout the country, that certain meetings which were held a day or two ago in Dublin had put an end to the Liberal party and to Ito Irish policy—(laughter)—and that they had nothing elm to do now except to recant their errors and humbly beg pardon for their mistakes. Those meet- ings were no doubt of an interesting description. They enjoyed great, and in them days unusual, advantages' in Ireland. (Laughter.) The police protected and did not disperse them, and they hail in their favour all the authority and the influence which was possessed by the Government in that bureaucratic land; and he had not seen it anywhere stated that there was a police reporter present on the occasion. (Laughter.) The meeting, especially the one held in Leinster Hall, waes head under special advantages, and they were informed by the "Times" that there were assembled ha that meeting and the overflow meeting some 8,000 persons. He dared' say it was so. He dared say those gentlemen were col- lected from every part of the country, brought vast distances, and, he understood, even from foreign parts— (laughter)--and their presence in such large numbers afforded Lord •Hartington an opportunity of assuring the English people with the greatest possible em- phasis that there were persons in Ireland who were opposed to Home Rule. Well, it was quite unnecemary that Lord Hartington should give them that information. They knew that there were persons in Ireland who were opposed to Home Rule, and they had never been such fools as to deny it. They knew (meetly their proportion. They knew perfectly well that out of the 101 members representing the people of Ire- land—he left out for the purpose of this calculatioa the two members for the University of Dublin-85 were in favour of Rome Rule and 16 against it. (Cheers.) They never had denied that, indeed the repeated statement of it had been one of their main arguments' in Wont, of, dealing with Home Rule at the present time. They Weir that in the election of 1885, taking the six divisions, two of the county and four of the city of Dublin, that about one-third of the electors voted against the Natioaal *an- didates, and they knew also that in 1888 the anti-Hone Rulers only ventured to contest two out of the six divisions, and in these two they polled less, when tate question of Home Rule was directly before the country, than in the year 188 i. Thev knew perfectly well that the vast majority of the lanewners of that country were opposed to the policy of Home Rule. They knew also that the Fellows of Trinitv College were opposed to , Home Rule, although the 86L/1011 Fellow had long been a staunch Home Ruler sad took the chair at a meeting the other day which welcomed his honourable friend, Mr. Illingerorth, and the other English members who went to Ireland. no. were Ow aware that there were aeon- siderable number of gentlemen of the Bar who did not support the Home Rule movement, although they knew very well that there were many members of that distin- guished profession, and many eminent members, in Lee- land warmly in favour of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule policy. (Cheers.) Lord Hartington laid great stress upon the gentlemen representing the commercial inter- ests who attended his meeting. The lost thing he (Lord Ripon) should be inclined to do would be to underrate the importance of the opinions of gentlemen who were con- nected with trade and industrial undertakings, whether in thie country or in Ireland, but it remained to be seen how far those gentlemen who appeared upon that occa- sion might be taken to represent the whole body of in- dustrial and commercial union in Ireland. (Hear, hear.) He observed last Saturday a letter in the "Daily News, from Mr. Handel Comsham, the member for one of the di- visions of Bristol, and he said that one of the things which most struck him in Ireland—and he had been re- cently there—was that the commercial and the industrial classes were becoming convinced that there was no chance of tranquility in Ireland, no chance of a satisfac- tory state of things for the conduct of commercial affairs, until Home Rule had been granted. <Applause.) All that they knew very well. They know also that in the proportion of at least five to one the representatives of the Irish people were in favour of Home Rule.; and they knew, therefore, by that, and by a hundred other exam- ples, Which could easily ho given if time allowed, the Irish people, speaking broadly, had set their hearts on the management of their own affairs. (Cheers) Their forces remained unshaken, and their duty remained unchanged, by anything that peered upon the occasion to which he had referred. But Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain had recently propounded a novel theory—a theory ef unanimity—.a theory that it was necessary that there should be practical unanimity in a country before any constitutional changta could be in- troduced, That was a theory unknown to the British , constitution. (Cheers.) He rased hardly say to that 1 audience, so largely composed as it was of working men, that there could not be any doctrine more absolutely fatal to public interests; than such a one. (Cheers.) This doctrine, if it meant anything at all, meant that there should be an overwhelming desire on the part of the people of a country for a measure which they believed would be greatly to their advantage, and he did not think that they were ever likely to have a more over- whelming unanimity than that which was presented by the proportion of 8 to 16 in Ireland. There was an overwhelming unanimity of feeling in the country in favour of a particular measure, but because a small minority did not think so, the measure wita not allowed. Was there perfect unanimity at the passing of the Reform Bill in 1832? Was there perfect unanimity when. the Corn Laws were repealed? Had there been unanimity of opinion with regard to the measures of religious freedom that had been passed during the last century? No. Was there perfect unanimity the other day when the battle was being fought for the extension of the suffrage and the reform of our representation which took place in 1884-5? Let them go a little closer to Ireland with re- gard to this question of unanimity, and let him ask this question—" Was there unanimity in Ireland when the Unionawas established?" (Cries of "No.") He was not going to say anything about the way in which the measure was carried; he was not geing to say anything of the powerful means that were used for carrying the measure; he would simply say that that measure was opposed to the last by some of the noblest men in Ire- land, by men like Grafton and Plunkett, and others. Were they to be told that when the Union was carried, in the teeth of an opposition of that description, it met the wishes of the great and vast majority of the Irish people? The theory was an utterly untenable one. (He'vkr, hear.) Again, take for instance the disestablish- of the Irish Church. was there perfect unanimity about that? The Irish Clecrrch was disestablished by a Govern- ment of which Lord Hartington and Mr. Goschen were members, and of which he himself was a member—and that measure was opposed by landowners, , by the fellows of Trinity College, by a no inconsiderable portion of the Bar, by a good many people connected with commerce, and especially by those who arrogated to themselves the title of loyal. 'Phe Government of that day did not concede an Imperial veto the Orange fac- tion of that time, and why should they be asked to con- cede it to them. now? (Cheers.) Lord Hartington, in his speech the other day, exhorted the Irish people to place their confidence in the Parliament sitting at West- minster, and to leave them to deal with Irish affairs, in the certain assurance that they would deal with them in the best possible manner, and in accordance with the wishes of the Irish people. It seemed to him that that was a little late in the day. (Hear, hear.) The Union was passed in 1800. The support and consentof Ireland was obtained on the promise that theyahould be eman- cipated. The promise was broken; the pledge was not kept. How about the land question. Had Parliament been so very ready to deal with that question and remedy the evils of it? There was once a famous com- mission appointed by Sir Robert Peel's Government, a Tory commission appointed by a Tory Government, and it reported in 1845, and it laid before the country, fairly and honestly, all the monstrous evils of the Irish land system, but nothing was; done that really tended to re- move those evils until the Act of 1871. No successful attempt was made in the British Parliament to deal with the enormous evils of that question for a period of some twenty or thirty years after the time at which the whole facts of the case had been brought before their know- ledge. He was in Parliament himself for many years when the Irish land question was being continually dis- cussed, and he used to support Irish members in their endeavours to get some measure of justice. If the ques- tion had been dealt with in 1852 or 1853, it could have been settled upon a very moderate basis, and every re- quirement might easily have been met, and. it would have prevented all the evils that had since occurred, all the ill-feeling that had been going on from then to now, and all the monstrous wickedness that had since then been perpetrated in Ireland. (Cheers.) The question , of local government in Ireland had been before Parlia- Iment for the lest thirty or forty years, no one had had anything to say in favour of the present system of local government in Ireland, and yet nothing had been done.

Again, the municipal franchise in Ireland was a moa- strous thing, and excluded a great body of the people from management be theirdoced eairis.. Let them look for si moment at the prs.4.eat,eind let them leek at toed Hartington's own es-induct of late with regard to reme- dial legislation for Ireland. Lord Harlington said that there was no remedy proposed by the Irish members of Parliament, which Parliament was unwilling to concede: The noble lord's memory: must have failed him. He cer- tainly understood that in the autumn of 1886 the Irish members pressed upon the Government in the strongest possible manner the state of agricultural affairs in that country, and warned them 'of the approach- ing winter. Mr. Parnell brought in a bill with a view to meeting the evils that he foresaw. The Government, supported by Lord Harlington,. not only rejected Mr. Parnell's bill, but refused to listen to his wirnings, and it was to them, and td those who sup- ported them, that the country owed the lamentable scenes at Glenbeigh and Bodykso, and it eves to them also the Government owed the Plan of Campaign. That was one of the most recent instances of the manner in which Parliament dealt with Irish affairs. And why? Because it did not understand Ahem. Because it never had listened, and never would listen with respect, to the opinions of the representatives of Ireland. (Cheers.) What were the prospects of the future with regard to Ireland ? Lord Harlington himself had told them that they should not have any amelioration of their system of local self-government until they gave up their national aspirations. Look at the imprisonment of Mi. O'Brien, who was a trusted leader of the Irish people. 'They know the circumstances—the shameful, mean, and unworthy circtunetancee—connected with the imprisonment of ' which they had been hearing of late. Was there not something in that calculated to drive men mad. Look again at the gross insults which had been levied full against the Irish members. Look an the language that was used about them by the Tory and 'the Hnioxist 'Pre.es, and by members of Parliament and others speak- ing iii the country, and look at the way in which, when members were anxious that the charges against them should be inquired into by the House of Commons, the majority of that House refused in a manner in which they would nob have refused in the case of any other person. Look again at the suppreesions of public meet- , ings. Look, too, at the Press prosecutions, and look at I the prosecutioa of the Lord Mayor of Dublin, a distia- guished gentleman, a man of eminence, and of spotless character. (Cheers). It was only due to the wisdom of the magistrate before whom he was tried the other day, that he, like Mr. O'Brien had not been committed to'hard labour. This refu.sal to condemn the Lord Mayor of Dublin to hard labour showed in the face of the world that it was in the power of the officers of the Gov- ernment to relieve political prisoners from such an in-' dignity if they thought fit. There was one small matter I —although it vvas a serious one for the people concerned, which had been brought up lately, which he should like to speak about.. They had seen instances lately of news- agents and newsvendors being prosecuted for selling cer- tain newspaper; in Ireland that contained reports of the meetings of suppressed branches of the National League. He was, not going into the question of whether it was a reasonable law that persons should be prosecuted for publishing reports of meetings of any kind, but he thought, at the mei time, that it was AA unreasonable law. Whet ha *anted be point out was the position of thee, aewsegente seed neyrarendors, Of coulee these re- ports were not contained in every number of the frith newspapers, but appeared from time to time. The newt- agent received by the morning train the Rapers which he pet upon his stall for saleeoreold at a station to per- sons who travelled in the trains. Wrie it seriously ex- pected that these persons, before they sold the meriting papa*, would open them and read them through for the purpose of seeing whether they contained any report of a meeting which , might by any chance have been proclaimed. He never heard of such a monstrous thing, and could not conceive it. Anyone who travelled by rail and bought papers must see how absurd gnat a system was, and how eminently calculated it was to irritate. That was to say, according to Ir. Goschen, to drive people mad. (Laughter and cheers. Than again, the government , were striking right and left at the National League. He looked with great alarm at the state of things in Ireland becauselles believed that the power of the Natioital League was being used for the purpose of repressingadd stopping outrage, and that if that power was broken, the danger of the situation would be greatly increased. He trusted that the Irish people would have the good sense and forbearance to abstain from outrage, and that they would show how futile such things were to the mums. Mr. Gosichen said the other day that he had still to learn that the condemnation of the League was an insult to the Irish people. 'Wolf, if Mr. Goschen meant by those words that he had still to learn the close attach.gent of the Irislz. people to the National League, if he meant that he still had to !earn how strong was the hold that the League had upon the people of Ireland, then all that be could say was that Mr. Ooschen did not know the A B C of the situation in Ireland. (Cheers.) They had here only one other proof of how difficult it seemed to be for Englishmen to understand the Irish people. He did not tit all suppose, or believe for a moment that, of late years at all events, there had been any other wish on the part of the English people, and even the ling,lish parliament, than to do justice to Ireland. The evil had been that they had not 'under- stood the real state of things in Ireland that they had not properly understood the feelings, the trials, and the wishes of the Irish people, and therefore they had been constantly misled. From the sentences of Mr. Csosthen they had the Strongest proof that on the part of Her Majesty's government that state of things would con- tinue, for even all the startling events of the last two years had not warned them of the real state of things, I that existed in that country, andthefeelings of the Irish. Those two great men of whom he had been speaking had distinctly declared that they would have nothing to do with the aspirations and desires of the Irish people, and they left no other prospect than the continuance of the 'present system of coercion. He observed that they were very careful not to go into the policy of that system. They did not' talk in defence of the proceedings at Mit- chelstowa, or against Mr. O'Brien, or against the Lord Mayor of Dublin. They left all those things to Dublin Castle and the resident magistrates, and confined them- selves to a very general statement in respect to their de- termination to maintain law and order by the methods to which they were now resorting. But if the,Tories and their supporters had no policy for Ireland save a policy of perpetual coercion the Liberals had. (Cheers.) They had a policy founded upon experience and based upon fact, and calculated to satisfy the aspirations of the Irish people, And to make them one of the strangest in- struments for the union of Great Britain and Ireland. (Cheers.) That policy was Home Rule. (Renewed cheers.) Now, what was lime Rule? Home Rule, in the firet place, was not separatien, and no one knew that better than those who were always calling those of the Liberal party separatists. Hard words would break no bones, and if it pleased Lord Harlington and his friends to call them separatists, he for his part would be very sorry to; deprive them of that pleasure. A policy of separation of Ireland from England was. one that was not to be entertained. He admitted that there had been men who had advocated a policy of separation who had despaired of ever obtaining justice from England, and who had, therefore, desired to be absolutely cut off; but even theses men, he should think, must have always, recognised the despairing nature of that remedy in re- gard to the interests of Ireland, and how fatal to her in a political, a commercial, and an industrial point of view must be her separation from this country. The policy of Home Rule was averse to separa- tion—(hear, hear)—and, given Home Rule, the Irish people would refuse to listen for one moment to anyone who might still desire to preach to them the doctrine of separation. (Cheers.) His idea. of Home Rule was that it was a. eystem that should be car- ried out by meane of a legislature in Dublin. It should have the management and the control of the legislation in regard to the internal affairs of the country. All Im- perial affairs would remain, as now, with the Imperial Parliament, and with them the Irish legislature would have nothing to do. That Imperial Parliament would still be maintained. It was supreme over all parts of her Majesty's kingdom, and it would remain supreme to the end. (Cheers.) All that would be given over to the Irish legielature would be the management and control of such matters as Parliament might decide to be matters intimately connected with the internal affairs of Ireland. He thought that it would probably be the wisest course to set out in distinct form what were the subjects with ' which the Irish legislature were to deal, provided only that those subjects were made sufficiently wide in scope to honestly and fairly give the management of their own affairs to the Irish people. Within the limits; of the matters thus transferred to the management of the Irish legislature, Ireland should be governed and adminis- tered in accordance with the wishes of the Irish people, constitutionally expressed. This was a definition - . what, as it seemed to him, was meant by Home Rule, and that, he believed, would be accepted by the Irish people as a settlement of this great question. Speaking at Rawten.stall, on Saturday night, Lord Harlington alluded to a question that had been greatly discussed in regard to this matter—the question of what should be done with the Irish members now in the Imperial Parlia- ment. Lord.Hartington objected to their being left there or removed, andthue did not throw much light on the: question of what course should be taken. (Laughter.) Of course what Lord Hartiugton meant was that he ob- jected to Home Rule altogether. There were a great many people who honestly believed that it wouldbe take to exclude the Irish members from the Imperial Parlia- ment. Mr. Gladstone had said that thequestion might be scaled, so far as the main feature of Home Rule Bill was concerned, bv leaving the Irish members'exactly' as it present, and leaving the question to be determined by practical experience, and the working of the measure after it had been passed. They should endeavour to give contentment to Ireland, and to satisfy the national aspi- rations of her people. ,They should substitute for the outward form of union that existed at present a real and substantial union—(cheers)—founded upon a solid ba,aie, upog the hearty assent of the people. In conclusion, be would appeal from Lord Harlington to a great Whig—to Lord Grey—to the Lord Grey who carried the.first great reform bill, to whom this country owed for that great work such a,deep debt of gratitude. What did he say about the queetion of union between England and' Ire- land when he Nees a member of the House of Comenone. He said by a union he meant something mere' thazt a

mere word; a union not of terms, but of hearts, affec- tions, and interests, which would tend to the general 'welfare of the British Vmpire,. would increase the real /Strength of the country, and give security against dan- ger, whereas the tendency of a union in name only would be to disunite and to create disaffection and distress. These, the ma.rquisadded, were the wordsof a real states- man, who defined the policy of true Liberals:: (Cheers.) It was only by just and kind legislation that they could hope to secure peace and prosperity to Ireland, and the unity and strength of the United Kingdom. (Cheers.) Mr. A. .1. SYMONDS, who next addressed the meeting, said that the Marquis of Ripon had succeisfelly shown the position that Lord Hartington and the so-called Unionists had taken on the Home Rule question. Lord' Hartington had stated that he was a Unionist first and a Liberal afterwards, but Lord Ripon had plainly shown them that the Liberals were the real Unionists,. True Liberalism meant government of the people, :for the people, and by the people—(cheers)--and the Liberal party were not going to yield that proud title. To them belonged that name, ana in folloiting out those princi- ples they were the true Liberals and the true Unionists, (Cheers.) If itwal right for the people on this side of the channel to govern themselves, why should not it also be right for the people on the other side to govern them- selves. Mr. Groschen spoke strongly indeed at Manchester the other day upon the question of separation, but why, he would ask, would not Mr. Goschen give the 'lrish a chance of prosperity by allowing 'them the laws that they desired. (Cheers.) If he would give them that chance, then, perhaps, they would find that the Irish people would be willing ,to give obedience to the laws when they were passed. There tad been laws and laws passed, but any man in that room would feel bound to disobey such laws if they were attempted to be piit Into force now. (Applause.) Did Mr. Goschen know anything about the Revolution of 1688? (Hear, hear.) He talked about the liberties which their fathers had won for them; but he would like to know where Mr. Goschen's forefathers were when the liberties of England were won. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Let Mr. Goechen and Lord Hartington stand aside, if they were going to bring foul calumny on a name of which the, Liberal party were proud. Let them remember that a few years rot Tory Govern- ment produced Peterloo •, and that a few Years of Tory Gov, ernment produced Mitchelatovrn. They inWarrington that night said that these things must not be. If the Gov- ernment persisted in the system of tyranny. and oppres-' mien that they had been practising, if they went on sup- preeing public meetings and putting down newspapers; and if they went on putting Irish members into prison there were English members of Parliament ready to take their places: and if they put the English• members nf Parliament into prison, there were plenty of volunteers, even in that room, who would take their places. (Cheers.) The die was cast, and the battle was waging. They mind everyone take their share and he appealed to all alike to bear his and her share—because in this great fight that was going on in Ireland the women and the children were also suffering. It was for those who cared for freedom and justice to stand by their greet leader in this cause. They must not be content with merely shouting approval of the resolution, but they must work as hard aS they could to re- turn Mr. John Crosfield as their member at the next election, ((heers.) They must show that in England at least the old spirit of freedona and justice I was alive, and that Warrington amongst other places would fight for victory. (Cheers.) Mr. C. S. Rueriess then rose to move a resolution.' Ple.l thought that it would not be out of place if he expreased On behalf of the Liberals of Warrington the profound re- gret with which they heard of the death of Lord Dal- housie. (Hear, hear.) In his death the country and the Qtteren had lost a faithful and devoted servant, and the 4 Liberal party a loyal and true supporter. (Cheers.)' The resolution he had been asked to move was as fol- loVes :--" That the best thanks of the meeting be tendered to the Most Hon. the Marquis of Ripon, K.G., for his able ' and interesting address. (Applause.) The stirring and vigorous words of the. noble Marquis were still in their , minds, and he should not-attempt to say anything that , might in any way efface them. They must let the result of that , meeting be that they would work for the cause the Marquis lad come down to Warrington td propagate, aed work for the grand old man who was striving to carry peace, happiness, and prosperity to Ireland. (Cheers.)

Mr. A. H. CROSFIBLD, who had a very hearty reoep- , tion, seconded the resolution. He was; he said, obliged to the Chairman for giving him an opportunity of saving a word in favour of the cause which the Liberal; of War- rington, beyond all other muses, at the present time were fighting for. Mr. Gladstone had said that this cause was in a great measure a fight between the lIIRSPeS and tke classes, but they had the great satisfa,ction of knowing that there were distinguished and important exceptions to that definition; and they were glad to know that those exceptions were net confined to those who passively supported Home Rule. There were amongst them them who had worked hard for the CallfrB, and they looked upon that as an example it ,would be well for them to follow. (Cheers.) They wore handicapped in a great measure by the influene,e of the elapses and of the majority of the employers of labour. Influence was brought to bear in a great measure by working on the prejudices instead of upon the reason of the people: and if the Liberals were to win they nsu.st deal with them with reason, and bring their opponents to the deadlock of logic. (Cheers.) Mr. g. CHLMBIRS supported the resolution,thoroughly endorsing what had been said by themover and seconder. The lesson to he derived from his Lordship's speech was that they should do what they could in their own spherit of life to further the use of Liberalism, and the cause of justice to Ireland. He hoped that the day was far distant when the democracy of this country would, refuse to listen to the appeals of their fellow-countryzuen. (Cheers.) The resolution was then passed with cheers. It was briefly acknowledged by the Marquis of Ripon, who then proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman.
Thi reeolution having been seconded by Mr. Jour; CROgFIBLD, and carried, the meeting. WU brought to a conclusion. ,

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday. There were pre- sent Messrs. Greening (in the chair), Balharry, Blaekhurst, Jolley, Isherwood, Derbyshire, Owen, finalist', J. Houghton, Clarke, Ratcliffe; S. Sutton (assistant clerk), Ward (workhouse master).

div.head: TES CIIIIISTNIAS DINNER.-TEB. BEBE QUESTION.
div.p: TES CIIIIISTNIAS DINNER.-TEB. BEBE QUESTION.

The House Committee recommended thf-it the inmates of the Workhouse should have their. usual Christmas din- ner provided for them.—The CHAIRMAN asked if this *-•.! eluded an allowance of beer.—Mr. JOLLEY 'said ho should certainly recommend that those inmates who wished it should have an allowance of boor. Ho liked a glass o 4 beer himself, and he should like to see those in the Work'- house treated on the same footing. The cost was so trifling as to be hardly worth discussmg.—Tho CHAIRMAN said that perhaps Mr. Isherwood could tell them whether anything was said about beer at the committet\ meet- ing.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said he was the only one present at the meeting, and the beer question never entered his head at the time. He was the only member presdst at the committee meeting, and he simply took the minute of last year. He should certainly not recommend or sup- port the allowance of beer.—M. BLACHEURST was sorry. the queStion had been raised. There was not much in it, and it would be no great harm whether beer was al- lowed or not.—ln answer to Mr. Clarke, the CHAIRMAN said he believed beer had only been disallowed once in six or seven- years.-s.tr. RATCLIFFH spoke in favour of the inmates being allowed beer with their Christmas din- ner.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON also supported the allowance, and said he had never heard of the slightest bad effects from the inmates having beer—Mr. Istranwoon saill he sheuld vote against the allowance.—Mr. Datievatuan Moved that beer be not allowed the 'inmates at their Christmas dinner. He moved that on principle, and not beoause he did not like a glass of beer. He .considered the reasons given by Mr. Jolley and Mr. Houghton as frivolous. Because they liked.a glass of beer was no reason why the ratepayers should be called upon to pay for a glass of beer for people, Many of whom had brought themselves into the Workhouse through drink. He Was sorry to hear that menabers of that Board seemed to Wish to perpetuate the drinking customs of the country, which had done so much harm.—The CHAIRMAN. said he had very great pleasure in seconding Mr. Darby: shire's proposal. He, like Mr. Darbythire, did not go on' the ground that he-either liked the beer or did not. Per, lisps he did-like it, but he had lived many vfairs now without it, and he always had his dinner on (..)hristinae Day without it. Ho was of opinion that the great ila- orit the people in the Workhouse were brought them, thiangh dnnk.—M77lTiTitiffireilT" They are past all that ! now.—The CHAIRMAN was not, so sure of that, !as he lately saw three women--inniates of the house—rolling drunk in the streets. •In another case he know a man who had been allowed out came in in such beastly stato of drunkenness that the Workhouse Master very properly I said he should not go out again for two months. Ho (the ! chairman) could remember a year o,n which': no 'drink 4as allowed, and the doctor told them that he had `had /lksa trouble With the people after the Christmas of 4hat ! year 'than 'he had had for years. There were many ikhe,r Boards of Guardians that did not allow beer to be ! given; and at Manchester Workhouse with its immense number of inmates there had not been a drop of drink allowed for years.—Mr. JoLLsr said if it was a mere question of expense ho would pay that himself .—The CHAIRMAN said it was not a ,question of expcnse.—Mx. JOLLEY said there were people in that workhowe who had come there through other circumstances than'druzi- kenness.—The CHAIRMAN Very fey.—Mr. JOLLEY said they must not say that all the inmates had come glare through drink. rink, like other things, when taken in excess was a curse, 'bet when taken in such moderation as he argued for, he maintained could do no harm, while a great deal of pleasure would be afforded..,-Mr. BLACK.- muter said that as heliad no strong feeling in the Mat- ter, he should not vote either way, but leave those who felt more strongly to decide.—A vote was taken when Messrs. Jolley' Owen, Kilslaall, Houghton and Ratcliffe (5) voted in l'avour of the allowance of beer, Alltrtfie- Chairman 'and Messrs. Darby-shire , Isherwood, and Clarke (4), against. It was accordingly decided that the beer was to be alloweii. , . . ,

SCHOOL }miss. The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 6 new and 86 old cases.--On the motion of Mr. BLACKHURST this motion was adopted. 'MR rADOATE SCHOOLS.• Mr. Mines, superintendent of the Padgate Industrial Schools, reported that the general health of the children was good, but that there were a few cases of chilblains, and one child was suffering from whooping cough. Mr. Pickavance had presented to the schools four copies of the " Boy's Own Paper" and "Young England."---On the motion of lir. DARBYSHIRE, seconded by the CHAlR- mexi it was decided that the saholars and officers at Padgate Schools should have their usual Christmas din- ner.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE remarked that the -" usual " Christmas dinner at the schools did not include beer, while the " usual " dinner at the Workhouse did include beer. .

THE RESIGNATION OF BR. GIBSON. A letter was read from the Local Goveriunent Board stating that they had accepted the resignation of Mr. ,Gibson of the °dice of Guardian for Thelwall, and inti- mating that they would in due course issue itn order directing the election of another Guardian in place of Mr. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: IVARRpcGTON FARMERS' CLUB.
div.p: IVARRpcGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

A general meeting of the members ot this Club was held on Wednesday evening in the large Exchange-room of the Farmers' Stores, Cornhill, Warrington. Mr W. Whitlow presided, and there was a geed attendance of members.—The flow. Sue. (Mr J. L. Stelfox) said he had received a reply from the Chairman of the Ship Canal Company (Lord Egerton) to the letter he sent at the request of the Club asking that a reduction might be made in the rate ef tariffs ' charged by the Bridgewater 'Navigation for the carriage of agricultural produce. Lord Egerton wrote that he was as an agricultur- ist, in entire sympathy with the objects of the letter, but as a trading body which had to return a dividend to its shareholders the Bridgewater Navi- gation oould not at the present time make any sub- stantial changes in its rates, while carefully con- sidering any suggestion that might be made for the encouragement of the agricultual traffic on the canal.—Some discussion next ,took place as to a proposal that factories in which surplus milk could be utilised should be established, and it was uNniately agreed that the secretary should write to neighbouring landowners to ascertain if they would be willing to assist in the carrying out of such a schercie.—The Hos. SECRETARy next read a paper, in which he dealt with the distressed 'state of agriculture, and urged the necessity of adopting a prompt remedy. Dealing with the loss of national wealth resulting from agricultural depression, and basing his re- marks upon the " incomplete and unsatisfactory compilation of statistics' which Government issued under the name of "Agricultural Returns," Mr. Stelfox said that 3,200,000 acres of land had been lost to corn and other crops, although now re- turned under permanent pasture. These unproduc- tive acres represented a monetary loss of about, .£9,600,000, which would otherwise have been avail- able for division amongst landlords, farmers, and farm labourers. They further caused a loss of .£6,4oo,ooo,which would have been available for the purchase of manures and seeds and fQr the pay- ment of the varioua petty expenses incidental to the farming pursuit. Well might our cotton spinners- and their operatives; our woollen and linen manufacturers and their workmeh ; our iron masters and their employes: our colliefilr proprietors and their colliers, one and all complain of lack of demand and employment, .when they 'saw £16,000,000, which should be annually springing from the soil of a sadden withdrawn from circula- tion and percolation throughout the length and breadth of their social structure. (Applause.)— Some discussion took place on the paper, in which the Chairman, and Messrs. Percival, W. Derbyshire, J. Marsh, Davidson, and others took part. All the speakers spoke in complimentary terms .of the paper, and it was agreed that it shovld be printed and circulated by the (secretary. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proceedings.

div.head: OFfItISTMAB BOOKS, &c.
div.p: OFfItISTMAB BOOKS, &c.

Messrs Griffith, Farran, & Co., St. Paul's Church- 'Yard, London, have issued a series of ,Christmas books which are likely to be in great demand during the com- ing season. They are "beautiful exceedingly," and , whoever loots through the books and then at the prices will confess they are cheap. The first volume we lay our hands on is The "Old Corner" Annual (3s 6d), which is appropriately described as 4,‘, a, collection of pictures, stories, and verses for little folk." The frontispice is a coloured picture of three girls telling" twilight stories by the fireside. it is very finely finished, and the same must be said of the full-page pictures, coloured and in "black and white," throughout the book. Twenty years am) such a book was not to be had for love or money. Fine art as applied to book illustration was nothing like so fine. Bach month is hit off 'with a suitable set of varies suitably illustrated. The storks are for the most part in prose, and are capitally told. "His Little Royal Highness" (6s), is a substantial volume a some 200 pages. It is from the pen of .Ruth Ogden, and it is specially illustrated by. W. Reaney, who has followed the story through all its turns with a most skilful hand. Those who are on the look nut for some- thing which will arrest and preserve the interest of cliii- dren will do well to turn to this lengthy but admirable story. The book is handsomely bound in brown and gold; and bears' on -the front 'a picture of "the ship- wrecked: crew." •, .

"The Little Wonder Box" (3s 6d) is appropriately named. It is a box containing six books of stories-1i Jean Ingelovi. They are in stiff covers of green and gold. They are besides illustrated; each book contains some 50 pages, and one or more stories. The six wonders are in the following order, and Will, we are quite sure, be found sufficiently wonderful by the little reader :—The Prince's Dream, The Fairs: who Judged her Neighbours,. The Ophie of the Woods, The Snowflake and the Water-lily, • A Lost Wand, and Rocking the Cradle. The Little Wen.- , der Box will be heartily welcomed in 'families where several wish.to be reading at the same time. ' "The Christmas Box" (25.'6c1.) is a volume of pictures , and stories edited by Arthur Holme. The frontispieee is a brightly dressed, winsome girl—and it is typical of thil ' contents of the Christmas Box. Some of the pictures , are really marvelleus in their photographic detail, and soft, light, and shade. Let the critic look at the full page picture, "Bobby's in the river," and say if he ever saw anything finer in a child's 3ook. The coloured plates in this volume are numerous and very pretty. It should be added that the odds and ends, in prose and verse, have been carefully written with a view to being as instructive as they are amusing. " In the Land of Nod" (2.5. ed.) is the title of another of these entertaining volumes. It is a sort of "Alice in Wonderland," but quite original in its way.. It is written by Ada C. Maizetti, who is exceedingly lively i and clever n this kind of syork. The illustrations; are by F. C. Gould, who has evidently been well pleased to wander in "The Land of Nod," for his drawings are as quizzical as the text. What can be more comical in its • way than the frontispiece "Toadland .Junction," with the fat toad of a porter in" Confab" with the little girl? The volume is handsomely bound, and well printed on strong toned, paper. "The Christmas Gallery" is the name given toe series of beautiful cards, published, as are the books above noticed, by Messrs. Griffith, Farran, and Co. They are issued in boxes, each box containing eight catds, and ' the price' of each set is two shillings.. The Cards are larger than tho ordinary cabinet Size, and. it, can be said, of each picture that it is a masterpiece, of chromo-litho- graphy. Drawing and colouring are th)roughly artistic, and the result is a series of pictures that are unrivalled in their way. They are sure to find their way into frames and albums—with an eye to permanent preservation. In the first series vre have chubby boys and girls from one to two years of age. Here is a bright- wide-awake youngster, who, with finger on his lip, stares straight-at you. Another is being prepared for the bath, and a third has gone to sleep; and so on. The second Series introduces boys and girls a few years old, and ye have pretty faceS and pretty costumes, blondes and brunettes being agreeably intermingled. In series three, the chil- dren have got to an age when they can be indulged with pets, and thus we • have them nursing a kitten, a pug, a parrot, a dove, or a4oll. The fourth set is a series of dainty school girls, most daintily arrayed—tilieg:of beauty everyone of them.. Messrs. Griffiths and Marian will, if we mistake not, make "a palpable hit l' by the issueof "The Children's Gallery," 'for it is as novel as it is'Leautiful. ,' . . . ;' • Messrs. J. S. Virtue . and Co., Ivy-lane, London, have issued a series of cheap, but profusely illustrated books in handsome stiff colours. r Our Noah's Ark" contains capital pictures of our dumb friends, with appropriate, stories as to their habits and characteristic 4. The frontispiece ,"Iri pesSetsioh " is a fine engraving of an empty mansion. with deer gathered in front of the closed door. "Stories from Foreign Lands for Little Folks at Herne," is just what its title purports; but si-e Way add that children of larger growth will be pleased alike with stories and illustrations. , 'Short stories for Sun- s day Beading" is a somewhat ' similar volume, ith the , difference that .the tales are. of a more setio ;lass. "YAW Luggeishall, or the Lightship," is from t e pen of ' W. H. G. Kingston, who has had a wide experience' in works of this class It is specially illustrated with ,plates of a high class., ' .The frontispiece, " Home agaih,' is a realbr. charminglictitre.. The whole series can be torifi- 'leii-fly reConiiiierTda: . " Seribnees Magazine for December is a Christmas number, every article lulls) issue being complete. . It is ' very strong both as to 4,14 , and illustration. Mr. L. ~

div.p: Stevenson contributes a wierd story in verse, with tk title of " Ticonderooa," and Bret Harte has a charac. teristic sketch—" A drift from Redwood Camp." Florence with Romola," and "In Dickens-land," iwug interest many readers. and there is a story by C' Burner called "The Zadoc Pine Lab Our Union , which is much more, interesting than the title. "Law Lane," by Sarah Orne Jeivett, 1.9 another excellent illustrated story. It should be added that Mr. Austin Debron hag a charming " Song to tho Lute," but this by pa u3eant4 exhausts the lisb of contributions. '• • The Christmas Number of Truth (Is.) is one' of tile_ liveliest if not the liveliest of the annuals. It is inas ver7, übual, and the subject is" Jirbilee Junketing's!: Very smartly written, and very cleverly illustrsrea-7: the more, prominent men of the day figuring in one or another under conditions provocative of '.;ulinSi Several of the full-page plates are in colours, and wst; finished. The foatures of Viscount Cross are caught a nicety, and afterwards we have the following rolloc, ing verso, which we quote as a fair specimen of annual : I've been bundled about not a little of late, For I own that I'm not any use; But I still have insisted on serving the State, Though I'm not, as I said, any use. , That is, to the State I'm nob useful, you see; But the State, let me say, is most useful to me; And that's why I like to a 3Bnister be, • Although I am not any use! First they tried me at this, then they tried me at that' But I wasn't -the least bit of use; And I soon made a mess of whate'er I was at, For I wasn't the least bit of use. So, finding I muddled official affairs, And, wishing to ease the of Government cares, " Why; they made me a Viscount, and kiclos ul" • . stairs. For they said I was no other use. But I soon let them know I was not to be bmibed, • Although I was not any use; And though the poor Marquis an interview shirk'dr He found it was not. any use: - For I fussed and I fumed till he said with a ggh, - "'Cross hasmulled all, the rest—let him India try! And so I arm here—if you wish to know why— Because I am not any use! •

When the ancient empire of Atahualm existed in all its glory, and before its overthrovi by' the rapacious Menlo, ottle extraordinary virtues of the' Pearl of South America " wet:e as well known to the then natives as to the Peruvians of the present day. Indeed, its great and .atinfitted worth led to its being used in all public ceremonies as an acceitable offering to their ,deity—the Sun God. The leaves of .this marvellous shrub. When ready for mi:rket; are 'transpoited on inules up the steep mountain sides, across the icy and desolate plateaux, and through the passes of the Bolivian Andes mountains, many of them 134)00 and 14,000, feet above the level of the sea, and then downwards on the other side of nib mountains into Peru , for shipment from the port. of Callao (Lima.) div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE,
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE,

_ WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Alderman Chandley. ' DELINKENNESS.—A young woman, Ellen Elliott, who had only been out of goal a few hours when arrested, was charged with having been drunk on Friday at Market Gate. On promising to leave the toWn at once she was discharged with a ca,ution.—A woman 'named Frances Richardson, " who said she belonged to SOutliport, charged with a similar offence on. Friday night, was also discharged. LARCENY.—A wothan named Anne Clarke was charged with having stolen a pair of boots from the stall it; the market of Mr. josepli Frisby, boot and shoemaker. on the previous Saturday night. The 'accused waS sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour, but after- wards, on the application of her father, who stated that was In ill-health, the decision was altered to a fine of 20s and costs. Mosnov.—Before the Mayor (Alderman T. H. Sutton), Cotificillors Greening, J. Pierpciint. DRUNKENNESS".—The -foll Owing were 'dealt with for this offence :—Bridget Lally, on Town Hill, on Saturday night, fined 108. and costs; George Makin, in Dial-street, on Saturday, tined ss. including costs; Patrick Mahar and John Riley, in Rodney-street, each fined ss. and costs. SLEEPING Orr-v.—Thomas Roach, who was charged with having been found sleeping out at Bewsey Forge on Sunday morning, was dismissed with a:caution. MISCELLANEOUS—James Cartledg_e,for beingdiBorderls7 by fighting in Queen-street, on the 30th ult, was bound over.to keep the peace for six months.---Ann Hamblett and Eleanor Walsh were summoned for having been disorderly in Dutton-street, and were ordered' to pay the costs.—Thomas Booth and Thomas Hines.'were each fined is, including costs,. for allowing the chintnies of their dwelling-houses to be on fire.--Charles Grove was fined 5s and costs for using obscPne language in Factory-lane on the 20th of August. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. R. W. Francomb. Anuxxxxxiss.—A young man named James Hans- bury, was charged with being drunk and diAo,rderly. on .the previous.....d ,ti ay., and ,alle of ss. and costs was un- posed. ARRESTED ON Suserciori. A middle-aged working- man named Martin Burke, was charged with- being in possession of a pair of trousers, shirt, cap, and handker- chief supposed to be stolen. It appeared from the evi- dence that a woman had been sent by the accused on Monday afternoon to pawn the articles mentionedibut as her replies were not considered satisfactory, Constable Halstead was called in, and eventually Burke was ar- rested. Burke denied that the articles were stolen, al- leged that he had purchased them in St-Helens on Satur- day, and was only temporarily partingevith them when he sent them to the pawn in order that he might raise money for his lodgings.—He was discharged on entering into his own recognizances to appear in answer to the' charge if again called upon. WEDNESDAY—Before Alderman Chandley and Messrs. Fairclough and Garnett. Dianievvvess.---The folh.wing were dealt with for this offence :—Mary Ann • Sniith, in Foundry-street, on the morning previous.•fined 5s and costs; Elizabeth Leyland, in Horsernarket-street, on the previous after- noon, fined 10s and costs; Thomas Cook, in Mersey- street, on the previous night, fined 55 and costs; and Samuel Simpson, in Bewsey-street, fined 58 and costs. A WELL-TO-DO MENDICANT.—John -.Glessbath was brought up on a charge of begging, in Sankey-street, on the night previeus. Constable Mortoghan followed bim into a shop, and heard him relate a pitiful story of how he had walked from Manohester to get work on the Ship Canal. When apprehended he said that he had not suffi- cient money with which to pay for his lodgings, but the sum of 15s 21. d was found in his possession, He was sent to prison for 14 days. TRIIRSDAY.—Before Alderman Webster, and Councillors Platt, Greening, and Litton. $ CHARGE OF STEALING DRUGS.— Andrew Mackenzie Guthrie was charged with stealing a quantity of drugs, of the value of £l2 Is. 5d., the property of Messrs. Win. John Bush ancrCo., London.—The case was remanded till Monday, the prisoner in the meantime tabs detained in Walton good. FALSE DECLARATION.-1 soldier named Luke Mullin was remanded till Monday on a charge of obtain-. ing certain pay from Government ou a false declara- tion. FRIDAY.-13efore Alderman Chandley, Dr. Gornall, and Mr. It. Garnett. ALLEGED ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF GOODS. —John Hardy was summoned for having fraulliulently removed his goods from the house 42, Naylor-street, with intent to avoid a distraint for rent. The case was dismissed. A Crimes Coml.—Edith Smith was summoned by , Charlotte Lee, who charged her with having stolen 4s, from her by means of a trick on the 27th ult.. Com- plainant alleged that on that day defendant came to her house in a frightened condition, and said she waspreased for 4s with which to get a bundle of clothinwout of pawn. She had stamps to the value of 78 ed, and asked for 4s to be advanced on them. Complainant gave her the money, but instead of giving her the stamps defend- ant took them with her also, saying that she would get them changed and return the money. It transpired that the complainant had subsequently treated the mat- ter as a debt, and she was told that that fact took the case out of the jurisdiction of the court. Defendant, ',owever, expressed willingness to refund the money, and ,
D R.

tie case waidismissed on -that understanding. - A Nsionnona's Qtisnast.—Jessie Mitchell was sum- moned for having assaulted Elizabeth (Heave on the 2nd instant. The parties are neighbours living in Napier- street, and a quarrel arose over trivial matters. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant.—The case was dismissed. u WIFE DESERTIONV—WiIIiam Patten, tanner, was sum- moned by his wife, Ann Patten, for having deserted her on the 12th ult.—The case was dismissed on the parties promising to endeavour to live comfortably together. OvEncnownwo.—John Stringer, summoned for this offence, was ordered to abate it, and pay Be. Bd., the costs. MAINTENANCE.—WiIIiam Allen was summoned for hav- ing failed to comply with an order directing ' him to pay 12s. a week towards the maintainknce of his wife. The order was made on the 10th Oct., and nothing had been paid under it since.—The magistrates ordered that the defendant should now pay 15e. a week, and pay the costa.

• WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WRDNESDAY.—Before Mr. T. Comber and Mr. J. Tinsley. • DEDISKENNESS.—Forthis offence, committed at Burton- wood, on the 20th ult., Michael Ryan was fined 5s and costs; James Stokes and John Stokes, for having been drunk and disorderly at Orford, on the 26th, ult., were each fined lOs and costs ; Thomas Johnson,who.wa.s sum- ,moned for having been drunk on the highway at Pen- keth, on the Ist in.st, VMS fined 26 6d and costs ; and for a similar offence at Croft, on the 3rd inst., James Yates was fined 5s and costs. THE DOGS' ORDEll.—Thomas Jennings was summoned for having a dog at large, unmuzzied, contrary to the order of the Local Authority', on the 27th ult. Defend- ant said that he had acted in ignorance, lie was ordered to pay a fine of is and costs. No LICENSE.—Peter Wadsworth, Rixton, was fined 5:4 and costs for having kept a dog without having a license. , HUNGER AND THEFT.—EIIis Vaughan (17), a stranger to the district, was charged with having, on the sth inst.,'stolen a loaf of bread from, the shop of Robert Lees, grocer and provision dealer, Raton. Prisoner said that hunger had driven him to commit the offence. He was cautioned, and bound over to appear if called Upon. •

Thomas in the chair), the Inspector of .Nuisances reparted that he had examined and tested the drainage of certain premi. in Church-street, and found that such drainage discharged into Church-street Brook. Directions were given for an estimate to be obtained the cost of connecting the said drainage with the main, sewer. The Inspector also reported that he found the . quantity of water made by the running pipe in Howley-. lane, Overton, had greatly diminished. He had had tfie, covers taken off to ascertain the cause. The falling of, the water, in the Inspector's opinion, was due to the springs above being weak and low. Various plans were submitted and considered. 410.-

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon. There were present Mr. J. Fisher (chairman), Revs. T. Chambers and C. W. Wooll, Messrs. W. Middlehurst. W. Tyrer, J. Lowe, J. Buckley, J. Hanson, J. Ellison, J. Burcliall,W. Daine, E. Syder, J. Griffiths, W. Swift, R. A. Graves, W. G. Ashton, J. Leatherbarrow, C. B. Johnson, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 516 inmates of the house this week; 552 last week, and 475 in the corresponding week la.styear. He also acknow- ledged the receipt of ten couples of rabbits, for the sick inmates, from Mr. H. R. d'A Willis. Castisrmas DINNER.—The Rev. T. Chambers moved that the inmates be regaled with their Christmas dinner on Monday, 26th December.—Mr. Daine seconded the motion, which was passed, and the t hairman invited as many Guardians to attend as could make it cotmveient to do so. Ties SECURITY OF OFF/CIAIS.—The Local Government Board wrote inquiring whether the Guardians had called upon their inquiry officers to give security for the faith- ful discharge of their duties, and the letter was referred to the Finance Committee. MEDICAL OFFICER FOR WOOLTON.—A letter was 'read from the Local Government Board, sanctioning the ap- pointment of Dr. S. J.Stiott, as medical officer for Wool- ton, at a salary of £43 per annum. .
