I This concluded the businesi. . • THE SALVATION ARMY FUNERAL AT ST. HELENS. MEMORIAL SERVICES.
the

The St. Helens CorpatoLthe Salvation Army held sPecial services on Sunday last, having reference to their late, Captain, 'her Worth, "hose death and funeral was rendrteci in our last isiue. . Ilnfortiin- ately the weather was Inclement, and the outdoor gatherings' were net as largely attended as would have been ths case had the weather been more favourable. Thr.oughout the day the services were ~, • " under„the: leadership Of Staff Captain Surtee of London, who • was assisted by the newly-appointed officers of the St. Helens Corps, Captain Hunt and Lieutenant Treamer. . • • In the forenoon an open-air meeting was held on the Market ground, at which there was a fair attendance. The soldiers subsequently marched to the barracks ii 2 Lowe-street, where a "holiness meeting": was conducted. The afternoon services commenced with' an- open-air meeting at Parr, followed by a-well attended service in the barracks; 1 .• s The principal service of the, day was held in the bar- racks in the evening. The large room was literally packed to its utmost capacity; a large number of people rbeing unable to gain admission. The service throughout was of an affecting character. Among those present [were Mrs:Worth and her five little children, and a eor- old feeling of antipathy towards them was expressed on every hand. The proceedings commenced with sing- ing and prayer, after which Brother Hutchings, in the course of a brief address, said they were met on a solemn occasion, to mourn the loss of a dear officer, but it was not so much to praise the dead as to benefit the living. Captain Worth had left a eau which was most difficult to fill, for he believed he had bean one of the best officers In the Salvation Army. He was glad, because Captain Worth had been genuine ; he was as good as he seemed to . be; and there were no two ways about him. Pie concluded by appealing to all who were unsaved to seek salvation.— Staff Captain Surtees remarked that while they. did not want to praise the dead, they wanted the dead to benefit, those who were left. There was a time when the late !Captain Worth was not a Salvation Army Officer, and when he was a Christless, Godless lad, but' he was at last brought to a knowledge of the Lord. They wanted the memory of Captain Worth's memorial services to go 9 right through the days of time., intoxtbe longer day of eternity,. when hundreds and -thousands Would be saved as a result of that service.—After a*fetv words tfo from a local Soldier, the late Captain ,Worth's favourite song "We shall conquer in the blood of the Lamb" was ' impressively sung.—Captain Hunt afterwards spoke, observing that he could not SAT much about Captain Worth from personal knowledge, but •ItO ehuld say a little respecting his death, and when he was drawing I near to the river of death he knew it . was .well with his soul by the testimony he gave. A month ago, when oCartain Worth stood upon that platform they little expected that death would so soon visit .81, Peter- street, but God had done all for His hononr and 'glory. He would ask them not to let their hearts be 1 ti oubled and that message of Christ would apply to Mrs I Worth and her family. There was a possibility of their again grasping the fiend of Captaie Worth on that celes- tial shore where there wag no death or pain, and where there would be no more parting.—Another hymn was vile.. after which Staff-captain Surtees gave an address founded on the 6th, 7th. and Bth verses of the 4th chap- ter of II Timothy. Staff-captain Surtees, in the course of his address, remarked that Captain Worth had the true , spirit of God within him, and though he could scarcely believe that he had gone when he first heard of his death he comforted himself with the thought that he had fought a good Wit, he had kept the faith and he had gone to his reward. Their loss . NFU indeed great, and they felt that a Prince had fallen-in Israel. Captain Worth was born in the county of Dur- ham, near Spenny Moor, and his early life was much like that of other lads. He was afterwards led into the Salvation Army at Stockton-on-Tees, and, he decided to give up home comforts for a: life of hardshiP in the Salvation Army, and to win men and women from dark- ness into the light. In a brief resume of his services Staff-captain Surtees said the late Captain Worth whilst at Bolton increased the number Of the Army soldiers from about 200 to 2,000, and he afterwards visited South Shields, London, Sheerness. and other towns. From July, 1880, up to the time of his death; he had been at about sixteen stations, and at each place he had worked hard and well for the Lord. He had always been allowed to stop at each station Vie full length of time, and that spoke volumes for him. They had highly valued. him, and while he was Worth by name, he was worthy by nature. He had had a hard fight and had gone to his reward. As they had sung that afternoon "He fought like a warrior; he died at his post." At Guernsey Captain Worth started a work for fallen women, and God had magnificently blessed the work in that directitm. He prayed God to help them all to fdllow in their late captain's footsteps, anti concluded by making an earnest appeal to those pre- sent 'to seek salvation while it may be found.—Mrs Worth spoke a few affecting words as to the loss she had sustained, but she would never retreat from the good work she had taken in hand.—The service was con-
chided with singing, followed by a prayer rneelng. • ,

div.head: ALLEGED RITUALISTIC PRACTICES AT
div.p: ALLEGED RITUALISTIC PRACTICES AT
RUNCORN.

LIVELY • MEETING. On Thursday evening, Mr. R. Stewart Clough, of London, delivered a lecture in Runcorn Public Hall on the subject of Holland's struggles for civil and religious liberty. Notwithstanding the exceedingly inclement nature Of the weather, a good audience assembled, no doubt attracted by the announcement that an address would be delivered on "Ritu- alism with special r9ference to Runcorn." Mr. Robert Foulkes, of Frodsham, was the chairman, and he commenced the proceed- ings by stating that he was a member of the' Evangelical Protestant Union. Their friends, the Ritualists, he said, spurned the word " Pro- testant, ' and he instituted a comparison between Ritualism and Roman Catholicism, showing by copious quotations from Books and pamphlets their great similarity in tholight and mode of w)rship. The question of the eastward position was an • important one for the people of Runcorn. It was the position of a sacri- ficing priest, AI there was no sacrificing priest in the Church of England. •The Holy Scriptures were the key of the 39 articles, and the Ritualists would be glad to see the whole of the 39 swept out to-morrow. He hoped as long as he lived the Articles would remain in the Prayer Book. Allud- ing fo inclining the 'head before a cross or crucifix, Mr Foulkes said the Vicar of Runcorn—(" Draw it mild, Robert" applause)—would not admit that anybody worshipped the cross, (Applause.) He referred the Vicar to Canon Blakeley, one of the .chief men the country had ever seen. (A voice: "According to low church!) He was a LOW: Churchmaii, and what he said Was 'sound., ("Sometimes.") , Mr. Foulkes saiol he was in a' peg- tion to prove every statement he had made. (Ap- plause.) (Mr. Key: If you are a Churchman you believe in apostolic 'succoiaion.) Yes, replied Mr. Foulkes. (Mr. Key: Then there is an answer for you at once.) Mr. Foalkqs .said he had not come there to discuss thr mattO with him. ..They'were bound to keep the ten Commandments for the ' sake of ourselves, our country, and'our God. (Ap- Vause.) Mr. Wilson said the letter and not the spirit of the Vicar's remarks had been reported. ,(Applause.) The Vitar said if men would read the newspapers on the Sunday, let them read in the afternoon. Mr. Clough then delivered an eloquent lecture on the subject of Hollancts struggle for liberty. The lecture was appropriately illustrated with lime- light views. In concluidon Mt. Clough 'asked these , present to defend the church from Ritualiiiticiind; Popish innovation, and they could not do that better than by aiding the Church Association, 'which' had donfso much in nipping heresy in the bud.:. PATRICROFT. The final preparations Aare being mule for the commencement of the canal works in the Barton and Eccles districts. A large crane and other mate- rial ready for use arrived at Patricroft goods yard on Tuesday, and it is generally expected that in about a week a commencement with the actual cutting will be made. The surveyor for this section has already taken up his residence ;a Eccles. and every day receives applications from navvies for employtnent. On Monday Mr. Walker, the contrac- tor, visited Barton, and thence proceeded to Irlam and Cadishead, at which .places suitable buildings have been taken for office purposes. Accommoda- tion for the housing of navvies is/now being pro- vided. In this section one of the greatest difficul- ties to be encountered during the progress of the works will have to be faced—viz., the erection of the swing bridge over the aqueduct at Barton.
UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

An event of considerable interest to the members of this denomination took place on Saturday and Sunday last. An orchestral band and a number of vocalists from Glossop. near Manchester, paid a fra- ternal visit to the Rev. E. Hall, their former pastor, and combined business with pleasure by giving concerts at both Runcorn and Widnes in aid of the circuit funds. Zion Schoolroom, Oakland-street, Widnes, was crowded with an appreciative audi- ence on Saturday evening: when the first concert was given. Mr. I. S. Thumps presided, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. E. Hall and Mr. T. Snape. After an appropriate address had I been delivered by the Chairman, the band under the leadership of Mr. C. Hall performed the overture, "Cheval de Bronze," and during the evening also contributed several other pieces of high class music in most admirable style. The audience derived much enjoyment from the descriptive piece, "Life on the ocean." in which numerous popular airs were introduced with good effect. The principal vocalists were Miss Hall and Messrs. E. Waterhouse, W. • Fielding, and J. Makin, who rendered songs duets, and glees in a manner which called forth

ENTERTAINMENT AT WARORAVE.—Ort Monday evening an entertainment was given in the Wargrave Schools, under the auspices of the local branch of the Church of England Temperance Society: There was a good attend- ance, and the Rev. Canon Whitley, Rector, presided. During the evening Mr. R. A. Naylor, of Thelwall, gave an address, and Mr. James Davies read an Interesting communication from the Scilly Islands. An excel- lent programme of recitations • and readings was gone through.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER:
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER:
EMON.plirlir CORRESPONDENT.) . 1./ I L 23, Old Broad-street, E.C.

The depression which has hung like a cloud over the markets for a long time past seems to hvecleared up at the last settlement, and prices are now more buoyant all round than they have.been for,months. There is only one subject winch-receives anything like attention just now, and that is metal shares. Gold, silver, copper, and tin are each and all in the ascendant. The phenomenal rise in At-Oodles has given an impetus to gold mining speculation and the result has been two or three com- panies, which are certainly very much better than the average run of gold mines. One is the new Sheba, which adjoins the famous Sheba Reef, whose shares stand at an enormous premium., Tin has its representative in the Pahang Corporation Co., which has acquired valuable concessions in the Malay Peninsula. The capital of this company has nearly all been obtained as the wealth of the property is simply enormous. Our advice respecting Don Pedro's has pro zed more • than satisfactory. When we first recommended these shares,they stood at'los, to-day they are over £1 and we can safely advise purchase at this price, as we hear they are almost certain to go to £2. Home rails have been particularly firm during the week, but at the time of writin,g they are flat. The feature of the week in Eng- lish nuts has been the remarkable rise in Hull and Barns- ley stock, which has been the subject of considei ,ble speculation. On Wednesday there was a rumour which teems to be well grounded, that this line will be taken by the Midland Company. Onthe strength of this the stock jumped from 301 to 391. This is the stock which has been very much puffed of late by the firm of outside brokers. • In the excitement of speculation in gold shares there is one company which has been ovenlooka. ; this is Pines Altos, a very promising mine, whose shares now stand roughly at 17s. They are almost certain to go up and a purchasewould be a wise stroke. The West Sheba Reef Gold Mining Company has been formed to work and develone a valuable mining pro- perty, consisting of twelve ill claims, designated ~and duly registered inthe Government Mining Books of the De %sap District in the Transvaal, South Africa,and held by . the vendors under the terms of the gold mining laws of the South African Republic. The twelve claims are ad- jacent to the now famous Sheba Reef Gold Mining Com- pany's property, and a continuation of this Reef has been struck on thevi claims. The position of the West Sheba Reef Gold Mining Company's property is .such that when it is effectually worked should prove as successful an undertaking as the older company, which has just made a distribution of 15 per cent. out of the profits for one month, and whose £1 shares are now dealt in at

£4O. The Pahang Corporation has t 'en torreedlo purchase the mining and planting rights over certain districts in the State of Pahang, on the eastern side of the Malay Peninsula; to develope and work such portion or por- tions of the property as may be found desirable, and further, to sell or lease portions of the property to com- panies or individuals. The concession extends over anl area estimated at about 2,000 square miles, and contains numerous and most extensive lodes of tin, copper, silver- lead, and it is believed of silver and gold, as also a vast t. ',et of very rich agricultural land, well adapted for growing Inpioca, coffee, and other tropical pro- ducts. At present it is pa6posed to confine the company's operatious, almost eicluaively to working the tin lodes and • the stream tin which is found in the valleys and flat lands. The Working of the stream tin requires no machinery, and it can be separated with very simple appliances which are con- structed on the spot. Such large quantities of stream tin are immediately available that a very handsome in- come is derivable at once from this source alone, taking las a basis the price tin stood at a few weeks ago, when it was not above £9O a ton; with straits tin at £165 a ton the immeeiate profits to the company should prove enormous. The capital of the company Is £200,000 in shares of £1 each; the vendors are so t4atisfied as to She' results, that, with the exception of £lO,OOO, they take their entire interest in,sharesef the company.

THE " GHOST." Sir,—No doubt you will have heard the expression "When the ghost walks" made by persons who wish you to understand that they mean when their usual weekly stipend will coins into their possession, otherwise pay day, and I believe that the saying is now in very common use, especially in theatrical circles. Could any of your readers say how long it has been in use, or have any of them any idea how it originated? I had thought that perhaps it was a recently introduced slang term, but on glancing at a novel by Miss Braddon (the date of publication is not given) I find the words "The Ghpat6" used with exactly the same meaning as they ar#4l6*uisod. I have never befort) seen this in print, Ipad ask for information on the subject out of mere . CURIOSITY.
Warringbon, Dec. Ist, 1587.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

Jastict. standetn afar off— . • Equity cannot enter."—lsaiah, . It is very sad to ve,ad the report of the meeting of the School Board in last Saturday's paper. Miss Simkin has been an assistant in the Board schools for nearly three years. She took the infants at Mill-brow for one year, and since that she has taken standard I. of boys and girls at Greenway-road. She is a thoroughly good teacher of infants, and the Board have no fault at all to find with her. She is strictly punctual, a good discipli- narian, cheerful and pleasant in her manner, and a great favourite with the children. She is always on good terms with the other teachers. She earned the singing graht for Greenwav-road achool last year. Her testi- monials are as good as any teacher could wish for. Her certificate is the same as Miss Kennan's. Miss Kennan is an assistant in one of the girls' Schools at Widnes, and has never taught in an infants' school. Mr. Imison appears to consider this a special qualificas a. I understand she, cannot teach singing. J con- .l. Miss Simkin's results quite as good as Miss Ken- ..an's. " In Runcorn there are three denominational achoola where the better class of children go. As a rule the poorest and most ignorant go to the Board schools. In Widnes there are three large Board schools, and only one denominational school.: In Runcorn the schools have not been long established, and the children in standard I. are very ignorant. The average attendance in Runcorn is only about 72 per cent. In Widnes the schools are well established, and have a first-rate staff of teacher; in every department. The average attendance is about 90 per cent. Miss Simkin had a class of 72, of which 10 wee boat children. She presented 66. She had two failures, of which one was a boat child, and passed 92 _ cent, not having had any assistance. I understand is three years since Miss Kerman presented about 50 standard 111, or IV, girls, and passed cent. percent. with the assistance of an advanced pupil teacher, that two years ago she passed 94 per cent., and last year 99 per cent. • tk When Miss Hatchinson, t head teacher, left, about i 15th October, Miss Simkin requested to take Char& I of the mixed school till the e of the year, nothing be- ing said about any addition t her salary, the clerk inti- mating to her, as instructed to do by the chairman, that she would most likely be appOinted head mistress of Mill-brow infants' school, as four out of six members of the Board were in favour of the arrangement. This did not include Miss Simkin's seconder, so that at that time five out of six members were in favour of the appoint- ment. Since that she has lost the chance of another good situation. She lives with her widowed mother, and IS now thrown out of a situation altogether. Miss Ken. nan's .531417 will Mt he much more than she Would have received fit Widnes. • it.. ought to be knoWil that Ni OS kennan is a teacher in the Sunday school Where the chairman is superintendent, and that her brother is in the employ of her seconder 4 the Board. During nearly 40 years' connection with thel day schools, having been nine years a member of the Board (three years as chairman), I have never known such a case before. How Canon Barclay and the Other members of the Board year; ago would have scorned to be parties to such a transaction! I should ;ike to ask the chairman how it is more "practicable" or "work- able" to appoint Miss Kennan than Miss Simkin? What an idea for one member to refuse to vote for Miss Simkin because the clerk had told her she would most likely have the appointment! Is this justice or equity? It is to be hoped that the four gentlemen who have done this thing have different ideas as to right and wrong lso-( where from what they have as members of the Schoor Board. The remainder of the proceedings of the Board were so extraordinary that it does not appear necessaior to say anything in their condemnation.—l am, yours faith- fully, Runcorn. 30th Nov., 1887.

POLICE SERGEANT COMMINS has boon off duty since Monday last, stlffering severely from brenchitis and catarrh, and has been under the attendance of Dr. Pat- terson, of Earlestown. Tim WELSH PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL.—Under'ihe aus-, pices Of the Welsh Presbyterian Chapel, Tamwerth-street, Earlestown, a concert of an unusually excellent character will be given on Monday evening next. SMASHING A PLATE GLASS WINDOW:-John Plekavance, hailing from Prescot, was charged at the Warrington Occasional Courthouse, on Monday, with being drunk and'disorderly, and refusing to quit the Prince of Wales Hotel, Earle-street, Earlestown, when requested ; and he ' was further charged with breaking a pane of glass, and doing damage to the amount of 225. The prisoner, on Saturday afternoon, went into the Prince of Wales Hotel under the influence of drink. He became very vio- lent, and refused to leave. Joseph Dale, an assistant, ordered him out, but the prisoner seized one of the swing doors and banged it from side to side until the glass was smashed.—He WILS fined 5s and costs for the drunkenness, and was committed to prison for fourteen days, without the option of a fine, for the wilful damage. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.—Under the auspices of the Congregational Band of Hope a public entertainment was given in the Congregational Schtol- room, Crow-lane, on Wednesday evening. , The enter- tainers wore members of ,the Ashton Congregational Band of Hope, and the Rev. H. Wilson, of Ashton, pre- sided; .There was a good attendance.. The choir, during the evening, efficiently sang "Bear on the temperance banner," "Hark, the 'lark," "Bright flowing water," and "Sleep while the soft evening breezes blow." Recitations by Miss Z. Pennington ("Beautifutsnow"). and Miss M. E: Pennington ("Searching for the golden street") were highly appreciated. Mr. R. Roper, Mr. James Penning- ton, and Misses Z. and M. E. Pennington, Roper, and Hodgkiss nicely sang selections of music; while violin and concertina duets by Masters James and John Kay were loudly applauded. kfeature of the evening was a pleasant dialogue, entitled "The Flower Queen's Court," in which the primrose,. daisy, pansy, lily, and bluebell were represented. An enjoyable entertainment con- cluded with cordial thanks to the entertainers •and chairman, on the motion of Mr. A. L. Logan, of War. grave. EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT TEMPERANCE ANNUAL MEETING.—The annual meeting of the tarles- town and District Band of Hope and Temperance Union was held in the Temperance Hall, Bridge-street, on Fri-, day evening. There was a good attendance of repre- sentatives from the affiliated societies,, and Mr. J. H. Graham, president, occupied the chair. Mr. W. Pearson, secretary, in his annual report, referred to the position and work of the union during the past year, showing that an active movement had been carried on by numer- ous open air and indoor gatherings, which had been largely attended, the distribution of temperance litera- ture, Arc. although a good work had been done, for which the workers deserved thanks, he thought they might still have done better, and he urged all by re- newed earnestness andkictivity to push forward the good work in which they were engaged. (Applause.) The financial statement, showing a good hal-, ance in hand, was presented by Mr, George Clarke. The auditors (Messrs. John Judson and William Clare) reported that the accounts were correct, and the books had been well kept.' The report and balance sheet were unanimously adopted. Reports on the position of the associated societies were next presented after which thanks„wero tendered to the local press for their reports of the work of the Union during the year. The election' lof officers for the ensuing year resulted as follows President, Mr. J. H. Graham ; vice-president, Mr. John Taylor ; secretary, Mr. William Pearson ; treasurer, Mr. George Clarke ; assistant secretaries, Mr. 0. Pickett and Mr. E. Newman; auditors, Messrs. J. Judson and Joseph Morris. The committee was elected s lows :—Messrs. J. Judson (sons of Temperance), 0. Pio- kett (Wesleyan), J. Taylor (Primitive Methodist), J. Morris (Baptist), R. Jones (Congregational); F. Urea (Good Templars); and W, Jameson (Gospel Mission). Thanks were tendered to la.st year's officers for their ser- vices, and to the chairman for presiding. I.lmost any one of these various deposits Would constitute a very conSidemble and valuable mine. • At Wigan, on Thursday night, Mr. Baldwin, captain of the Wigan Association Football Club, was knocked down by a cab and killed. - New York newspapers have advices from Washington: that the Fishery Commission is hopelessly unable to ar- rive at an agreement. The unofficial register of the unemployed in London isk not making much progress. So far only some 6,000 per-i sons have asked for work. ' The Marquis and Marchioness of Salisbury and the Duke of Norfolk, who have been on a visit to the Queen at Windsor Castle, left on Friday morning for London. A heavy snowfall is reported from Alstone,,Cumber- land. The roads are blocked with snow, which is, level with the fences. It is feared that many sheep: have perished. A meeting of the Joint Committee of Fiscal Reform Socipties was held, on Friday, at the Westminster Palace Hotel. It ended in a squabble as to the expenditure of the £lOO,OOO now being raised. On Thursday night, thieves gained an entrance to the house of Mr. James Derham, of Sneyd Park, near Bris- tol, and stole jewellery valued at about £l,OOO. No arrests have been made, nor any clue to the robbers found. TRAGEDY AT SOUTHSEI.—At Southsea, On Thursday night, a man, whose name is unknown, sh It a woman named Moor, with whom he cohabited, and afterwards committed suicide by shooting himself. Jealously is assigned as the cause of the tragedy. The ironmasters of West Cumberland district held a meeting at Workington, on Friday, and decided that, in consequence of an advance in the price of iron, to with- draw the notice of reduction of 2/ per cent in wages of blast furnacemen. This decision will avert the threat- ened strike. ATTEMPT TO BLOW UP A BRITISH FORT. The Halifax (Nova Scotia) correspondent of the New York "Tribune" telegraphs that an attempt has just been made to blow up one of the large forts at that port. "hough the nefarious design failed of its full intention, considerable damage was done to buildings and stores. THE FRENCH CRISIS. PARIS, FRIDAY.—In consequence of M. Goblet's with- drawal, President Carnot has summoned M. Fallieres, who has requested to be allowed until this evening be- fore finally replying to the President's request that he should undertake the formation of a new Cabinet.

SWINE -FEVEIR.—On Thursday morning it was reported to the police authorities of Lymm that swine fever had broken out on the premises of Mr. Samuel Pennington, at Warburton. • WESLEYAN BAND OT HOPH.—Mr. B. Parr presided over a meeting of this Band of Hope, held on Wednesday evening, Mr. Wilkinson, of Heatley, and Mr. John Brere- ton ,of Sandy-lane, gave short addresses, and a musical programme was rendered. POLICE.—On Wednesday afternoon a lad 'named Ed- ward Brazendale was brought up before Mr. T. P. ,Norris, at Lymm Police Court, charged with stealing and dis- posing a to another lad a pack of cards, the pro- perty of Mr. T. Ardern, of Eagle-brow.—He. was re- manded on bail to the Petty Sessions, to beheld on .the 16th inst PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—On Sunday afternoon service of song, entitled "Gems from the hfe of John Ashworth," was given by the cfhoir of the abnve-named place of worship, under the leadership of ;Mr. T. Apple- ton. The solos were undertaken by Miss M. Clare and Mrs. T. Appleton. Mr.. G. L. Welford gave the connec- tive readings. At the close a collection was made in aid of the choir bind. • Awarasa Sunnsx Dicavit.—On Saturday morning Mrs. Clarke, wife of Mr. George Clarke, head gardener to Mr. Peter Stubs, of Statham Lodge, died very suddenly. Not feelihg very well, she went to consult Dr. ,Brabazon at his house. On her arrival she waited in the Surgery for the doctor, who had gone to see a patient in the village. After a- short interval Mrs. Brabazon thinking she heard someone come in, went into the surgery, and fcand Mrs. Clarke lying helpless on the floor. She called for assistance, and Dr. Brabazon areiving at that moment went into the surgery, only to find the unfor- tunate woman just expiring from what proved to be heart disease. Her remains were at once conveyed to her home in Statham. MUTUAL TIOROVEMENT Socrierr.—On Monday evening theweekly meeting of this society wzts held in the Wes- leyan schoolroom, Lymm, Mi.. Knowles presiding. Mr. Daniel Brown read an essay, entitled "A retrospective sketch of 'Lymm and neighbourhood." Not more than 60 years a.go, the essayist remarked, there was no lake such as they had now; Snuggling, fifty to seventy years ago, was largely carried on, and several houses near the canal, co Id, the malayist stated, no* be pointed out as dePts for the reception of smuggled goods, in these same houses being secret chambers. Mr. Dodds, proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the essayist :which Was seconded by Mr. Brown, senr., supported by Messrs. Welford and Knowles, and carried. SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A WIFE.—At the Altrincham Police Court, on Tuesday, Joseph Whitehead, a labourer in the employ of the Lymm Local Board, was brought up tinder warrant charged with unlawfully assaulting his wife, Emma Whitehead.—The complainant stated that she lived at Reddish-lane, Heatley. and had been married to the prisoner eight years. On Saturday last the prisoner came home at about five o'clock in the even- ing. He was drunk, and when he had had his tea he returned to the beerhouse. Later in the evening she' went for him, and when he came intci the road he struck her over the eye, anti then he struck her about the head and shotilders.-In cross-exa minationthe complainant denied that she threw a glass at her husband and cut his face.—Other evidence having been given, Mr. Mills said the magistrates were quite satisfied that the prisoner assaulted his wife. The prisoner would be sent to Knuts- ford for a month with hard labour, and at the expiration of that term he would be Wund over in his own recogs nizanees of £lO to keep the peace for six months. . „ .
